PREFACE The purpose of the first edition of Chancery Practice in New 

Jersey was to provide material for a course in equity pleading and practice in New Jersey Law School. A second edition is now offered with an additional purpose, viz., to make available to practitioners in the form of a ready-reference manual, the rapidly increasing number of cases which relate to the practice of the Court of Chancery of New Jersey. An attempt has been made to group accurately the reported decisions and to state faithfully the practice in so far, and only in so far, as it is thus reported. Nothing is offered ex cathedra. All matter in the text is to be taken strictly in connection with the authority cited in the footnotes. Doubtless errors have been made. The writer will be indebted to anyone who takes the trouble to bring such to his attention. 

It is proposed to supplement this volume at a later date with a book. of forms. With that in mind, references to many of the important forms have been included in appropriate places in the text. The 

New Jersey decisions are cited both in the official state reports and in the National Reporter System in order that all citations may be quickly available. The references in the footnotes to Story and 

Daniell refer, respectively, to the tenth and sixth editions. 

Certain proceedings in chancery such as foreclosure of mortgages, divorce actions, receiverships, lunacy inquisitions, and others, are beyond the compass of a handbook on chancery practice. Accordingly, these proceedings have been considered herein only in a general way. An effort has been made also to keep down the text matter in bulk by referring to, rather than by restating, the provisions of the Chancery Act and the Chancery Rules. The writer desires to express his appreciation to Sidney Kirschen, Esq., a member of the Newark 

Bar, for invaluable assistance in preparing the manuscript. 

NEWARK, N. J., January 3, 1933. 

LEWIS TYREE.

1. Chancery Practice in General. 

Ch. Zabriskie remarked in an early case that "proceedings in equity are conducted with less regard to mere matters of form and technical objections than proceedings at law." But this cannot be construed to mean that there are no rules governing the form of equity pleadings. Ch. Vroom: "The rules of pleading in a court of equity, are not so technical and precise as in courts of law. The general powers of this court, and its peculiar modes of administering relief, authorize and require a greater degree of liberality than would be expedient in the courts of common law. Still, when principles have by repeated adjudications become settled, and especially when they are founded in justice and the fitness of things, it is quite as important that those principles should be preserved in this as in other courts." 2

The necessity for and the function of rules in equity has been thus stated by J. Story: "It is obvious, that, in every system of jurisprudence, professing to provide for the due administration of public justice, some forms of proceeding must be established, to bring the matters in controversy between the parties, who are interested therein, before the tribunal, by which they are to be adjudicated. 

1. Evans v. Evans, 23 N. J. Eq. 71; see, Ransom v. Geer, 30 N. J. Eq. 249. 

2. Marselis v. Morris Canal, etc., Co., 1 N. J. Eq. 31.

And for the sake of the despatch of business, as well as for its due arrangement with reference to the rights and convenience of all the suitors, many regulations must be adopted, to induce certainty, order, accuracy, and uniformity in these proceedings. Hence it will be found, that the jurisprudence of every civilized country, ancient and modern, has established certain modes, in which the complaints and defences of parties are to be brought before the public tribunals; and has authorized the latter, by rules and orders, to prescribe the time, the manner, and the circumstances, in which every suit is to proceed, from its first institution to its final determination. "This is emphatically true in the jurisprudence of England and America; and is not only exemplified in the proceedings in suits at common law, but in those also which are governed by the larger and more liberal doctrines of equity. Indeed, in the latter, as well as in the former, there are many rules altogether founded in artificial reasoning, but which, nevertheless, may be affirmed, with few exceptions, to be greatly promotive of public justice, and subservient to private convenience. If, here and there, any of them work an apparent hardship or mischief, it will, on close examination, be found that they also accomplish much general and permanent good; and in this respect they partake only of the infirmity of all general rules, which must, in particular cases, give rise to some inequalities, and shut out some individual equities and rights.":

J. Story further distinguishes the much misused terms, pleading and practice: "By the pleadings we are to understand the written allegations of the respective parties in the suit, that is to say, the written statement of the plaintiff, containing, in a due legal form, the facts of the case on which he grounds his title to relief, or to some equitable interposition or aid from the court; and the written answer or defence of the defendant to the charges of the plaintiff, either denying them altogether, or admitting them, and relying on some other matters, as a bar to the suit, or admitting them, and insisting upon the want of title in the plaintiff to the relief sought, or to the interpositions or aid of the court; and the written reply thereto by the plaintiff. By the practice in a suit in equity we are to understand all the various proceedings in the suit, whether by the positive rules, or the usage of the court, and whether interlocutory or otherwise, 66 

3. Story, Eq. Pl., §§ 1, 2. V. C. Bentley : In the ordinary run of litiga tions, orderly procedure and the dispatch of business necessitate the imposition of general rules that are rigidly adhered to, except when the result of such adherence will work an injustice. 

Paper & Textile Mach. Co. v. 

Newlin, 101 N. J. Eq. 115, 137 Atl. 314.

3 which may become necessary or proper for the due conduct thereof from the beginning to the final determination thereof."4 

2. Comparison with Pleading at Common Law. 

Many differences existing between practice in the Chancery Courts and the highly developed common law pleading may be noted. The common law system served to reduce the parties to an ultimate single issue, and to create a purely bilateral or two-sided controversy always. Equity pleading aimed at neither end. Thus in equity pleading are not found those remote stages of pleading which carried the parties in a law action through a rejoinder—a surrejoinder, a rebutter, and a surrebutter stage. Equity pleading in this respect is simplicity itself. Thus except in rare cases are there more than three stages in the pleadings-the bill, answer, and replication. And the last stage is purely a formal joinder of issue, general in character, for special replications setting up new matter (and calling for additional answer by the defendant) were abolished very early in the history of equity pleading. 

With respect to that adverseness between two contending sides, again equity pleading is strikingly dissimilar to pleading at law. 

Judgments at law were restricted in character and necessarily either for or against. Whereas in equity, relief accorded by decree followed no fixed form but was malleable; the decree could be so adapted as to work out any intermediate result being neither for nor against. 

By reason of the same flexibility of procedure equity could deal with many conflicting claimants. It could also decree fully in any case and thus settle the entire controversy provided all parties were before the court. The adverseness of parties in equity therefore is unimportant; that a party is joined as defendant, when in fact a real party complainant, or vice versa, was not a misjoinder for equity could shape its decree to meet the facts.5 

Not only might a litigation in equity involve many more parties 

4. Story, Eq. Pl., § 4. 

5. Under the Chancery Rules it is provided that a proper party complainant, declining to join as plaintiff, may be joined as defendant, the reason therefor being stated in the bill. Chancery Rule 5. If not so stated, the omission may be cured by amendment. Kirkpatrick v. Kirkpatrick, 106 N. J. Eq. 391, 151 

Atl. 48.

The classification of parties in the drawing of the bill is not binding on the court with respect to their competency as witnesses under section 4 of the Evidence Act; their antagonism of interests and not adverseness on the pleadings is the test of their competency as witnesses as to transactions with a decedent. Kempton v. Bartine, 59 N. J. Eq. 149, 44 Atl. 461, 45 Atl. 966; 

Kirkpatrick v. Kirkpatrick, supra.

with varied, dissimilar and conflicting interests inter se, but a suit in equity could raise many issues all more or less collateral, but involved in the principal controversy. Equity delighted to do justice fully, and with that end in mind, would draw into a pending suit all necessary and proper parties in order to deal effectively and finally with the subject matter of the cause. In this respect, procedure at law designed, as previously stated to reduce the parties ultimately to a single issue, is in striking contrast.

Another difference in the procedure arises from the different composition of the two courts: In law there is a careful segregation of issues into issues of law, and issues of fact, for in this way only could a line of demarcation be drawn between the respective functions of judge and jury. In chancery, the Chancellor tries all questions of law and fact. But when sitting as a jury, the Chancellor has the right to discredit the testimony of a witness, and when there is reason. therefor, to disbelieve him altogether. It may be that under certain circumstances, trial by jury is allowable in chancery. Parties in equity may demand such as of right and the practice of the Chancellor submitting a question of fact to a jury, i.e., a feigned issue, has existed since early times."

In law the plaintiff had a choice of different forms of action and at common law the selection of the proper form of action was a matter of utmost importance. Whereas in equity jurisdiction is invoked in one manner chiefly-by bill of complaint which lends itself to a statement of any cause cognizable in equity. In law, the declaration and the writ must correspond, and if the writ fell, the declaration failed also; whereas in equity the bill is the foundation of the suit, and if the writ of subpoena is defective for any reason, the stability of the bill is unaffected. 

The relief that a law court could afford was fixed according to its various writs and limited in the enforcement to action by the sheriff, whereas relief in equity by the very terms of the decree is plastic, flexible and adaptable to any situation no matter how complex or peculiar in character. 

Other differences growing out of the difference in jurisdiction between courts of law and equity, and differences between their

Originally pleading in equity lacked formality and rigidity but in Lord Eldon's time, the rules of pleading enthralled the courts of chancery. 3. Equity Systems Generally. 

Equity in a restricted sense is defined as a branch of remedial justice administered by tribunals distinct from common law courts and empowered to decree equity in the sense of impartial justice.10 In some states as in New Jersey, the complete separation of law and equity is preserved as it was originally in the Chancery Court of England. In other states law and equity are administered in the same court and under the same procedure, as in New York. In still another group of states, the same judge sits as common law judge one day, and on the next he sits as chancellor; each court is a separate entity with distinct records, docket, etc., but with the same home and judge who presides at law. Such a system is found in Virginia.¹¹ This latter system is found also in the Federal Courts where the equity procedure is prescribed by a complete set of Federal Equity Rules, adopted in 1913. 

4. The Court of Chancery of New Jersey. 

The Court of Chancery is created by and under the Constitution of 1844.12 It is well established that the Legislature cannot impair the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, nor the powers of the court, as they existed at the time of the adoption of the Constitution.13 

By reason of this fact, there is much latitude in the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery.14 The Court of Chancery is the Chancellor of the State of New Jersey-a corporation sole.15 The Chancellor

In reality and in contemplation of law, they act as independent judges in chancery, have their own calendars, hear causes, write their own opinions and then advise the Chancellor to sign the decree they make, which necessarily he does as the only way to keep pace with the business of the court.

5. Statutory Proceedings in Chancery. 

Certain proceedings are begun and conducted before the Chancellor and vice chancellors under statutes and which are not heard as matters in the Court of Chancery proper, viz., an application to a vice chancellor for a writ of habeas corpus,35 an application to the Chancellor in capital cases for a writ of error, 36 etc.36a In these cases the Chancellor acts as a statutory magistrate or statutory agent; the vice chancellors also act not only as headmasters of the Court of Chancery, but also in special capacity as statutory agents.36b Nevertheless in such statutory proceedings, all writs, pleadings, orders, decrees, and other papers therein, shall be filed with the Clerk in Chancery and shall be records of his office; and such proceedings and decrees shall be enrolled the same as in causes pending in the Court of Chancery, and the clerk shall make certified copies of any or all of such statutory proceedings when requested, and such copies, so certified, shall have the same force and effect as certified copies of proceedings in causes in the Court of Chancery.37 

6. The Chancery Rules. 

Under the authority of the Chancery Act, a set of Chancery Rules was adopted in 1916 which changed much of the earlier practice, and superseded the previously existing rules of the Court of Chancery.38

9 43 law.39 The object of the rules is to simplify the practice, and this was done by adopting rules which brush aside much that formerly was technical and obstructive, and which broaden the procedure, so that rights may be promptly determined whenever the issue may be conveniently presented.40 Neither the Chancery Act, nor the Chancery Rules, however, dispense with precise pleading; simplified pleading does not permit shiftless pleading.41 Under the Chancery 

Rules not only a simplified but a complete system of procedure is intended; 42 but in so far as any matter of procedure is not therein provided for, or not otherwise changed, the rules of practice in the English High Court of Chancery as they anciently obtained continue to apply to practice in the Court of Chancery of New Jersey." In those pleadings where new names have been substituted for old, the new pleadings continue to be subject to many, if not most, of the old rules that governed the old pleadings.44 Fundamental questions of pleading are not disposed of by a mere change of name and an understanding of the old practice in chancery is necessary to understand and apply the present rules. But the rules, as adopted, are of course but a means to an end, for the rules expressly provide that they shall be considered as general rules for the government of the court and the conduct of causes, and as the design of them is to facilitate business and advance justice, they may be relaxed or dispensed with by the court in any case where it shall be manifest to the court that a strict adherence to them will work surprise or injustice.45 Under this rule vice chancellors, as judges in chancery, may relax the rules of practice but this power, however, exists only after jurisdiction by the vice chancellor has been acquired; they cannot dispense with the

7. Venue in Chancery. 

The Court of Chancery, like the Supreme Court and the Prerogative Court, is a court of statewide jurisdiction and is "in every county and municipality of the state.49 The Court of Chancery is regarded as being in continuous session, all terms of court, regular and special, having been abolished.50 By reason of the fact that no statute prescribes any rule of venue, any matter may be presented to the Chancellor, himself, regardless of venue.51 Preliminary applicacations, however, should, whenever practicable, be made to a vice chancellor of the vicinage.52 Reference of a cause for final hearing is, however, subject to no rule of venue; the Chancellor may accordingly refer a foreclosure of a mortgage on property situated in one county to a vice chancellor sitting in another county, and the inconvenience of the hearing is not a ground for re-reference.53 54 Matters heard by vice chancellors without an order of reference, however, are subject to a rule of venue. The rule is not one prescribed by statute but one prescribed by the Chancellor in the Chancery Rules for the regulation of matters brought forthwith before vice chancellors, and accordingly is not binding on the Chancellor.55 

The requirement appertains to those proceedings brought before a vice chancellor for (a) a writ of habeas corpus, (b) a writ ne exeat, (c) the appointment of a receiver of an insolvent corporation, etc.56

8. The Transfer of Causes. 

59 Under the early chancery practice, a cause of action improperly brought in equity being cognizable at law only (and vice versa), could not be transferred to a law court under inherent any of equity.5 power

In such a case, the complainant's bill would be dismissed for the want of jurisdiction and he would be put to a new suit at law.60 By statute, however, a cause erroneously instituted in the wrong forum may be transferred to the proper court without the expense and delay of a dismissal and re-institution of the suit. The practice under the New Jersey Transfer of Causes Act is to transfer the record of the cause and all papers filed therein, for hearing in the proper court, which shall proceed therein as if the cause had been originally brought in that court. Such a transfer in a proper case may be made at any stage of the proceedings. On a transfer to the Court of Chancery, the practice with respect to the form of the pleadings is to conform to the procedure in chancery by the filing of appropriate papers, viz., a bill of complaint, petition, etc., on which issue is joined.62 Parties defendant being already before the court need not, however, be served with the usual subpoena. The statute expressly empowers the Court of Chancery to make rules for transfers from the Court of Chancery.63 

Under the Chancery Rules no cause can be transferred to the Supreme Court, or other inferior court of law, without an order for that purpose.

When a cause is transferred from any of the law courts to the Court of Chancery, the Clerk of the Court of Chancery shall give a receipt in writing describing the papers so received; and 64

A cause may be transferred from equity to law only when and because the Court of Chancery is without jurisdiction, and the case is cognizable at law only; if jurisdiction is concurrent at law and in chancery, even though a special equity is involved, there may be no transfer from the law court.6 66 Nor in an action triable at law can the defendant by setting up an equitable defence oust the law court of jurisdiction; transference of a cause from law to chancery can be made under the Transfer Act only when the transferring court. is without jurisdiction to try the cause.67 

If, in spite of jurisdiction in the transferring court, a cause is erroneously transferred to the Court of Chancery, the bill in equity will be dismissed on that ground alone; a fortiori, if the bill on its face presents no case for equity, the remedy at law being adequate.68 

Nor in such a case can the Court of Chancery enter a decree in favor of the complainant (even though he be entitled to it at law), and direct the law court to enter a judgment accordingly; that is for the law court to determine in accordance with the verdict of the jury.69 

An order of the Court of Chancery transferring a cause to law is an appealable order, and if on appeal the Court of Chancery is found to have cognizance of the cause, it will be remanded to the Court of 

Chancery for adjudication.70

Order of Transfer of Chancery Cause to Supreme Court.] 9. Feigned Issue: Jury Trial In Equity. 

The Court of Chancery has the inherent power to refer a question of fact to a jury for a verdict thereon.75 Under the early practice, this was called a feigned issue, or an issue out of chancery.76 Originally the trial was conducted in equity or as the Chancellor might direct. It was the object of the issue to inform the conscience of the court where there was a doubt as to a question of fact.78 The office of the jury in equity is not definitely and finally to settle a question of fact, the verdict being merely persuasive; 79 the Chancellor is free to accept or ignore it, or order a new trial.80 This practice in New Jersey is regulated by statute under which the issue is sent to a court of law for trial according to the practice of that court.81

10. Jurisdiction: Defined. 

66 66 It is not the purpose herein to undertake to define the scope of equity jurisdiction. It is not amiss, however, to point out the different meanings in which the word "jurisdiction" is used, with reference to the particular procedural question that may be involved. 

I. Jurisdiction, as most often used, means “ jurisdiction of the subject matter." By this is meant "the right to speak "; " the power to hear and determine a cause ; or, as Beasley, C. J., states it: The right to adjudicate concerning the subject matter in a given case.” 11 

Without such power the judgment of the court is void and a nullity, i.e. coram non judice. Whether the Court of Chancery has jurisdiction in a given case is a matter of organic, i.e. constitutional law in New Jersey.12 Instances when the Court of Chancery is without jurisdiction of the subject matter are: trial of legal title to land,¹ a fraudulently procured will,14 etc.15 When the bill presents a cause without the jurisdiction of the court in this sense, the lack of jurisdiction of the subject matter may be raised by a motion to dismiss the bill. III. Jurisdiction may also be used to mean "the power to pronounce the particular judgment," or decree, in a particular cause. 

This is a matter of the form of the pleadings, for the Court of Chancery is without jurisdiction to enter a decree not conformable to the pleadings.20 The lack of power may be either to pronounce the particular decree which it undertakes to pronounce, or to pronounce any decree whatsoever, in the cause.27 Jurisdiction may be lacking in this same sense, when, although jurisdiction of the subject matter and parties exists, there is lacking power to pronounce a particular sentence because of established court procedure; as for example, the power to convict for one crime when the presentment and indictment was of another.28 If the Court of Chancery assumes to act in the absence of the power so to do, i.e. enters a decree not conformable with the pleadings or inconsistent with established modes of procedure,. the proper mode of objecting is by an appeal.29 The decree in such a case would seem to be open to collateral attack.30

11. The Function of the Bill. 

The purpose of the bill of complaint is to state in extenso the complainant's case in order that the defendant may answer, and that the issues be fixed. The complainant in the taking of proof will be limited to the allegations of the bill; or, as it is stated, the allegata and the probata must agree.¹ The bill will also limit relief accorded for the Court of Chancery may decree relief only on the case as set out in the bill.2 A bill defective in its essential allegations, how- "6 

1. J. Story: 'Every fact essential to the plaintiff's title to maintain the bill, and obtain the relief, must be stated in the bill, otherwise the defect will be fatal. For no facts are properly in issue, unless charged in the bill; and of course, no proofs can be generally offered of facts not in the bill; nor can relief be granted for matters not charged, although they may be apparent from other parts of the pleadings and evidence; for the court pronounces its decree secundum allegata et probata. The reason of this is, that the defendant may be apprised by the bill, what the suggestions and allegations are, against which he is to prepare his defense." Eq. Pl., § 257. 

2. Thus if a bill alleges fraud, and that is its whole theory, and the facts make out merely a case of an unauthorized misrepresentation by an agent, 21

ever, may be amended under the liberal equity practice in this respect, but a careful pleader should avoid the embarrassment, delay and expense occasioned by an amendment correcting faults in the original bill.3 

12. The Parts of the Bill: In General. 

An orderly presentation of a case in equity will require the bill to be divided into parts, each part serving a particular purpose. 

The inclusion of each part" in every bill is not, however, necessary, but is contingent upon the nature of the case presented and the relief desired. These "parts do not each fall into separate paragraphs as compositional units, and therefore, are not numbered under the practice which requires the paragraphs to be numbered. 

In modern practice, the use of some of the "parts" is obsolete; the use of other parts is purely formal, carrying over as a relic of the past. The parts of the bill are as follows: (1) the address, (2) the introduction, (3) the stating part, (4) the confederacy clause, (5) the charging part, (6) the jurisdiction clause, (7) the interrogatory part, (8) the prayer for relief, (9) the prayer for process, (10) signature of counsel.¹ 66

II. The Introductory Part. This part serves to set out the name of the complainant, or complainants, their places of residences, and the capacity in which they sue, if it is a special one. If the complainant is under a disability, the introduction should so state. When an infant sues by next friend, the address of the next friend should be given. An executor, administrator, or trustee, suing as such, should so describe himself. Good pleading requires that parties be designated by their full names-without initials-certainly by one Christian name to be followed by the surname. Married women should be described by their full Christian names and husband's surname without prefix, viz., "Mary Anne Jones;" and not "Mrs.

John Jones." The complainant refers to himself in the bill after naming himself as above, in the third person, e.g., "the complainant"; but in a petition, as "your petitioner." When jurisdiction depends on the residence of the complainant, the omission of the residence renders the bill defective.10 And in all cases, the correct residence is necessary for the proper service of notices, orders and process in connection with the suit. III. The Stating Part. In this part of the bill the complainant sets forth in extenso all the facts that go to make the complainant's right in equity. It is, therefore, the most important part of the bill. 

Here" should be set forth all the facts fundamentally material to the complainant's cause, actually essential to it as a portion of its very consistency, and none others." 12 These facts should be stated with fullness and particularity but not with prolixity.13 The requirement that the substance of the complainant's cause of action appear in the stating part of the bill is, like most rules of equity pleading, not inflexible.14 If it appears that the complainant has omitted facts that are material to the issue, the court may order such facts set forth in the pleadings, or if documents, that they be annexed to the bill.15 The pleader under the rules must strike a nice balance between stating the ultimate facts of the case with sufficient fullness and particularity and without suppression, at the same time not offending the rules against prolixity and repetition. Undue amplifications or enlargements of matter that has already been sufficiently stated in the pleading, increase costs and may be stricken on motion.10 The practice of repeating statements in other parts of the bill, or other pleadings, is expressly forbidden under the Chancery Rules; such matter may be referred to in lieu of repetition.17 One of the objects of the Chancery Rules is to shorten and simplify pleadings; 18 but if the pleader errs too far in the direction of brevity, adequate provision for the benefit of his adversary is afforded by other of the Chancery Rules.19 Upon violation of rules of pleading with respect to prolixity, repetition, etc., the court may on its own initiative order amendments of such defects upon terms or make such other order in the premises as may be just.20

V. The Charging Part. The importance of the charging part is largely historical. Originally it served two purposes: (1) to get discovery either by way of a pure bill of discovery, or discovery incidental to other relief; (2) to meet anticipated defenses. Its first purpose, i.c. discovery, in modern practice has been largely superseded by the more efficient mode of getting discovery through interrogatories. The second purpose was to meet expected defenses of the defendant. This was made necessary because of the fact that in the replication to the defendant's answer, the complainant from very early times, would be limited to a formal traverse or denial of the answer; if the complainant wished to reply thereto by setting up new matter by way of confession and avoidance, he could not reply specially (i.e. by special replication); he could do so only by amending his bill, and thereby incorporating the new matter; this latter practice was subject to (1) the discretion of the court in permitting the bill to be amended, and (2) extra expense and delay.22 To overcome, therefore, these difficulties, the complainant, in his original bill would anticipate the defendant's defenses by "charging that they would be, etc.," and then setting up the new matter by way of reply thereto, as for example, when the expected defense was infancy, to show a new promise in writing following the defendant's majority.23 Since special replications under the present practice (save as an answer to a counterclaim) can be filed only upon leave of court, it would seem to be still desirable practice to charge anticipated defenses in the bill, and set up at the same time in the bill the ultimate facts in reply thereto, thus raising the real ultimate issue in the bill itself.24 But

VI. The Jurisdiction Part. This clause was a formal averment of jurisdiction, e.g., whereas the complainant has no adequate relief at law and is without adequate remedy save in a court of equity, etc. 

It was, of course, the pleader's legal conclusion from the facts stated and could not confer jurisdiction; that must result from the facts of the case.20 The present practice is to include the jurisdiction clause, not as a necessary but as a merely formal averment.27 

VII. The Interrogatory Part. This part, sometimes called the interrogating clause, or prayer for answer, called upon the defendant to answer all matters alleged in the bill. Under the early practice, the prayer was invariably for answer under oath for it was here that a court of equity could exercise one of its most valuable powersnamely to search the defendant's conscience under oath. To crossexamine the defendant further in detail and to prevent evasion by the defendant, the complainant could propound to the defendant specific interrogatories which the defendant was required to answer under oath.28 The peculiar value of this function of the bill will be more fully appreciated, if it be recalled that this practice existed at a time when all parties to a cause, merely as such, were incompetent as witnesses. Although the incompetency of parties as witnesses has been removed under the Evidence Act and generally, and in spite of the further fact that it is the usual practice to waive answer under oath, it is still permissible practice to incorporate in the interrogatory clause (e.g. the prayer for answer) specific interrogatories calling for answers under oath.29 Nor has the extension to law courts of the practice of interrogatories, in any way lessened the ancient jurisdiction in equity with respect thereto. But the use of interrogatories in the present-day bill of complaint is of considerably lessened importance and frequency than formerly, and the "interrogatory part" ordinarily consists merely of a general demand for answer. 

Its importance consists largely of the fact that it is here that the defendants are named and presented to the court; a function formerly served by the prayer for answer.30

VIII. The Prayer for Relief. The prayer for relief of the bill may be either for general relief, or special relief, or both.31 A prayer for general relief is a prayer for any relief that to the court may seem "fit and proper." A prayer for special relief, sets out in terms the specific equitable relief or remedy that the complainant desires and to which he deems himself entitled, viz., a preliminary injunction, specific performance, a writ ne exeat, etc. If the complainant is mistaken as to the proper relief, but is still under the facts of his case, entitled to some equitable relief, that relief ordinarily will be accorded under the prayer for general relief. For this reason, the complainant should pray for special relief in the alternative. 

Formerly,32 it was indispensable to add to the prayer for special relief, a prayer for general relief; otherwise, only the special relief prayed for could be granted, the pleader being limited to the special relief requested. Under the present practice, however, any relief appropriate in the case may be granted although it was not the specific relief requested, and this without the inclusion of a prayer for other and general relief.33 Under the present practice a prayer for “such further and other relief," or for general relief in the premises, as it is usually designated, is not to be regarded as improper; its inclusion is merely unnecessary. 

It often happens that a pleader is uncertain in his own mind as to the true nature of his rights and the proper relief to which he is entitled. In this quandary, under the rules of equity pleading, he may have two theories in his bill, i.e., he may state his case under both theories, but disjunctively, and pray for relief in the alternative, according to which conception of his rights the court finds to be the true one. Such a bill is called a "bill of double aspect.' " 34 Under the Chancery Rules inconsistent causes of action are expressly

Even before the adoption of the present Chancery Rules, the rule of common law pleading that pleadings must not be in the alternative" was not insisted upon in equity pleading.

Present divorce practice permits the alleging of separate grounds in a single petition. Hart v. Hart, 99 N. J. Eq. 373, 131 Atl. 903; cf., Snover v. Snover, 10 N. J. Eq. 261.

allowed provided they are stated in the alternative.35 The court is not limited to a choice of either of these two conceptions, but may take a third view of the complainant's case, and grant relief accordingly. But this rule does not permit in all cases full cumulative relief, viz., on one bill, reformation of a contract may not be had, followed by a further decree for specific performance thereof.36 It should be noted that this practice of pleading a single cause of action doubly, is not a joinder of different causes of action which is allowed. under the Chancery Rules.37

The relief that the complainant desires, and the only relief that may be granted, even though not specifically prayed for, is relief that is agreeable to the case as made out in the bill.38 The relief granted must be consistent with the complainant's theory of his bill to prevent surprise or harm to the opposing party.39 It is this rule that renders it desirable for a complainant who is doubtful of the true nature of his case, to present it to the court in the form of a bill of double aspect, which will not necessitate a departure from his original theory, and will not operate to surprise or prejudice the defendant.40

15. Oath to the Bill.

The general rule is that a bill or petition in chancery is not required to be sworn to.5 57 But in many suits, by reason either of statute or because of the character of the relief sought, the bill must be sworn to, i.e., verified by an affidavit of the complainant, or by someone else having the requisite knowledge.58 In some of these instances the affidavit is of a special fact pertinent in the case, viz., as an affidavit of non-collusion in divorce actions, etc.; whereas, in other cases, the bill is verified in common form, meaning thereby that the bill in its entirety is sworn to as true.5 Pending a full discussion of these special cases where an affidavit to the bill or petition is required, it will suffice at this point to enumerate the usual instances of a sworn bill: (1) Bill of interpleader (affidavit of non-collusion),60 (2) bill or petition seeking ex parte relief under Chancery Rule 130, viz., for a writ ne exeat, writ of habeas corpus, a preliminary injunction,61 

etc., (3) Bill seeking discovery,62 (4) Bill of review,63 (5) Bill or

16. Form of Affidavits.

If, however, the affidavit sets forth (a) the sources of the information and (b) the grounds of the belief, and (c) are accompanied by the affidavit of some person having actual knowledge of the facts, they are allowed as sufficient.72 Affidavits are subject to the usual rules of evidence which exclude hearsay evidence, conclusions, and argumentative statements.73 It is irregular for the solicitor of record of the complainant (or petitioner) to take the complainant's affidavit; but this rule is one of judicial

18. The Bill Distinguished from the Petition. 

The bill of complaint is really a petition but by another name.83 

In equity pleading generally, a bill is to be distinguished from a petition, mainly in the formality of averment that is required in a bill; a petition is informal both in its averments and prayers for relief. 

The petition is largely employed in the matrimonial suits, both actions for divorce and both actions for nullity being instituted by petition, the bill being used only for separate maintenance under Section 26 of the Divorce Act.84 In matrimonial causes, parties defendant are served by citation and not by subpoena, which is the process employed when the suit is by bill.85 Another difference to be noted is that whereas, on bill and subpoena, the time fixed for answering is twenty days from the date of the service, in cases of petition and citation, the time fixed for answering is twenty days from the return day in the citation.86 In suits by petition other than in matrimonial causes, the process is usually a rule to show cause served on the defendant and requiring answer in less than the twenty days allowed on bill and subpoena.87 A further difference between the bill and petition is to be found in the fact that only a counsellor can sign a bill, whereas an

20. Classification of Bills. 

Bills in equity are variously classified and described. The following classification represents the usual distinctions: 

(A) Original Bills. 

(B) Bills not Original. 

(C) Bills in the Nature of Original Bill. 

(A) Original Bills which originate the cause in equity are in turn further classified: 

(I) Bills seeking Relief. 

(II) Bills not Seeking Relief.

21. Pleading Legal Conclusions; Fraud, etc. 

The bill must state facts and not conclusions of law.19 The most usual error is for the pleader to aver fraud generally and not allege the facts constituting fraud.20 Fraud must never be pleaded eo nomine. Fraud is never presumed;21 and if fraud is to be spelled from the facts," the pleader must do the spelling." 22 The rule that fraud must be pleaded with full particularity, alleging fully items and dates, is applied also to allegations of (a) misrepresentation, (b) breach of trust, (c) wilful default, or, (d) undue influence.23 The fullness of allegation is necessary to give the defendant full opportunity to deny, explain or disprove them.24 Allegations of conspiracy must also be made with full particularity.25 Other allegations that offend the rule prohibiting the pleading of legal conclusions are: alleging "an encumbrance" on title;20 alleging an act to be "without power" (i.e., unauthorizedly);27 alleging usury; that the statute of limitations barred the cause of action; alleging acts done "by com-

Answer (in Lieu of Plea) Setting up Fraud.] 22. Pleading Documents. 

No bill, or other pleading, should recite records, deeds or documents in full, but only so much and such parts thereof as may be necessary for the clear exhibition of the case, or the construction of the document, omitting all parts not relevant to the relief sought, or the defense set up; and no pleading shall repeat documents or parts of documents set forth in any previous pleading, but if the same are not fully or accurately set forth, may add such parts as may be necessary to complete or correct the same.32 In pleading any document, a copy thereof may be annexed to the bill, or other pleading and referred to therein with like effect as if it were recited at length.33 Such copies which are annexed as "Exhibits," or "Schedules," etc., constitute a part of the record and are considered in determining the legal sufficiency of the bill on a motion to strike the bill.34 Many formal defects and omissions from the bill itself

This is an innovation on the earlier practice to which a bill of particulars was unknown, for only from a comparatively recent date has a bill of particulars been allowable in equity practice.45 Whether a bill of particulars will be allowed, is within the discretion of the Court of Chancery.46 The rules applicable to a bill of particulars at law, from which court equity obtained the practice, in general would seem to apply in equity since the procedure in equity is assimilated to that at law.47 It should be noted under the chancery practice, either party may demand a bill of particulars with respect to the matter of any pleading. 

It would seem that generally and subject to the discretion of the court, application by the defendant for a bill of particulars should be made before the defendant files his answer; or if the application is by the complainant, before he files his replication.48 The purpose of a bill of particulars is of course to enable a party to meet properly a pleading, and is to be distinguished from interrogatories which are designed to enable a party to prepare for the hearing and are propounded, under the Chancery Rules after issue has been joined.¹

defects in pleading. In case the bill seeks discovery the complainant may set out collateral facts, justifying the discovery desired, which would be impertinent if the bill required answer without oath.51 

The case should be particularly clear to warrant expunging matter from pleadings as impertinent, because if error is done in expunging, the error is irremediable; if left in, the court may still at the hearing set the matter right in point of costs.52 The best test for impertinence is, in the language of Chancellor Kent, "whether the subject of the allegation could be put in issue and would be matter proper to be given in evidence between the parties." 53

When matter in an answer is objected to as impertinent, it must be shown, to sustain the objection, that the matter criticised is so unrelated to the complainant's claim as to be unworthy of any consideration as a defense.54 But if the complainant calls for an answer to impertinent matter he must take the answer, though it be impertinent, and cannot object thereto.55 But matter in an answer not called for, which serves no useful purpose and encumbers the record, is impertinence.56 Where there are substantial doubts, especially in the case of the bill, they should be resolved in favor of pertinency, and nothing should be expunged from the answer, which if proved, might influence the judgment of the court, as to whether the complainant is entitled to relief-even down to the question of whether he shall have relief with or without costs.57 

Scandal is alleged matter offending the senses, "unbecoming the dignity of the court to hear." 58 But if material to the primary issue of the suit, it is not to be regarded as scandal, although if standing alone, it would be prima facie scandalous and offensive to the decorum of the court. And even if material, yet if the matter is stated in an unnecessarily offensive manner, it will be scandal.59 

Allegations of conduct offensive to good manners or morals, or

Under the earlier practice, objection to an answer on the ground of impertinence or scandal, was made by exception; to a bill or crossbill, by demurrer.62 Under the present chancery rules objection in all cases is made by a motion to strike out the part, not the whole of the pleading, objected to as impertinent or scandalous.63 

Even though no motion is made by a party, the court may sua sponte strike out the objectionable part.64 It was to prevent scandal and impertinence in the bill, that the practice originated of having counsel sign pleadings as a certification thereof.65 The action of the Chancellor in striking out impertinent matter is appealable, but will be reversed only in a clear case, manifestly injurious to the substantial rights of the party complaining.66

27. Allegations on Information and Belief. 

Averments of fact in a bill may be on information and belief. An allegation (a) that the complainant has been informed, and (b) that he believes, etc., and (c) therefore charges as true certain facts, is held to be a sufficient averment, as a rule.82 But an allegation of adultery in divorce actions merely on information and belief is not held to be a sufficient averment under the rule that in allegations of adultery in divorce actions, the charge must be made specifically and with particularity.83 It should be noted that a mere allegation that the complainant has been informed that, etc., without an allegation that the complainant believes the facts alleged, or without a charge of their truth, is inefficacious.84 Such allegations to be well-pleaded should give further, the source of the information and the grounds of the belief; or should be supported by affidavits of some person having actual knowledge of the facts.85 Whether a bill consisting entirely of allegations founded on information and belief, unaccompanied by any allegations of fact, would stand on a motion to strike in lieu of demurrer was a question raised by Ch. Magie, but not answered. Allegations on information and belief are not taken as confessed on a motion to strike in lieu of demurrer.87 Adverse parties to pleadings under the Chancery Rules are deemed to admit all material allegations of fact in a pleading, unless they either deny

28. Right of Voluntary Dismissal. 

A complainant may, after bringing his suit to a hearing, or at any time in the proceeding, prior to the entry of final decree, upon notice to the defendant, move to dismiss his suit upon the payment of all costs to the defendant.9 It does not lie in the mouth of the defendant to object thereto, for the dismissal of the original bill carries with it, the dismissal of the defendant's answer on which he is entitled to no affirmative relief whatsoever.91 Even if the complainant in his original bill has made admissions advantageous to the defendant, the complainant may still withdraw his own bill upon the payment of costs; in such a case, the complainant's right to dismiss will be on terms, viz., that the dismissal shall be without prejudice to the defendant's right to the benefit of the admissions contained in the bill in any subsequent proceedings that the defendant might take with respect to the subject matter of the bill.92 On a voluntary dismissal by the complainant, it is not within the power of the Court of Chancery to award counsel fees.93

29. Dismissal by the Court. 

.11 8 .12

The Court of Chancery under an inherent power may of its own motion-ex mero motu, dismiss a bill of complaint although the defendant makes no objection to proceeding with the suit. This power in a proper case may be exercised by the court at any stage of the suit-yet it may within its discretion retain the cause after a hearing has been had on the merits, the defendant having submitted to jurisdiction, although ample grounds exist for its dismissal. Among the grounds that may warrant dismissal by the court are: the prematurely filing in equity of a bill of complaint;10 that the complainant's case is without equity;¹¹ the existence of an adequate remedy at law; that the complainant does not come into equity with clean hands;13 failure to prosecute a cause with reasonable diligence ;14 inequitable conduct, viz., where a non-resident filed a bill but refused to submit to cross-examination as a witness;15 formal defects of the bill such as objectionable multifariousness, etc.16 The order of the court may, however, be in terms without prejudice to the right of the complainant to file a new bill.17 Dismissal by the court is also provided for under the Chancery Rules in the following cases: when the complainant fails to appear at the time and place designated for a hearing (upon advice to this effect) by the Chancellor;18 for failure to file a replication within the time allowed;19 for failure to revive a suit

30. Effect of Dismissal: Res Adjudicata. 

24 It is usual to include in a decree of dismissal as ordinary practice a provision that the dismissal is without prejudice to the filing of a new bill.22 This is especially true when the bill is dismissed for formal defects such as dismissal on demurrer for failure to amend properly a sworn bill.23 If the order of dismissal omits a stipulation that the dismissal is without prejudice, then the complainant may file a new bill based on the same facts as those set forth in the original bill, provided that the first bill was dismissed on a ground which did not go to the merits of the case. If after a hearing on the merits, a suit in equity is dismissed for failure of proof, such dismissal is taken ordinarily to be an effectual bar to the bringing of a new suit on the same cause of action, the cause being res adjudicata so long as the order of dismissal stands unreversed.2 

25 Nor can the rule be nullified by changing in the bill the character of the relief sought, as, for example, seeking a decree for separate maintenance under Section 26 of the Divorce Act alleging the same facts formerly set up in a petition for a divorce a mensa et thoro, the original petition having been dismissed for failure of proof.26 If a cause is heard, however, on its merits either in bill or counterclaim, and dismissed as unsubstantiated, the cause is res adjudicata with respect to further proceedings either in equity or at law.27 The test of whether the

4b: Order Dismissing Suit in Equity Without Prejudice.] 31. Joinder of Causes: Multifariousness. 

By reason of that "extreme flexibility" of equity procedure which permits in one cause, several issues involving any number of parties, as well as other fundamental principles of equity jurisprudence, notably, that one designed to prevent a multiplicity of suits, it is not surprising that different causes of action may be joined in one bill of complaint, even to a greater extent than at law. When a bill or a counterclaim joins improperly two or more causes of action, the bill is described as multifarious.30 The defect, i.e., multifariousness, is one of form and not of substance. Although formerly the rules relating to multifariousness were quite strict, the tendency in modern the hearing and filing of conclusions by the Vice Chancellor but before entry of final decree. Friedlander v. Lehr, 98 N. J. Eq. 359, 129 Atl. 241. Further litigation when res adjudicata may constitute contempt. Mendel v. Berwyn 

Estates, 109 N. J. Eq. 11, 156 Atl. 324. 

28. Hoffmeier & Son v. Trost, 83 N. J. L. 358, 85 Atl. 221. See, further,

Chapter VI, The Answer in Lieu of Plea, infra. 

29. Weinstein v. Blanchard, 9 N. J. Misc. R. 113, 152 Atl. 787 (and cases cited); Savage v. Edgar, 85 N. J. Eq. 420, 97 Atl. 164. 

30. J. Story: "By multifariousness in a bill is meant the improperly joining in one bill distinct and independent matters, and thereby confounding them; as, for example, the uniting, in one bill of several matters, perfectly distinct and unconnected, against one defendant, or the demand of several matters of a distinct and independent nature against several defendants in the same bill. In the latter case, the proceeding would be oppressive, because it would tend to load each defendant with an unnecessary burden of costs, by swelling the pleadings with the statement of the several claims of the other defendants with which he has no connection. In the former case, the defendant would be compellable to unite, in his answer and defense, different matters wholly unconnected with each other; and thus the proofs, applicable to each, would be apt to be confounded with each other, and great delays would be occasioned by waiting for the proofs respecting one of the matters, when the others might be fully ripe for hearing. Indeed, courts of equity, in cases of this sort, are anxious to preserve some analogy to the comparative simplicity of proceedings at the common law, and thus to prevent confusion in their own pleadings, as well as in their own decrees." Eq. Pl., § 271.

equity procedure is to encourage and favor the joinder of separate causes of action in a single bill.31

Multifariousness may be encountered in three forms of increasing seriousness: (1) The joinder in one bill of several causes of action independent of each other but by the same plaintiff and against the same defendant. (2) The joinder in one bill of several causes of action independent of each other by several complainants against one defendant. (3) The joinder of independent causes of action by several complainants against several defendants all of whom are pot jointly or equally interested in all the matters to be litigated. It will be perceived that the last case stated presents the greatest difficulty, whereas the first case involves the least objectionable joinder.32 

Under the early practice the first joinder stated above, would or would not be permitted within the discretion of the court according to whether the two causes could be conveniently heard together.33 

Where the different causes arise out of the same transaction, the joinder thereof in one bill, by the same complainant against a single defendant would not only be permissible—it would be proper.34 And under the early practice, the rule against multifariousness was applied not as an inflexible rule of pleading, but only when the causes joined. could not be conveniently heard together.35

The Chancery Act adopted in 1915 was intended to liberalize the practice of joining different causes of action in a single bill. Under the provisions of this act, along with supplementary rules adopted by

J. Depue: "The rule with regard to multifariousness, whether arising from the misjoinder of causes of action or of defendants therein, is not an inflexible rule of practice or procedure, but is a rule founded in general convenience, which rests upon a consideration of what will best promote the administration of justice without multiplying unnecessary litigation on the one hand, or drawing suitors into needless and unnecessary expenses on the other. . . . In allowing or disallowing objections of this kind, the courts are guided by the consideration whether there is a subject-matter in dispute, in which all the defendants are interested, which is capable of being determined in a single issue, and the determination of which, in that method, would not involve the defendants severally in the needless expenses of the litigation of matters in which they have no concern." the Court of Chancery, the old-time objection of multifariousness has been substantially done away with.36 The provisions of the act, having as an object the simplification of chancery procedure by uniting in one bill all manner of complaint, is liberally construed to effectuate its purpose.37

A distinction, however, must be taken between the joinder of different causes of action in a single bill against the same defendant, and a joinder against different defendants. It is in the first case, that the practice is most liberal; the requirement in this case is one merely of convenience; the causes joined may be unrelated and arising out of separate transactions, having no common question of law or fact.38 Thus a foreclosure of four separate mortgages by one complainant who held all the mortgages against the same defendant was permitted in a single bill.39 The joinder of different causes against the same defendant is, however, subject to special limitations and exceptions set out in the Chancery Rules, in addition to the general limitation of convenience. Thus, claims by a trustee in bankruptcy as such, must not be joined with any claim by him in another capacity;40 claims by or against any executor or administrator, as such, must not be joined with claims by him or against him personally-Unless the latter claims arose with reference to the estate of his testator or intestate;41 in a suit for divorce or annulment of marriage no non-matrimonial cause of action shall be joined.4 42 When different causes of actions are joined in one bill against different defendants, however, the practice of joinder is permitted only when the causes joined “have a common question of law or fact, and arose out of the same transaction or series of transactions." 43

32. Consolidation of Causes. 

64 The Court of Chancery possesses the inherent power to consolidate causes that may be conveniently heard together independent of any statutory authority. An order for consolidation may be entered with or without the consent of the complainant, or complainants.65 

Consolidation is not a matter of right but within the discretion 66 of the court. The effect of consolidation is not a fusion of the suits consolidated, but rather a hearing together, the records on the several causes not being actually united.67 Causes with different complainants may be consolidated when to do so would save costs and delay.68 

The order of consolidation is obtained on motion of counsel, or on suggestion of counsel in open court, or entered by the court sua sponte.69 Typical causes in which consolidation may be ordered are: foreclosures on different parcels by one complainant against one defendant;70 foreclosures on different parcels with different parties in interest; 71 bills by different creditors for a receiver of an insolvent

33. Function.

The amended bill has many uses-but the chief one is to cure omissions and correct defects of the original bill. Thus, when the complaint imperfectly pleaded a foreign statute, the complainant was granted leave, on request during the trial, to amend the bill by properly pleading such statute, so as to render the statute admissible in evidence.¹ In a suit so set aside a fraudulent conveyance, if the bill omits, a necessary allegation, viz., that the creditor was thereby hindered, delayed, etc."; or, if, in a suit to quiet title, the bill omits an allegation of peaceable possession,3 or, in a suit to sequester assets of a non-resident, the bill fails to state the complainant's residence, the defects may be cured by apt amendments even at the hearing if these facts be established by proof. Additional prayers and new parties can also be added, if otherwise proper, by amending the bill.5 Amendment is also proper to correct a mistake in pro- 2

34. Power of the Court of Chancery to Amend.

The power of the Court of Chancery to permit an amendment is an inherent power.

It has been evolved as a matter of practice and is not regulated by statute, except a provision that amendments may be on terms. This statutory provision, however, is merely declaratory of the inherent power of equity.10 "On terms" simply means that all amendments shall be made with or without costs, and on such equitable terms as the court shall direct. Under the Chancery Rules it is the practice that in all cases not otherwise provided, in which the defendant shall have answered the complainant's bill and the complainant shall obtain leave to amend, if such amendment require a new or further answer, then the complainant shall pay costs to be taxed.11 

35. Making a New Case. 

A fundamental rule of equity pleading reaffirmed in numerous cases is that the complainant cannot by an amended bill make out a new case different from that made by the original bill.12 This means thereby obtains further knowledge of facts or circumstances which may aid him in the cause, he may amend his bill and proceed according to the information thus obtained; and in general, any imperfection in the frame of a bill may be remedied as occasion shall require, provided the application for that purpose be made in proper time: Coop., Eq. Pl., 333. Before replication, the order to amend is granted, of course." Buckley v. Corse, 1 N. J. Eq. 504.

Van Fleet: "Courts of equity have always exercised a very liberal discretion in allowing pleadings to be amended. In deciding whether leave shall be granted to amend a bill or not, they disregard mere matters of form and simply consider whether the amendment is necessary or not to reach the real and substantial merits of the case. The duty of the court in such cases is to see to it that the pleadings are put in such form that the real matter in controversy may be fairly tried and justly decided. Cooper, in his treatise on 

Equity Pleading, states the rule regulating the amendment of bills as follows: 'If the plaintiff, after he has filed his bill, finds that he has omitted to state any matter which he ought to have stated, he may supply such defect by amending his bill. Or, if after the defendant has put in his answer the plaintiff thereby obtains new lights as to the circumstances of his case, he may amend his bill, in order to shape his case accordingly. And, in general, any imperfection in the frame of a bill may be remedied as often as occasion shall require.' Coop., Eq. Pl., § 332. Judge Story states the rule in the same words. Story, Eq. 38. Time for Amending: Amending to Meet the Evidence. 

66 As a matter of rule, an amended bill may be allowed at almost any time in order that the real controversy may be fairly tried and justly decided.31 Ch. Green: The question presented is whether the amendments proposed are proper to be made at this stage of the proceedings. Before the pleadings are brought to a termination, that is before the issue is finally made up between the parties, amendments, where the pleadings on file have not been sworn to, are permitted with the utmost liberality, as the purposes of the party may require. The complainant may vary his case by amendment in any way he pleases, however inconsistent with or repugnant to the original bill. A bill to set aside a deed has been permitted by amendment to be made a bill to establish the deed. A bill to invalidate the encumbrance of a mortgage has been converted into a bill to redeem the mortgage. "At this stage of the proceedings . . . it is difficult to draw a line beyond which the complainant may not pass in changing his case. And it seems absolutely essential to the ends of justice that this extreme degree of indulgence should be allowed, for from the character of the proceedings, the merits of the complainant's case are not unfrequently disclosed by the answer. And even after issue joined, and before the taking of testimony, the complainant will be permitted to withdraw his replication and amend his bill, as his case may require. But after witnesses have been examined, the time for allowing amendments, except the addition of defendants or such as do not substantially alter the case, has gone by. 

28. Boehme v. Rall, 51 N. J. Eq. 541, 26 Atl. 832. 

29. Schuler v. So. Iron & Steel Co., 77 N. J. Eq. 113, 76 Atl. 239 (discussed by V. C. Garrison but not passed upon). 

30. Schaffer v. Krestovnikow, 89 N. J. Eq. 549, 105 Atl. 239. 

31. Fearey v. Hayes, 44 N. J. Eq. 425, 15 Atl. 592.

"From this time, if there be an imperfection in the frame of the bill, if the case as stated is insufficient to warrant the relief sought for or to ground a complete decree, if some other point appears necessary to be made, or some additional discovery is found requisite, the complainant must resort to a supplemental bill. The time for amendment has passed. This is not a mere arbitrary rule, but rests upon clear and familiar principle, and is a valuable safeguard of the rights of parties. The evidence must be confined to the issue. The allegations and proofs must correspond. To prove a charge not made by the bill, and to make a charge not sustained by proof, are alike inoperative to sustain a decree. In one case there is no evidence; in the other it is rejected as impertinent. The complainant fails alike in both cases for want of proof. 66 As already stated, it is a recognized exception to the general rule, that if a bill is defective for want of parties, the complainant will be permitted to amend by adding the proper parties. So when a matter has not been put in issue by the bill with sufficient precision, the court, upon the hearing, has given leave to amend. So the complainant will be permitted, upon the hearing, to amend his prayer for relief, or any clerical mistake or mis-statement. But neither of these amendments vary the issue between the parties, nor as a general rule do they at all affect the relevancy of the evidence offered. 

But except in the case of infants, who are permitted to amend without restriction, the general principle is clear, that amendments are not permitted which will vary the issue between the parties, or substantially vary the charges of the bill. Even after general demurrer for want of equity, amendments are granted only where there is some defect as to parties, or some omission or mistake of a fact or circumstance connected with the substance of the case, but not forming the substance itself. There is a class of cases in which, by recent practice, more liberality of amendment has been allowed. Thus, where upon the final hearing, or even after appeal, it appears clearly from the evidence, that the complainant has a case which entitles him to relief, but which, by reason of some defect or omission in the charges or allegations of the bill, is not brought fairly within the issue, he will be permitted to adapt the allegations of the bill to the case as proven. It is within this class of cases that the complainant seeks to bring the present application. I find no case of such order being made before the testimony is closed. There is a very decided objection to permitting a complainant to vary his allegation and mould

the issue according to the real or supposed exigency of the case, while the testimony is being taken." 32

The power of amending at the final hearing to meet proofs different than as contemplated in the original bill is exercisable only when the ends of justice render it absolutely necessary, and its exercise will not substantially impair or abridge the right of the defense.33 C. J. 

Beasley doubted this power to amend at or after a final hearing in a case where the amendment would materially falsify the facts originally pleaded; 34 or in the language of V. C. Reed, the amendment must not set out facts "inconsistent with," but "only cumulative " of, the facts originally pleaded.35 If the proposed amendment makes a new case, or states new and additional claims to relief, amendment will not be permitted; the complainant must proceed by original bill, or a petition for a rehearing.36 It would seem therefore, that in no case, may the bill be amended after a final decree has been entered and enrolled.37 After a final hearing and the vice chancellor has filed his conclusions, but before the entry of the decree advised, it is also too late to amend in the absence of any special equity.38

40. Amending of Right: Leave of Court. 

Before subpoena issues, the complainant may amend his bill of course and without motion or rule, and without costs. After subpoena issues the complainant may, without notice, unless upon application for the order notice is directed to be given, obtain an order to amend his bill at any time before answer is filed or notice of objection is served, and upon such terms as may be imposed by the order.44 

If the defendant puts in an answer, which is objected to as insufficient, and the defendant submits to answer further, or the answer shall be adjudged insufficient, the complainant may, in either case, amend his bill of course, and without costs, and the defendant shall answer the amended bill; and if the defendant shall answer in lieu of plea, or shall move to strike out the bill, and such answer or motion shall be overruled, the complainant may, before the filing of an answer amend his bill of course, and without costs.45

41. Effect of Amending. 

When the original bill is amended, the allegations of the original bill do not bind the complainant as admissions; the allegations of the record, or amended bill do so bind him.51 Injunction bills may be amended without prejudice to the injunction.52 The right to relief on an amended bill is determined in the light of conditions existing at the time the amended bill was filed and not as of the time of the filing of the original bill.53 But in an action for divorce on the ground of desertion, the two-year period is computed from the time of the filing the original and not the amended petition.54

43. The Supplemental Bill. 

57 A strictly supplemental bill is always founded on facts that have occurred since the filing of an original bill.58 These additional facts may be necessary to aid the complainant in obtaining the relief originally sought, or in obtaining new and additional relief. Since the costs of a supplemental bill are less than an original bill, the former should be used whenever it can equally subserve the purposes of justice. Thus a bill by a mortgagee to restrain waste by the mortgagor may be filed before the mortgage is due; after the mortgage becomes due, the original bill being pending, the mortgagee can now file a supplemental bill praying for additional relief, viz., foreclosure.59 

But facts having occurred and being well within complainant's knowledge before the filing of the original bill, are not strictly matters upon which a supplemental bill, or bill in the nature thereof, can be based. 

As a basis for relief, they could be introduced regularly only by an application to amend the bill after notice. Such facts, if made the subject of a supplemental bill, would render it subject to a motion to strike in lieu of demurrer in so far as the relief sought by the supplemental bill, is based thereon. The defect would, of course, be purely formal in character.60 Nor in divorce actions can additional that parties once having personally appeared in a suit are before the court and are subject without further notice to all subsequent proceedings in the cause.

Although the distinction between an amended and a supplemental bill is not always observed, 62 yet this difference, strictly speaking, distinguishes them :-An additional or intervening right accruing to a complainant subsequent to the institution of the original suit should be set up by way of supplemental bill; whereas, an amended bill is to correct errors on the face of the bill, or to set up matters existing at the time of the filing of the original bill.63 The supplemental bill may vary the relief as circumstances may demand.64 Like the amended bill, the supplemental bill may bring in new parties.65

45. Service in General: Kinds. 

Service, or process, is the means of compelling a defendant to appear in court. It need not necessarily be a subpeona or other 72

writ. It may be an order, or notice, or rule to show cause.¹ Every state has power to prescribe a reasonable notice in order to subject a defendant to the jurisdiction of its courts.2 Until the Court of 

Chancery has acquired jurisdiction over the person by proper service no defendant is before the court. There are two kinds of service: (1) Subpoena personally served on the defendant within this state. (2) Constructive, or statutory service, by order of publication. 

In answer to the question of when jurisdiction can be acquired over the person of the defendant and for what purposes, the following propositions have been recognized by the Court of Chancery, as established by the Supreme Court of the United States: (1) That a personal judgment is without validity, if it be rendered by a state court in an action upon a money demand against a non-resident, proceeded against by publication, but not personally served with process within the state, and not appearing. (2) That no validity is imparted to such a judgment by the fact that the defendant has, at the time the action is commenced, property within the state upon which a levy can be made under the judgment. (3) In suits strictly in rem, that is, where the property itself, is conceived of as having done the wrong or as having been the instrument of its commission, is being proceeded against, and in suits quasi in rem, that is, where the suit is against the person in respect of the res, where, for example, it has for its object partition or the sale or other disposition of defendant's property within the jurisdiction to satisfy plaintiff's demand by enforcing a lien upon it, personal service within the jurisdiction or appearance is not necessary. The decree can, however, extend only to the property in controversy. But there is this dis-

Hayden, 101 N. J. Eq. 361, 139 Atl. 328.

There is a further case, illustrated, so far, by proceedings to quiet title. Here the suit is based upon a denial of any res in the defendant. In this class of cases the Supreme Court has taken a distinction. If the decree sought, be a decree operating in personam only, to be taken under the ordinary jurisdiction of equity, a decree, for instance, that the defendant make or cancel a conveyance; that defendant be restrained from asserting his claim, it can be made only after personal service within the jurisdiction or after appearance. But if the decree be taken under a statute which authorizes the court to determine the question of title and to decree it to the party entitled, then it binds without such service or appearance, if the statute has provided “a reasonable method of imparting notice." 5 

46. Service in Summary Proceedings. 

li Causes matured in a summary manner are created by statute. such actions on the clearest principles of justice no person can be deprived of his rights either of person or property without an opportunity of being heard, viz., of having notice of the suit. This is true even though the action is summary in nature and despite the fact that the statute creating the remedy, fails to provide specifically for service. The summary action is usually matured not by a subpoena, but by the service on the defendant of an order or rule to show cause fixing a return day on which return day a summary hearing is had on affidavits, proofs and allegations. Under modern practice this summary hearing which is matured in the vice chancellor's chambers often is, and always will be where justice so requires, a complete trial of the issues presented by the pleadings.10 After the summary final hearing no process of subpoena issues. The entire function of process has been performed by service of the statutory notice under the direction of the court. fendant by a writ of subpoena ad respondendum.16 Originally this writ was a writ of the common law to enforce the attendance of a witness to give evidence; later it was employed by the courts of chancery to compel the appearance of a defendant and oblige him to answer on oath, the allegations of the bill of complaint.17 

Thereafter it was the practice to make applications to the chancellor for writs of subpoena. Now, however, they are supplied in quantities to members of the bar as officers of the court. They are accordingly filled in and signed by the solicitor, which is deemed to be the equivalent to the ancient issuing of process, in analogy to the practice at law.18 Copies are provided for each defendant and the sheriff's return is on the original. 66 In practice usually the bill and subpoena are sent out at the same time, although it should be noted that the subpoena recites the prior filing of the bill of complaint. In such case the subpoena should be dated ahead at least a day. In New Jersey the statutory requirement is that no subpoena or other process for appearance shall issue out of the court of chancery until after the bill shall have been filed.” 19 

This statute, patterned after an English act of the reign of Queen Anne, was designed to correct the practice of issuing the subpoena before the filing of the bill. In case the subpoena issues before the filing of the bill, the defendant must move promptly to set aside the service; the defect is, however, a mere technical irregularity, and if the defendant takes any step in the suit without objecting to the service, the court will not thereafter interfere to correct it.20 That the provision of the statute is directory and not mandatory has been recently held by Ch. Walker, in a case21 in which he alludes to the practice of mailing the bill to the clerk in chancery and at the same time issuing the subpoena, filing the bill as of the preceding day, a practice which he had condemned in an earlier case.22
