By a recent statute,23 the practice of fixing a return day in the subpoena was changed; subpoenas now have no return day. They are served forthwith and time for answering is twenty days from date of service and not the return day as formerly. A citation, however, in divorce actions still fixes a return day. Before this change, it was held that if the teste of the subpoena is just one day prior to the filing of the bill, or even if the time be longer, the cause will proceed regularly in the absence of prompt objection by the defendant; but it is essential that the bill be actually filed before the return day of the subpoena, otherwise the time for answering would be curtailed below the twenty days allowed after the return day when defendant is in court, for he cannot know what to answer until he sees the bill.24

The names of all the defendants in the same cause shall be inserted in one subpoena, unless the defendants reside in different counties, in which case the names of all those who reside in the same county shall be inserted in the same subpoena.25 When the bill names a person as defendant in a special capacity, viz., executor, trustee, etc., and properly charges him as such, it is not a ground of objection that the subpoena was issued against the defendant generally, for the subpoena is but notice, and by inspecting the bill the defendant can inform himself of the nature of the cause of action.26 66 The subpoena under the statute must be served on the defendant 'by giving to him personally a copy or leaving a copy thereof at his dwelling-house or usual place of abode." 27 What constitutes a person's" dwelling-house or usual place of abode " is not always an easy question.2

50. Issuance of Second Subpoena. 

Where the first subpoena is returned non est inventus (“not found") a second subpoena may issue after the first is misspent, and no rule of procedure in chancery requires a court order therefor. The subpoena although issued out of and under the seal of the court is but a notice to the defendant to appear and is not a mandate to one of the court's officers. It may be issued by the solicitor in the cause, and the fair implication is that he may do so toties quoties until service; viz., until legal notice of the suit be given the defendant. 

Subpoena by reason of the established practice in this state may issue as often as necessary to bring the defendant into court and without a court order.44

54. Constructive Service: Publication. 

one in

Constructive service is also called substituted service, service by publication, statutory service, etc. It is employed to acquire a limited jurisdiction over proper parties to an equity suit in the following cases: (I) Persons not known by the complainant to be either dead or alive, and whereabouts unknown, their unknown heirs, devisees, and personal representatives." (II) The unknown heirs, devisees, and personal representatives of persons known or believed to be dead.78 (III) Absent or non-answering non-resident defendants, whose names are known. (IV) Non-answering resident defendants who are concealing themselves within the state. (V) Domestic corporation defendants where none of the officers or directors is resident of this state or can be found herein.79

55. The Notice. 

The notice to non-resident defendants required under the Chancery Act is intended to be a notice which shall apprise a defendant not only that he is sued, but also of the nature of the suit, and such notice must necessarily involve a disclosure of the res toward which the suit is directed.91 The same statute makes it the duty of the 

Chancellor to prescribe the exact form and scope of the notice by rule of court.92 In the discharge of this duty, the Chancellor has ordained that, "Such notice shall be entitled in the court only, not in the cause, shall be addressed to the absent defendants by name, shall state the date of the order, the name of the complainant and the time within which the absent defendants are required to appear and answer; the notice shall also state briefly, in general terms, the object of the suit, and why the persons to whom it is addressed are made defendants.

Such notice shall be signed with the name and postoffice address of the solicitor of the complainant, or of the complainant, if he has no solicitor." 93 No notice to a defendant in an action quasi in rem would be reasonable which did not disclose distinctly the res, and its relation to the defendant, and to the demand of the plaintiff.94 [See FORM 50: Notice to Non-Resident in Foreclosure; FORM 53: Notice to Non-Resident in Divorce Action.95 5 ] [See FORM 43: Affidavit of Address of Non-Resident]; Schaffer v. Hurd,

56. When Constructive Service is Permitted. 

Jurisdiction over the person of a defendant can be acquired as stated above only by process served on him within this state or by his voluntary appearance in court. The proceedings outlined in the previous sections do not confer jurisdiction over the person of defendant who is absent from this state. Any personal decree founded on such statutory service is a nullity.96 But jurisdiction over a res which has a situs in this state but belonging to a non-resident may be exercised in proceedings where the absent defendant is served under the statute. These latter actions are described as actions in rem and quasi in rem.

It was held, though, that in a bill to enforce a personal covenant, when resident and non-resident defendants were charged jointly and severally, the bill could be taken as confessed against the non-resident defendants who were served by publication, and a final decree entered therein, although the property of such non-resident defendants could not, of course, be taken under the decree.97 Even where the defendant is within the state, but the subpoena was returned "not found' upon affidavit by the sheriff of due and diligent inquiry, etc., it was held in an early case that an order of publication was warranted, the statute being applicable to persons domiciled within the state as well as to those whose domicile is beyond its borders.98 

57. Actions Quasi in Rem. 

66 V. C. Stevenson summarized the essential elements of an action quasi in rem in the following manner: (1) a res located within the territorial limits of the state in such a way that the state can, if it sees fit to do so, exercise absolute power to control and dispose of it; (2) a course of judicial procedure, the object and result of which are to subject the res to the power of the state directly by the judgment or decree which is entered, as distinguished from a course of procedure which only affects or disposes of the res by compelling a party to the action to control or dispose of the res, in accordance with the mandate of the judgment or decree; (3) a course of judicial procedure on its face directed specifically toward the res 

96. Lanning v. Twining, 71 N. J. Eq. 573, 64 Atl. 466. (Suit against non resident directors by receiver of a corporation to recover money lost by negligence of directors; held: an action in personam.) 

97. Kirkpatrick v. Post, 53 N. J. Eq. 591, 32 Atl. 267, aff'd, 53 N. J. Eq. 641, 33 Atl. 1059. But see 1 C. S., p. 416, § 18. 

98. Equitable Life Ass. Soc. Laird, 24 N. J. Eq. 319. See Stevens v. 

Television, 111 N. J. Eq. 306, 162 Atl. 248.

so as to disclose this res to the defendant when reasonably notified of the action." 1 4 

Illustrations: A suit for the specific performance of a contract for the sale of land is a suit quasi in rem, and proper service of nonresident defendants who neither appear voluntarily nor are served with process in this state, may be had by publication under the statute.2 Similarly, a suit to foreclose the equity of redemption,³ to partition land, to quiet title to real estate; 5 a suit to reform a life insurance policy within this state; a suit for divorce; a bill for separate maintenance under § 26 of the Divorce Act; 8 etc.9 Simi larly, is an action to establish a trust in shares of stock in a New Jersey corporation, when the trustee resides out of the state, and cannot be served with process but can only be served by order of publication under statute.10 But a bill by one co-depositor in a joint savings account against the debtor-bank cannot be heard on substituted service by publication, on any theory that the other depositor's right (the other depositor being either a non-resident or whereabouts unknown) has a situs in New Jersey.11 Similarly a suit by a lessee to fix the rental under a lease on failure of the arbitration provided for in the lease is not in rem or quasi in rem and substituted service is a nullity in such a case.1 12

60. Service on Corporations. 

In any suit begun in the Court of Chancery against a corporation of this state, process of subpoena or other writ or order served upon the president, vice-president, a director or the designated agent of the corporation or other officer thereof, shall be good and effective service on the corporation.48 This statutory mode of service prescribed in the Chancery Act is not repugnant to provisions of the General Corporation Act 49 providing another method of service, which are in pari materia and service made under either section is regular and lawful. Under the provision of the latter act, service may be made in chancery proceedings on the statutory agent of the corporation, domestic or foreign, and if the same shall have died, or moved away, then on the Secretary of State, or the Assistant Secretary if the Secretary is absent.50

In all proceedings by the Attorney General on behalf of the State for an injunction to restrain any corporation from the exercise of any franchise, or the transaction of any business within the state, until the payment of such state taxes as may be imposed, the five days' notice of such application required to be given the delinquent corpo-

61. The Return: Amendment: Etc. 

Writs of subpoena have no return day by recent statutory change. The rules fix no period for the return of other writs and process except in case of writs of execution which are returnable three months after their teste; writs of injunction and writs ne exeat, one month.5 Ordinarily a citation would not be returnable longer than three months, and it could not be returnable less than five days from its teste, for that is the minimum notice that the person served is entitled to between the service and the return day.55 If the return day of any writ shall happen to fall on Sunday, or a holiday, it shall be returnable on the next secular day, but, if by inadvertence or otherwise, any writs are made returnable on any such inhibited days, they shall be considered as having been made returnable on the next secular day, and may be amended by the clerk as of course and at any time.50

The statute 57 directs the sheriff to make return of all writs, and for failure to do so, the sheriff or other officer "who shall not sign such return shall be amerced, and also answer damages to the party." 58 The return if unsigned, even though accompanied by affidavit would seem to be void.59 The return of the sheriff, i.e., "served," is presumptive proof of service of the subpoena.60 If the

The truth of the sheriff's return can be controverted in the action by either of the parties as at law. But the truth of the return cannot be assailed collaterally; 62 objection, thereto, must be made in the suit itself, or in a direct course of appellate procedure.63 

If by reason of a clerical error, the subpoena itself is antedated, ahead of the date of the filing of the bill, although in fact it was not issued before the filing of the bill, the error may be corrected by amendment.64 Similarly errors in the sheriff's return may be corrected. Thus the return of the service recited the defendant's name incorrectly (as did the other papers in the cause) yet in fact, service was made on the real defendant; such an error can be amended on petition supported by affidavits showing the error to be purely clerical, etc., and an order of correction will be entered. Without such an order no final decree will be entered.65 The application for leave to make a "true and proper return" by correction will be denied, however, if the truth of the correction is controverted." 66 Citations continue to have a return day which must necessarily be at least five days after the date of the teste, to allow for the interval of five days between the date of the service and the return day, as directed by statute. It would fix a return day, at least a minimum of five days after its date, but perhaps no more days than is reasonable within which to expect service thereof by the sheriff, as required by the statute.

62. When an Equity Suit Is Pending. 

It is settled that the mere filing of a bill of complaint in equity is not the beginning of the suit.70 The essential step (as in actions at law 71) is the taking out of process. This is true notwithstanding the statutory requirement that the bill must be filed before the subpoena can issue.72 The difficult question is whether the subpoena must be actually served before the suit can properly be said to be "pending." Most of the cases have stated the rule to be that a cause is pending in chancery on filing of the bill, issue of the subpoena, and a bona fide attempt to serve the subpoena.73 The question is most accurately answered by considering the type of the suit and for what purpose the question is raised. In cases where a preliminary writ of injunction issues (not an ad interim order), the subpoena and injunction must both be served; if the subpoena be not served, the injunction will be dissolved. If the suit be in personam, it is not begun until service of the subpoena.75 But where the suit is in rem, or quasi in rem, and the court has jurisdiction of the res, the suit is regarded as begun upon the filing of the bill, issue of

63. Parties: In General. 

V. C. Grey: "There is a wide difference between the mode of procedure at law and in equity touching the bringing in of parties to a suit. At law, save in a very few instances, the defendants who are called upon to respond are selected by the plaintiffs in the suit, and the court accepts the record as thus made up; but in equity, if it appears that there is a person, not in court, who holds an outstanding interest, the court will stand the cause over until the bringing in of that party. In equity, every person interested in sustaining or defeating the object of the suit should be a party, and be heard before decree. The spirit of the procedure in equity is to settle once and for all, in one suit, all disputes concerning the object of the litigation. Lord Hardwicke directed a cause to stand over until the proper parties defendant were brought in, though the objection was admittedly (so far as the defendant was concerned) taken too late, on the ground that the court could not do justice without the presence of the absent parties, who appeared to have an interest in the object of the suit. Sir John Leach declared that, where the defect of parties is apparent on the record, the court will take the objection, though the defendant does not; for, on appeal, if there be a defect of parties, the court of appeals will send the case back." 86

No persons are parties as defendants to a bill in chancery except those against whom process is prayed, or who are specifically named and described as defendants in the bill.87"The plaintiff," said Lord 

Chancellor Parkes, "may complain and tell stories of whom he pleases; but they only are defendants against whom process is prayed." 88

The complainant should in his bill pray for process therefore against all persons interested in the subject of the controversy. If in doubt, it is better to join the party leaving it to the party joined to raise the objection of misjoinder, which if sustained

Depue, out of the constitution of a court of equity, which aims not so much to decide the issues between the litigating parties, as to embrace the whole subject and determine upon the rights of all parties interested, to make the determination complete and quiet all questions, so that the performance of the decree may be perfectly safe to those who are compelled to obey it, and also that future litigation may be prevented." 64. Necessary and Proper Parties Distinguished. 

Although there is some authority 91 for distinguishing necessary parties from those who are indispensable, the practice in New Jersey seems to be to regard necessary parties as those who are indispensable But the distinction between parties who are proper and those who are necessary, has been stated in numerous New Jersey decisions. The most often approved rule was stated by V. C. Pitney: "The learned judge [referring to a cited case] said that it was a familiar rule of equity pleading that all persons having a common interest and common object in the subject matter of a bill ought to be made parties or, if they are too numerous to render the joinder of all of them practicable, the bill should be brought by some in behalf of all, so that the rights of all may be duly adjudicated in the final decree'; the language there used, all persons having a common interest and common object in the subject matter of a bill,' seems to me to be a better general statement of the rule than to say that 'all persons having an interest in the subject matter' should be made parties. But I think that neither of them is strictly accurate, as was pointed out by Chancellor Zabriskie in commenting upon somewhat similar language used by the Court of Errors and Appeals he cites with approval the language of Justice Story 

89. Dean Lile's definition of parties: "All persons in being, and within reach of the process of the court, who are in anywise interested, legally or equitably, in the subject matter of the litigation, and whose interests may be directly affected by the proceedings, whether beneficially or detrimentally, or who might again litigate the precise matter adjudicated, should be made parties to the suit." Eq. Pl., § 85. 

90. Cutler v. Tuttle, 19 N. J. Eq. 549. 

91. Chester v. King, 2 N. J. Eq. 405, semble; Berryman v. Graham, 21 N. J. 

Eq. 370; Clephane, Eq. Pl. & Pr., § 10. 

92. Board of Com'rs of Somerville v. Johnson, 36 N. J. Eq. 211, at 214.

.6 that, it is not all persons who have an interest in the subject matter of the suit, but in general, those only who have an interest in the object of the suit, who are ordinarily required to be made parties'; and Mr. Calvert's language in his treatise on Parties (page 10): 

The propriety of a person being made a party depends upon his interest, not in the subject matter, but in the object of the suit.' A still better definition, perhaps, is that of Thomas J., The general doctrine in relation to parties in equity is often stated to be that all persons interested in the subject matter of the suit should. be made plaintiffs or defendants. This statement is too broad. It would be more accurate to say, persons interested in the object of the suit must be made parties; that is, persons who are parties to the interest involved in the issue, and who must necessarily be affected by the decree.'" 93

66. Proper Parties: (Illustrations). 

Parties who may be joined but need not be are proper parties. 

They are sometimes called formal parties. Parties joined, however, against whom the complainant does not ask for and is not entitled to relief, and as against whom the bill must be dismissed with costs upon demurrer are not proper parties. A person against whom a decree cannot be had should not be made a party. Within this rule would be an action in the Court of Chancery joining the United States as a necessary party; 7 proceeding against the Chancellor in his capacity as Ordinary; or, an action against a receiver as an officer of the Court of Chancery on the receiver's bond without the consent thereto of the Chancellor.9

69. Foreclosure (Continued): Unrecorded Encumbrances: Right of Intervention. 

Section 58 of the Chancery Act provides that proceedings in foreclosure shall bind all unrecorded encumbrancers although they are not made parties to the suit in the same manner as if they had been joined.43 The act applies to and cuts off all encumbrancers who claim through "any conveyance, mortgage, assignment, lien, or any instrument which by any provision of law could be recorded, registered, entered or filed in any public office of this state,44 and which is not recorded at the time of the filing of the bill to foreclose.45 The statute is intended to perfect the title in the foreclosure in accordance with the public records as such records disclose the existence of liens or incumbrances, and to protect forever the title made under the sheriff's sale as against any liens not thus disclosed.46 Although the statute serves to relieve the mortgaged premises when sold under of the bill with subpoena on the United States District Attorney by the Sheriff of Mercer County. In the event that a lienor has neglected to file or record his lien or encumbrances at the time the bill to foreclose is filed, the Chancery Act authorizes him to record his encumbrance forthwith, and thereupon to intervene by petition in the pending foreclosure.5+ [See 

FORM 90: Petition of Lienor to Intervene in a Foreclosure.] Prior recordation is ordinarily required as a condition to the right to intervene, but the requirement is relaxed when the instrument is lost, or in the wrongful possession of the complainant, and the inability of the lienor to record will not debar him from the benefit of the statute.55

The petition must set forth the instrument thus recorded, and the title and interest of the lienor in such a manner as to show that the petitioner has an interest in the subject matter of the foreclosure and is a proper party in that suit.56 The petition is to be supported by affidavit and the procedure governing the intervention is that controlling any intervention under Chancery Rule 13.57 At the hearing on the application to intervene, the court will not undertake a complete trial of petitioner's alleged rights: the issue is simply as to whether or not the petitioner is asserting a bona fide claim which he ought equitably to be permitted to have tried in the cause.58

70. Foreclosure (Continued): Bill For a Deficiency Against an 

Assuming Grantee.

In a foreclosure the grantee to whom the mortgaged property has been conveyed and who holds title to the equity of redemption at the time of the foreclosure, is a necessary party.62 But although joined as a party and despite the fact that he has assumed payment of the mortgage, no decree for a deficiency can be entered against the assuming grantee in the foreclosure suit.63 The mortgagee in enforcing the liability of the grantee for a deficiency must proceed by an original bill in equity. This right of the mortgagee is in addition to an action at law on the bond.

72. Quieting Title: Parties. 

In the usual suit to quiet title the complainant is the owner of both the legal and equitable title. But this is not necessarily true: the holder of the bare legal title may file a bill to quiet title under the statute as a proper party complainant. The holders of the equitable title in such a case should be made parties to the action. Conversely, the owner of the equitable title is also a proper party complainant, joining also as a party to the action, the holder of the legal title.5

73. Partition: Parties. 

All the owners of the joint estate to be partitioned are necessary parties.10

Where there are non-resident owners, or persons believed to be dead, their unknown heirs, are necessary parties, and can be served by order of publication, and the Court of Chancery will acquire jurisdiction to partition or sell the land affected.11 A trustee who under a will holds legal title with power of sale, to the land to be partitioned, is a necessary party even though the will has not been probated.12 When a person has an interest in the realty to be partitioned in two or more capacities, viz., as heir at law and as mortgagee, he should be made a party to the suit in both capacities.13 

Similarly, when it appears that the land of the decedent is subject to his debts, the administrator is a necessary party as such although he may be already a party in an individual capacity.¹ But if the joint estate is created by will, it not appearing that there are debts to which the land is subject, the personal representative of the estate is not a necessary party.15

74. Partition (Continued): Encumbrancers. 

A mortgagee with a lien on the whole premises is not a proper party.19 The Partition Act, although it authorizes a sale free of a lien on undivided shares, does not authorize a sale in partition free from the lien of a mortgage on the whole premises; the statutory right, therefore, to make mortgagees parties, extends only to mortgagees on undivided shares.20 Not only mortgagees, but all other creditors who have a lien on the undivided interest of any party whether by way of mortgage, judgment, decree, devise, or otherwise, are proper and necessary parties to the partition thereof if the property is to be sold clear of the lien.21 Although the lien of a mortgage on the whole premises is unaffected by a partition, yet when the lien is on an undivided share of one particular co-tenant, the lien, upon partition, shall be a charge only upon the share assigned such owner in division.22 Under the Partition Act, if the mortgagee on an undivided share is made a party, or is admitted on motion by any party,23 then a sale may be directed free from the lien of the encumbrance. 75. Modes of Objecting to Want of Parties. 

When the absence of a necessary party is apparent on the face of the bill, the objection is raised by motion to strike the bill in lieu of demurrer; if not apparent, then the defect may be brought before the court by answer in lieu of plea, and this defense is a plea in bar and goes to the whole bill.26 The proper decree, however, when further parties are necessary, is not that the bill be dismissed in the first instance, but an order that the cause stand over for the purpose of bringing in the necessary parties.27 If they are not then brought in within the period fixed by the order of the court, the bill of course must be dismissed.28 Even at the hearing the objection can be raised on motion that necessary parties are not joined in the cause; this motion would not be in lieu of demurrer, for the time for demurring is past, but a motion under a general equity rule of practice. Such a motion would amount to no more than a direction of the attention of the court to an alleged defect of parties which is so radical that the court of its own motion would hold the suit until the defect could be remedied, or, if irremediable, would dismiss the suit.29 From what has been said, it is apparent that the court itself can, in the absence of any objection from the parties, sua sponte arrest the suit for want of necessary parties.30 In case the party not joined is merely a proper or formal party, the objection must be taken in limine; if not then raised, the court will dispose of the cause in so far as it can with respect to the parties before it, but without prejudice to the rights of

76. Parties by Representation. 

Where parties in interest are numerous and widely scattered, but all are equally affected by the right to be litigated, it would be highly impracticable to require the joinder of all such persons either as complainants or defendants. In such a case one or a few can undertake to prosecute the suit for the benefit of and in behalf of all. 

Such a bill is called a class bill, and a decree entered in such a cause will beneficially affect all in the class notwithstanding some of them have not made themselves active parties in the suit.35 If a bill is filed by an individual of a numerous class in his own right, an amendment will generally be allowed so as to make such individual sue on behalf of himself and the rest of the class.36 66 This doctrine of representation of parties is sometimes called virtual representation." Although it is more usually found in cases of parties complainant, it may be invoked to join one or a few of a large and widely scattered group as parties defendant. In this latter case, all in the group of parties defendant are deemed to be before the court not for the purpose of entering personal decrees against all of them, but merely to enter a decree with respect to some res, trust fund, joint-right, etc., in which they are all equally interested. 

In litigating land limited over to persons not in esse, the joinder of the living owner of the first estate of inheritance brings in by repre-

42 41 43 39 A bill brought by one member of a benefit fund on behalf of himself and all other members of the benefit fund; a suit by one creditor for the benefit of all the creditors of a corporation to compel shareholders to pay their subscriptions to the capital stock in order to create a fund from which all the creditors (not complainant alone) can be paid their debts; 40 similarly one shareholder can file a bill for the benefit of all the shareholders; or one taxpayer can sue for the benefit of all; or, one bondholder can foreclose a trust mortgage for the benefit of all the bondholders; or, one creditor or stockholder can sue for the appointment of a receiver of an insolvent corporation.44 Under the Chancery Rules if a stockholder brings a representative suit, the complainant stockholder shall immediately, on filing the bill of complaint and issuing a subpoena to answer, give such notice of the pendency and object of the suit to the other stockholders as the Chancellor shall in each case by order direct.45 A single creditor may also file a bill for the benefit of all creditors to set aside a fraudulent conveyance.40

The right to intervene as a party is made conditional upon the petitioner's having "an interest or title which the decree will affect." 

This does not require a thorough and complete hearing, and a final and absolute determination that he has such an interest or title, prior to admitting him as a party. Such a course would be impracticable; in many cases, it would require a preliminary determination of the very issues which the complainant seeks to litigate. The rule does contemplate, however, that not every one shall be admitted as a party simply because he makes application. 79. Addition of Parties by the Court. 

When a complete determination of a controversy cannot be had without the presence of other parties, the court has the power at any stage of the proceedings to add new parties, directing them to be brought in, if their presence is necessary to a complete determination of the controversy.5 52 In all cases where it shall appear to the court that persons who might otherwise be deemed proper parties to the suit cannot be made parties by reason of their being out of the jurisdiction of the court, or incapable otherwise of being made parties, the court may, in its discretion, proceed in the cause without making such persons parties; and in such cases the decree shall be without prejudice to the rights of the absent parties.53 

80. An Infant Party. 

Infants, idiots and lunatics are the wards of court and the Chancellor is their general guardian.54 When they are brought into court, the jurisdiction parens patriae obtains.55 A bill may never be taken pro confesso as to such persons nor may it be voluntarily dismissed to their detriment.56 Nothing can be taken as admitted against an infant, either by failure of the guardian ad litem to answer, nor by actual answer filed by the guardian; neither guardian nor next friend can surrender by stipulation the infant's rights.57 Both an infant and a lunatic are served personally and such service should be in the presence of a competent person.58

An infant has no standing as a party complainant in equity; he must sue by guardian or next friend. If a bill is exhibited by an infant, the proper practice is, in case the defect is not apparent on the face of the bill, for the defendant to file answer in lieu of plea (formerly a plea to the person). The usual practice is for the defendant to move to have the bill dismissed with costs to be paid by

81. In General.

Modes of defense available to a defendant in a chancery suit. were formerly (1) a demurrer, (2) a plea, (3) an answer, (4) a disclaimer. In the present practice, a motion is substituted for a demurrer.¹ The plea is made by an answer in lieu of plea, and the answer and disclaimer remain as before.2 These changes are changes largely in name and the old rules continue to apply in most cases to the substituted pleadings. A demurrer, or a motion in lieu of demurrer, is said to be "an excuse for not pleading." It is an answer to the bill, yet in a technical sense it was not an answer. A peculiarity of equity pleading was that a demurrer was never interposed to a defensive pleading, viz., the plea and the answer.5 How 

1. Chancery Rule 67. 3 2. Chancery Rule 68 (every defense heretofore presentable by plea shall be made in the answer). 

3. Lully v. National Surety Co., 106 N. J. L. 81, 148 Atl. 762. 

4. Van Dyne v. Vreeland, 11 N. J. Eq. 370. 

5. Travers v. Ross, 14 N. J. Eq. 254. 124

the legal sufficiency of the plea and answer were tested in the early practice will be explained in later sections, and the effect of the present rules on this early practice will be considered." 

82. Historical. 

Formerly as at law, a general demurrer was used to test the legal sufficiency of a bill of complaint; a special demurrer was directed to defects of form and not to defects of substance. For both kinds of demurrer, the motion had been substituted under Chancery Rules promulgated by the Chancellor, many years before the adoption of the present Chancery Rules of 1915. Demurrers of course, are now abolished, but any pleading may be objected to on motion on the ground that it discloses no cause of action, or ground of defense in case the pleading objected to be defensive in character. In spite of the fact that defects of form as well as defects of substance, are both reached by motion, the distinction between defects in substance and defects of form continues to be of some importance in equity pleading as at law, as for example, a motion made to a bill for formal defects does not admit the matter alleged in the bill, but a motion in lieu of a demurrer does admit matter well pleaded." 

83. Speaking Demurrer. 

Since the function of a demurrer was to attack a bill for errors of law apparent on the face of the bill, either by reason of what appeared therein, or of what was lacking and omitted therefrom, or for obvious defects in the form of the bill, the demurrer could not set up matter not included in the bill. If the demurrer violated this rule it was called a "speaking demurrer." 10 If the demurrer restates facts differently from the allegations of the bill itself, and makes the new facts thus introduced the grounds of the demurrer to the bill, this is also, a speaking demurrer. The objections made to the bill, whether in the statement of the grounds of the demurrer, or in the argument of the demurrant's counsel in support of it, depend for their force, not upon the allegations of the bill, but upon the new facts introduced by the demurrant in the demurrer.

11 It violates that principle of correct pleading that a demurrer can be founded only on a fact or omission appearing in the bill.12 Similarly if any of the grounds of the demurrer deny facts charged in the bill.13 The rule of decision on a speaking demurrer, seems to have been to overrule the demurrer, unless the court could, after rejecting the new matter in the demurrer as surplusage, still sustain the demurrer without regard to the new facts set up.¹¹ The same rule is substantially applied to the motion, the present substitute for the demurrer, in the requirement that the motion cannot set up new matter either by affidavit or otherwise.15 11 

84. Motion to Strike Whole of Bill Bad Only in Part. 

Under the old practice if a demurrer was addressed to the whole of the bill, and not confined to that particular part of the bill that was demurrable, then the demurrer was too broad in covering the whole bill, and would be overruled.16 But if the demurrer was directed only to the improper part of the bill, a proper part being joined therewith, the demurrer to the improper would be sustained, but the bill would proceed with respect in the relief properly sought.¹ 17 

Similarly, in the case of a joint demurrer, the demurrer must be good as to both demurrants, or it is bad as to each.18

87. Demurrer Ore Tenus.

Under the early practice the demurrer was a written pleading and disclosed the grounds for the demurrer. In the argument, however, the demurrant was not limited to the grounds previously assigned in writing but could in open court assign other and additional grounds, the assigned grounds having proved untenable. 

This practice was known as demurring ore tenus.60 The practice, however, of reserving objections to the pleadings until the argument tended to delay the determination of the cause because, if the objection were put upon the record, the complainant might have concluded to amend at once, instead of awaiting a hearing upon the demurrer. Its effect was also to prevent proper preparation for argu-

60. Stillwell v. M'Neely, 2 N. J. Eq. 305, where under a general demurrer for the want of equity, a demurrer ore tenus was allowed for the want of parties. See Story, Eq. Pl., § 464; 21 C. J., § 483; Barrett v. Doughty, 25 N.

Under the present practice in New Jersey, not only must five days' written notice of a motion to strike be given, but this notice must state in writing "the particular grounds of objection." 64 It is inferable that this rule was designed to prevent the assigning of other and additional grounds at the argument in support of the motion. 

Certainly under the practice at law when specifications of the grounds of objection were subjoined to a demurrer, the party demurring at the argument, was confined to such grounds.65 Subject then to the general power of a court of equity to allow amendments to notices of motions to strike (discussed in Section 90, infra), and the flexible control it exercises over all matters of procedure, it may be fairly concluded, even in the absence of a precise ruling on the point since 1915, that the practice of demurring ore tenus, as such, even in the form of its counterpart, the motion, no longer exists under the present chancery practice. 

88. Assigning Grounds. 

Under the earlier practice demurrers set forth the grounds of demurring. If a general demurrer, the usual "want of equity" was assigned as the cause: viz., that the "bill does not make or state a case entitling the complainant to a decree and that the defendant is not bound to answer the same.' If a special demurrer, the particular defect or objection must be pointed out. Under the old practice defects of form were reached only by a special demurrer; defects " 66

Under the early rules adopted by the Court of Chancery of New Jersey, there is the same requirement: "Every demurrer, whether general or special, shall state the particular grounds of demurrer." 68 

This rule was taken to have the same scope and purpose as a similar order. in chancery in England, which was, in the language of V. C. 

Van Fleet, "to secure greater fairness and thoroughness in the discussion of questions arising on general demurrer than could be had under the old practice. Under the old practice, it sometimes happened that, although a general demurrer was well founded in point of law, yet the ground upon which it rested was so far beyond the line of vision of the ordinary practitioner that he could not see it without having it pointed out to him; and only lawyers of very extended experience, or unusual acumen, would readily discern it. A simple allegation of, want of equity gave the ordinary practitioner, in such a case, no information whatever of the ground on which his statement of his client's case would be attacked. The demurrer rather emboldened than disturbed him; for, not seeing the ground of the demurrer, he supposed none existed, and he would proceed to the argument of the demurrer in ignorance of the ground on which it rested, and generally without preparation; and the consequence was that in such cases the court was either compelled to defer the case for further argument or to decide it upon an imperfect argument. The purpose of the rule was to cure this mischief, by making it the duty of a demurrant, when he filed his demurrer, to make such a disclosure of the ground of his demurrer as would render it probable, when his demurrer came on for argument, that all the questions raised by it would be fully, fairly, and thoroughly discussed." 69

The present rule requires the notice of motion (which is, of course, in lieu of demurrer) to "state the particular grounds of objection.' "970 The practice, therefore, of acquainting the complainant with the grounds of the motion in advance is continued and it would seem remains subject substantially to the rules evolved with respect to the old demurrer, and the assigning of grounds therefor.

V. C. Van Fleet approved of the following rules: (1) An averment of mere want of equity would not in general be a sufficient specification of the grounds of demurring, but whether in any particular case it will be sufficient or not must depend entirely upon the form in which the complainant has stated his case in his bill; (2) that when the court finds, upon looking at the complainant's bill, that his right to relief is doubtful or uncertain, or that his equity is not obvious at first sight, then a simple statement of want of equity will, under the rule, constitute a sufficient specification of the ground of the demurrer; but where the defect or infirmity is obscure or latent, to such an extent that the court cannot, on inspecting the complainant's bill, readily discern it, there the rule requires the demurrant to point out, by a plain statement, the specific ground on which his demurrer is founded.72

The above limitation on the rule as first announced-that even though the defect of the bill is plain and obvious, yet under a general statement of want of equity as the assigned ground for demurring, defects collateral to the main issue, viz., laches, cannot be shown but must be plainly specified and particularized, was first announced by Ch. McGill. Van Houten v. Van

Complainant ordinarily will be given opportunity of proving the facts on a final hearing, including excuse for the delay, and the bill will not be stricken on motion before a hearing. Sobota v. Shaffer, 105 N. J. Eq. 459, 148 Atl. 196.

The limitation on the general rule just stated with respect to the defense of laches, as collateral to the main issue, and therefore requiring specification under the Chancery Rules even though plain on the face of the bill, was seemingly applied by Ch. Walker to a case where the demurrer had been based on want of equity, and the demurrant sought to show the existence of an adequate remedy at law. 

In such a case, the rule is that under a demurrer for want of equity, the existence of an adequate remedy at law is not available, the latter not having been specified as a ground for demurrer as required by the 

Chancery Rules. Ch. Walker: "It is at least doubtful, to my mind, whether the question of adequate remedy at law is not collateral to the main case, the same as laches, but, be this as it may, it seems that legal remedy, when relied upon as cause for demurrer in a chancery suit, must be specified as a cause of demurrer. [After discussing cases.] The rule, then, would seem to be this: Where the case made by the bill—that is, where all the facts, taken together—make a case in which it is doubtful if the complainant be entitled to relief, the bill may be assailed for want of equity under a general demurrer; but where the want of equity springs out of some concrete proposition, whether collateral to the bill, strictly speaking, or whether involved in the main case, then the cause of demurrer must be specified." 99-74 

74. Safford v. Barber, 74 N. J. Eq. 352, 70 Atl. 371, at p. 372; Knikel v. 

Spitz, 74 N. J. Eq. 581, 70 Atl. 992 (reaching a similar result on the ground that a specification of "want of equity" is too general and indefinite, to raise the objection that the remedy at law is adequate). Continental, etc., Tr. Co. v. 

Fulton Realty Co., 10 N. J. Misc. R. 1105, 162 Atl. 560.

V. C. Stevenson's discussion of Chancery Rules 209 and 213, which are embodied substantially in the present Chancery Rule 75, is particularly lucid: "The only specification in the demurrer is the common form,-for want of equity, viz., that the complainants have not in and by their said bill made or stated such case as entitles them, in a court of equity, to any relief against the defendant as to the matters in said bill, or any of such matters.' Prior to the argument of the demurrer the complainants moved to strike it out on the ground that it failed to comply with rule 209 of this court, which requires every demurrer to 'distinctly specify the ground or grounds of demurrer.' This preliminary objection is not well taken. It is well settled that a demurrer in the old form, which specifies as its basis only want of equity, is not in conflict with the above-mentioned rule. In other words, the statement in a demurrer that the bill does not set forth any case for equitable relief is a 'specification' of a ground of demurrer, within the meaning of the rule; but the question remains, what attack upon the bill will be permitted under such a specification? 

The object of the rule is to give reasonable notice to the complainant of the grounds upon which the sufficiency of his bill is to be called in question, to the end that he may prepare to meet the attack which is made, and that he may not waste his time in preparing to meet attacks which are not made. 

It follows that under the old form of demurrer for 'want of equity,' the demurrant may raise all objections to the complainant's case on the merits, as

The value of these rules of modern equity practice, which are assimilated to the practice at law, lies in the fact that large numbers of objections to bills which formerly were fatal under general demurrers, are now excluded from consideration unless they are distinctly pointed out and specified so that counsel for the complainant may speedily without loss of time amend his bill, or come prepared to defend his bill against the charge, oftentimes a mere technicality, which the defendant makes against it.75 And it seems to be fairly certain that most of the rules established when the demurrer was in use, and the motion was a merely elective substitute, continue to apply to the notice of motion which under the present rules is required to specify the grounds of objection.76 Certainly this is in accord with the practice at law and in keeping with the original purpose of the rules. 

90. Amendment of the Specification of Grounds. 

Although the specification does not disclose the particular ground on which the defendant wishes to rest his motion to strike the bill, yet, in a proper case, a court of equity has inherent power to allow "the grounds of the motion" to be amended, and to allow a motion made under the present Chancery Rule 67, in lieu of demurrer, to be continued, so as to permit the party making the motion to state additional grounds of objection." But to enable the defendant to amend his notice, application to the court for leave to amend must be made. The practice at law confines the "demurrant" at the hearing of his specified grounds of objection, but also allows for amendpresented in the bill of complaint, which are reasonably apparent upon a perusal of the bill and demurrer. No exact and rigid rule, from the nature of the case, can be laid down on this subject. It was not the intention of the rule to compel the demurrant to submit to his adversary his brief, or any particulars of his argument. The purpose was to notify the complainant only of the general subject-matter of the argument. If the bill and demurrer for want of equity do not give reasonable notice of any defect in or debatable question concerning the complainant's case as exhibited in his bill, then the demurrer is frivolous, but cannot be stricken out for non-compliance with rule 209. It is like a demurrer for laches, when no foundation for the charge of laches is contained in any allegation of the bill of complaint." Demarest v. 

Terhune, 62 N. J. Eq. 663, 50 Atl. 664, at p. 665. 

75. Beam v. Paterson, etc., Tr. Co., 81 N. J. Eq. 38, 88 Atl. 379.

91. Demurring in the Answer.

From the foregoing it must not be inferred that objections proper for a motion in lieu of demurrer must be made in that manner of not at all. On the contrary, since an early time the practice of "demurring in the answer " has been recognized in equity procedure.80 

The defendant then is at liberty to incorporate in his answer any objections of a substantial character that might have been the proper basis of a motion, and if he does so the objections are not deemed to be waived, but the benefit thereof saved to the final hearing.81 

78. 3 C. S., p. 4094 et seq.

80. Green, C. It seemed to be assumed upon the argument, that the objection for want of title in the complainant or other want of equity in the bill must be taken by demurrer. 'By a demurrer,' says Lord Riverdale, 'the defendant demands the judgment of the court, whether he shall be compelled to answer the complainant's bill or not. By an answer he controverts the case stated by the plaintiff, or, admitting the case made by the bill, submits to the judgment of the court upon it, or upon a new case made by the answer, or both.' Upon an answer, then the complainant is entitled to the opinion of the court upon the case made by the bill, as well as the case made by the answer, upon both or either. And it is not an unusual thing in practice for an answer in equity to conclude by the defendant's insisting that there is no equity in the complainant's bill and putting himself upon the judgment of the court respecting it. The practice rests upon sound policy. A demurrer admits the truth of the charges in the bill. A bill addresses itself to the conscience of the defendant, and when a bill contains charges of fraud or of other immorality implicating the character of the defendant, an upright man would forego his legal rights rather than avail himself of a legal objection which, if successful would deprive him of all opportunity of relieving his character by a denial of the charges." The distinction between matters well pleaded and matters not well pleaded should be noticed as important in this connection.90 (1) The most common instance of matter ill pleaded is the pleading of legal conclusions, viz., fraud, usury, etc., in haec verba. Thus a bill that merely avers fraud without setting forth the facts substantiating the pleader's conclusion, does not well plead the fraud, and the allegation of fraud, being a mere legal conclusion, would not be confessed by motion.91 Another instance of a legal conclusion not admitted on motion is where the bill of complaint undertakes to state the legal construction, character and effect of annexed documents; in such a case the documents will be read and construed by the court independently of the complainant's construction thereof.92 (2) Matters of fact alleged in a bill of complaint which run counter to facts of which the court takes judicial notice will be disregarded on a motion to strike the bill, as matter not well pleaded.93 (3) Matters of fact alleged in a bill not appropriate to the pending cause, as allegations of evidence in the case, when the bill is a bill of review for error of law apparent on the record, are not taken to be admitted on motion.94 (4) Matter alleged in a bill which is repugnant to or inconsistent with other facts appearing in affidavits, or annexed schedules or exhibits, accompanying the bill.95 (5) Allegations of fact pleaded on information and belief are not taken to be admitted on motion.96 If, on a motion to strike out a bill, the motion is accompanied with a denial of the facts as charged in the bill (i.e., a "speaking demurrer "), the denials are treated as surplusage, the motion being heard on the case as alleged.97

It should be noted that the motion admits the truth of all allegations

94. Adequate Remedy at Law as Ground for Motion to Strike a 

Bill: Timeliness. 

As has been already stated, the existence of an adequate remedy at law is a proper ground for a motion to strike the bill provided the notice of the motion properly specifies the adequacy of legal relief as the ground of the motion. Another limitation on the motion based on the sufficiency of the legal relief is that it must be made in limine.5 

In the absence of seasonable objection on the ground the remedy at law is adequate, the Court of Chancery will proceed to exercise its own unquestioned jurisdiction; the defendant by refraining at the first opportunity from objecting to the exercise of equitable jurisdiction will, if his objection be sustained now that the cause has proceeded to a hearing, compel the complainant to commence his litigation over in another court, and in the language of V. C. Stevenson, "may well be deemed to be stipulating or assenting to the proposition that the remedy at law is not adequate, and that therefore the complainant's case should be disposed of by the exercise of the jurisdiction of this court.' ." 95. Effect of Failure to Move to Strike. 

If the defect in the bill was one of form, and not of substance, such as would have been the ground for a special demurrer under the early practice, then not only was the demurrant required to specify the defect with reasonable certainty and distinctness but, failing to file a special demurrer upon filing only a general demurrer for want of equity, defects in form would not be considered, the latter being deemed to be waived by failure to demur specially.10 Similarly, the failure to file a general demurrer, under the earlier practice going to defects of substance, the defendant by answering to the merits (without saving in the answer the benefit of the objection), was deemed to waive the substantial objections that he might have made by motion had his motion been made in limine.11

He can move to strike out a bill instead of demurring to it, and must move to strike out while the pleadings are in that condition in which he can demur to the bill. The defend-

96. Demurrer Overruled by Answer. 

Under the early practice it was well settled that either a plea or answer overruled a demurrer. By overruled was meant that the demurrer was nullified, superseded or waived, by the filing simultaneously therewith either a plea or answer. Ch. Zabriskie :18 "It is not right that, by answering and omitting to demur, he [the defendant] should permit the complainant to take his testimony, and then, after his expense is incurred, take advantage of it on a final hearing The dicta in many of the cases, and of the text writers, that these matters may be taken advantage of by answer, as well as by demurrer, must be held to apply to answers for that purpose only; for it is a settled rule of equity pleading, that a defendant cannot answer and demur to the same part of a bill, and that an answer overrules a demurrer." 19 

Ch. McGill, in 1894, applied the same rule: "My conclusion upon the first ground of demurrer would lead me to sustain the demurrer were it not for the existence of the answer, which goes to the whole bill. I think that the answer overlaps and overrules the demurrer. It is the well-settled rule that a less favored mode of defense will yield to the more favored, i.e., a plea to an answer, and a demurrer to a plea or an answer. When more than one mode of defense is resorted to, no two must overlap, as the least overlapping is fatal to the less favored defenses

I cannot allow the demurrer because it is overruled by the answer." 20

97. Demurring to an Answer.

Under the early practice, no demurrer was interposed to an answer for the answer was a defensive pleading and equity had its own mode of testing the legal sufficiency of all defensive pleadings, as will be explained in succeeding chapters.24 Suffice it to say for the present, that under the existing chancery rules, a motion to strike out an answer will lie, so that in effect, the complainant may now demur to the answer.25 But if the objection to the answer is that it does not give the particulars or details claimed as constituting a defense, this objection cannot be urged on a motion to strike out an answer. This is true because the chancery rules provide a more efficacious mode of procedure of securing further particulars or details of the defendant's defense.26 Formerly, an answer that was impertinent, was excepted to by the complainant; exceptions to an answer are abolished by the present Chancery Rules 27 and the objection under the present practice would be made by a motion to strike the answer (in lieu of exceptions).28

98. Motion to Strike Pleadings as Sham or Frivolous. 

66 Under Section 117 of the Chancery Act, a motion may be made to strike out on notice any frivolous or sham defense." The court thereupon may enter a decree pro confesso, or allow the defendant to defend on terms, or enter any other order or decree in the premises as may be just.29 The hearing on such a motion is conducted in a summary manner.30 The proceeding is regarded as merely an inquiry whether there is an issue of fact to be tried, a distinction being recognized between the determination of whether there is a real issue to be tried, and the trial of the issue upon a motion: whether what in form is presented as an issue, is a real issue.31 This motion on the ground that the defense is sham, is not a motion in lieu of demurrer, and, therefore, is under the practice, supported by affidavits, documents, or other evidence.32 

Although the statute relating to sham pleadings makes no provision for the taking of evidence, the necessary implication of the statute is that evidence shall be taken, the evident intention of the statute being to assimilate the practice in equity to that at law.33 At the hearing, the rule of decision is to strike the answer-only if palpably false. An order striking an answer as sham is appealable to the 

Court of Errors and Appeals.35 A distinction, however, is taken between sham and frivolous pleadings. Ch. Walker: “While the courts sometimes use the terms 'frivolous' and sham' as meaning the same thing, and a motion to strike is often based on the ground that a plea is both frivolous and sham, there is nevertheless a clear distinction between the two in that a sham plea is good on its face, but false in fact, while a

100.' Motion Days. 

Motions are heard on motion days. Every Monday and Tuesday shall be motion days; every Monday at the Chancery Chambers in 

Jersey City; every Tuesday at the Chancery Chambers in Trenton and Atlantic City; every Monday, except August, at the Chancery 

Chambers in Camden; the first and third Mondays of each month, except August, at the Chancery Chambers in Paterson; every Tuesday, except August, at the Chancery Chambers in Newark.

When a regular motion-day shall fall upon a legal holiday, the day following shall be the motion-day. Motions may be heard on any of the days designated, by a Vice Chancellor sitting for the Chancellor, without previous special reference of the matter involved therein to him. Notices of motions shall designate the place of hearing, either as "the Chancery Chambers at (naming a place other than Trenton, assigned by the Calendar) or the "State House at Trenton," accordingly as the motion shall be intended to be made, and they shall also state that the motion will be made before the Chancellor," unless the case in which the motion is to be made shall theretofore have been specially referred to a Vice Chancellor or Advisory Master, in which case the notice shall state that the motionwill be made before the Vice Chancellor or Advisory Master, to whom such reference shall have been made.57

101. Function of the Plea: Historical. 

A plea was in effect an answer which reduced the issue between the parties to a single point.¹ Whereas a motion to strike the bill in lieu of demurrer is for matter apparent on the face of the bill, an essential requisite of a plea in chancery was that it should be founded upon new matter not apparent in the bill.2 Contrasted with the answer, the plea reduced the issue between the parties to a single point which, if sustained, was dispositive of the case, whereas an answer sets out in full all defenses available to the defendant, and also gives discovery if prayed for. Just as the motion may be thought of as an excuse for not pleading, just so the plea may be considered as an excuse for not answering. Lord Eldon: "The office of a plea, generally, is not to deny the equity, but to bring forward a fact which, if true, displaces it." 3

The plea was for the purpose of presenting a single state of facts which constituted one issue; if, therefore, it presented two or more defenses going to the same matter, it was bad for duplicity. A plea, however, presenting two defenses to the same matter in the bill under the early practice, was allowed with leave of court. If a 

1. Gilson v. Appleby, 78 N. J. Eq. 96, 78 Atl. 668. 

2. Kelly v. Masionis, 79 N. J. Eq. 644, 82 Atl. 329. 

3. Rowe v. Teed, 15 Ves. Jr. 372, 33 Eng. Rep. 794. 

4. Wooley v. Pemberton (Ct. Ch.), 10 Atl. 159. Such leave may be obtained on application made on notice to the complainant, and may be granted when a 151

6 double plea was filed without leave of court, and if the defect is not objected to, the defect is deemed to be waived.5 A plea raising a single issue which consisted of several or numerous facts or circumstances was not held to be duplicitous. In a leading case in the 

United States Supreme Court, involving a dispute between two states over their boundary line, the rule was followed, and a plea which united the two defenses of an accord and compromise and prescription was held to be bad for duplicity.7 

102. Practice Since 1915. The present Chancery Rules abolish the plea by that name. Every defense heretofore presentable by plea is made by an answer. If the only matter incorporated in the answer is matter that formerly was appropriate for the plea, then the pleading in strictness is called an answer in lieu of plea. Under the practice such an answer is entitled "Answer in lieu of plea." [See FORM 10: Answer (in Lieu of Plea) Setting Up Fraud.] The change is one largely in name, and the answer in lieu of plea is subject to many of the old rules applicable to the plea. Thus the answer in lieu of the plea should not usurp the function of the motion to strike in lieu of demurrer; if the facts on which the defendant rests his defense appear on the face of the bill, the proper mode of defense is by motion and not by answer in lieu of plea.10 The answer will be overruled, as a matter of form, if it merely discloses matters which appear on the face of the bill.11 Formerly it was equally objectionable for the plea to usurp the function of the answer by denying the facts of the bill and setting up an entirely different state of facts covering the whole subjectmatter of the bill.12 The effect of the present rules is to render this double plea will save the defendant inconvenience. Similarly, an answer entitled "in lieu of plea," but setting up two distinct defenses, would not be objectionably duplicitous as under the old practice. It would merely stand as an answer improperly described, and ordinarily misdescription of a pleading is not ground for striking.13 The answer in lieu of plea, like the plea, must still tender an issue on a material allegation; if not material, the answer will be overruled.

It will be noticed that the answer has been substituted for the plea. 

The Chancery Rules say "Every defense" made formerly by plea shall be made by answer. This would seem broad enough to include all manner of pleas-pleas in bar and also pleas in abatement. It should be noted in this connection, that whereas formerly jurisdiction to the person was questioned by plea reciting special appearance, that the practice now is to make this defense by petition for leave to appear specially and to move to quash the service.14 An answer in lieu of the old "plea to the jurisdiction " would be improper, since it would amount to a general appearance.15

The rules applicable to the mode of pleading the case in the bill apply to some extent to the plea. A plea should not be argumentative nor plead a defense in terms of legal conclusions. It is subject to the rules against prolixity, repetition, evasiveness and generalities in denials. Inferences arising from the averments of the plea are not effective as a part of the plea; the plea itself must aver every fact essential to make out a complete defense.42 In fact, averments are necessary to exclude intendments which would otherwise be made against the pleader.43

When the plea is defective in form only and objection is promptly made thereto by motion, it would seem, in lieu of special demurrer,44 limited by the restriction which the Federal Constitution imposes. Hence, when a plea to the jurisdiction of a federal court shows the defendant to be outside of the delegated authority, or such a plea in a state court shows him to be within the restricted class, it becomes unimportant whether any other tribunal can afford the relief sought. Moreover, no such special privilege as was required to oust the general jurisdictions in England exists among us." Wilson v. American Palace Car Co., supra.

105. Affirmative Defenses. 

When a plea sets up usury, the party asserting it has the burden of proof, since usury is an affirmative defense.47 It must be pleaded with precise formality, setting forth specifically the facts and circumstances of the bargain.48 If the answer fails to allege the particular facts and circumstances, it is frivolous and may be stricken on motion.19 [See FORM 14: Answer (in Lieu of Plea) Setting Up 

Usury.] Similarly, the plea of the defendant that he is a bona fide purchaser is an affirmative defense. The defendant should deny the fact of notice and every circumstance from which it can be inferred.50 

Notice must be denied even though it is not charged in the bill. The bona fides of the defendant must be distinctly proved.51 [See FORM 

15: Answer (in Lieu of Plea) Setting Up a Bona Fide Purchase.] 

Other affirmative defenses are: condonation in divorce actions; payment; 53 satisfaction; discharge; and want of consideration.54

106. Kinds of Pleas. 

Pleas under the old practice were classified as: (I) Affirmative pleas; (II) negative pleas, and (III) anomalous pleas. An affirmative plea, sometimes called a pure plea, is the plea which states new matter not apparent on the bill. It proceeds usually on the theory that, admitting the case stated in the bill to be true, the matter suggested by the plea affords a sufficient reason why the complainant should not have the relief he prays.56 A negative plea does not set up new matter. It merely by a denial puts in issue some fact or facts alleged in the complainant's bill and essential to the complainant's case. A typical negative plea is the denial of a partnership when an action for accounting is brought on the theory of a partnership.57 

An anomalous plea is one partly affirmative and partly negative. In an action of account, when the bill charges that the defendant will plead the statute of limitations, but goes on to aver that the defendant fraudulently concealed the claim on which the action of account rests, then a plea by the defendant setting up the statute of limitation and denying the fraud would be both affirmative and negative in character, and therefore anomalous.58 

With the abolition of the plea as such under the present Chancery Rules, the importance of this classification of pleas under the early

Such pleas are commonly classed as anomalous pleas, and must, as a rule where fraud is charged and discovery is sought, be accompanied by an answer in their support, specifically answering such averments of the bill as impute fraud, and making such discovery as the bill may require. 

Such an answer forms no part of the defense, but is a discovery of that evidence which the complainant has a right to require, as complainant is privileged to use such answer as evidence at the argument of the sufficiency of the plea, and also at a hearing to determine the truth of the plea." But an understanding of the differences between pleas under the early practice may be of help to the careful pleader who has some prior knowledge of its function and purport, when he undertakes the draftsmanship of an answer which is strictly in lieu of one type of plea. [See FORM 16: Answer (in Lieu of Plea) Setting Up Denial of Partnership to an Action for an Accounting.] 107. Supporting the Plea by Answer. 

Under the earlier practice, it was not true that the defendant by merely filing a plea could avoid giving discovery. If the bill prayed for discovery and propounded interrogatories, the plea was required to be supported by an answer. Even if the bill did not pray for discovery, but merely asked for an answer to every charge and matter contained in the bill, this might require an answer along with the plea to enable the complainant to make out his claim by means of any admissions the defendant might make.59 It will be noticed the function of the answer is merely to give the discovery and is not made as a defense; thus the rule, that an answer overrules a plea is not applicable.60 Although in the earlier books there were divergent views, it seems that both negative and anomalous pleas were required to be supported by an answer.61 Under the practice of today this old rule that a plea must be supported by an answer is meaningless, because (1) the plea is itself an answer, and (2) the disappearance of discovery is a distinctive feature of the answer.

109. Setting the Plea Down for Argument: An Issue of Law. 

The legal sufficiency of a plea was tested formerly by setting the plea down for argument, or for a hearing. It was a rule that a demurrer was never interposed to a defensive pleading. It thus happened that equity evolved this peculiar practice of setting a plea down for argument in lieu of a demurrer thereto. If the plea were objected to as sham or frivolous, however, a motion to strike the plea was the approved practice.66 Even in the absence of such a motion, the Court of Chancery could sua sponte strike a plea as sham or frivolous.67 65 The hearing of a cause on bill and plea (i.e., setting the plea down for argument) is substantially the same as if the complainant had demurred to the plea.68 Thus the complainant is bound by all the facts of the plea well pleaded.69 But with respect to an affirmative plea, the averments of the bill too, were accepted as true on a hearing on the legal sufficiency of the plea.70 If the plea were negative in character and denied allegations in the bill, then on a hearing on the bill and plea the rule was that the court took the uncontradicted parts of the bill and the allegations of the plea as verities, and decided according to the right upon the case as thus presented. 110. Setting the Plea Down for Argument: Rule of Decision.

111. Replication to the Plea: Rule of Decision.

112. Present Mode of Testing the Answer in Lieu of Plea. 

From the changes in the old practice noticed in the preceding section, it is fairly inferable that a plea is no longer tested by setting it down for argument. The rules provide that any pleading may be objected to by motion on the ground that it discloses no defense in point of law.90 This in effect allows a demurrer to a plea, a substantial change in the old practice.

Several other changes fairly attributable to the Chancery Rules of 1915 may be noted in this connection. As a corollary of the rule that by replying to a plea the complainant could not thereafter question the legal sufficiency of the plea no matter how deficient in point

Another recognized rule of the hearing on the plea under the old practice was that the legal sufficiency of a plea being questioned, the plea could get no help from the answer. That is to say, if the plea did not for example deny the fraud that was alleged in the bill, general denials of fraud in the answer which might have been filed in support of the plea could not be considered as forming a part of the plea, or in any way aiding a plea which did not deny the fraud.92 

The present rules in abolishing pleas and incorporating them in the answer would seem to make the old rule just stated of no importance, or meaningless.

An early case held that if a plea raised a question of jurisdiction of the person, at a hearing on the bill and plea the only things the court should look at were the matters set up in the bill and plea; the court refused to look at the files of the cause to determine whether a subpoena was returned "served" upon the pleading defendants, or whether an order of publication was entered in the cause.93 Questions of defective service are raised now by petition for leave to appear specially and move to quash the service, and it is doubtful to what extent, if any, the rule of the earlier case is still controlling, since pleas as such have been abolished. 

113. Advantage of Answer in Lieu of Plea.

Under the present practice in New Jersey, the defendant may (1) answer fully, and incorporate in the answer as a part thereof the matter pertinent to the plea; or, (2) the defendant may file an answer strictly in lieu of plea. The first mode of procedure has the disadvantage of postponing a hearing on the matter of the plea until a final hearing, unless the Chancellor exercises his discretion, and orders a hearing in advance on the matter of the plea.94 The disad-

114. Function of the Answer. 

Originally the purpose of an answer was threefold: (I) To serve as a defensive pleading in the cause, setting forth in full the defense or defenses of the defendant.¹ (II) To give discovery to the complainant. (III) To serve as evidence. Under the present practice its first function just stated is its important function. Its use to give discovery to the complainant is almost obsolete. Its purpose in standing as evidence in a cause is under the practice negligible, since the sworn answer is rarely filed, and the evidentiary value is now a matter of admissions. These particular functions will be more fully understood by a study of the following sections. 

115. A Sworn Answer as Evidence. 

One of the earliest of the equity powers was the power to compel discovery from a defendant. The procedure was by a bill asking

167 either for discovery only (i.e., a pure bill of discovery) or for discovery as incidental to other equitable relief. In both cases the bill usually would demand an answer under oath, for in no other way could the Chancellor search the defendant's conscience. In actions for discovery only, and not incidental to other relief, a sworn answer was invariably demanded; and in either case the answer, if sworn to, was evidence in the defendant's behalf.2 The two limitations to its value as evidence in the defendant's behalf were: (1) The matter of the answer must be responsive; (2) the matter of the answer sought to be used as evidence must not be nullified by or repugnant to other parts of the answer.³

The practice is generally—and existed in New Jersey before the adoption of the present Chancery Rules, to waive answer under oath.

The defendant must answer fully in such case but not under oath, and in such a case his answer is not evidence in his behalf. The very object of waiving an answer under oath was to overcome that value as evidence for the defendant that the answer would otherwise have.4 

When answer under oath is waived, the filing of a sworn answer is just as if the answer were unsworn.5 And if the complainant waived answer under oath but in the body of the bill addressed interrogatories to the defendant, and the defendant, in spite of the waiver, answered the interrogatories under oath, the answers at the most would constitute ex parte affidavits, which, if read without objection, might be treated as evidence in the cause. Unless the bill specifically prays for answer under oath, it is taken that a sworn answer is not desired.?

In so far as an answer is not responsive its averments must be established by proofs, even though answer under oath was called for and the answer was sworn to. In so far as it was responsive to the bill and interrogatories propounded, it would be evidence for the defendant and require superior testimony to overcome it.8 By superior testimony is meant that such allegations in the answer, being the direct and positive answer of the defendant to the charges of the complainant, must prevail unless overcome by two witnesses, or by

116. Collateral Effects of the Answer. 

18 Formal objections to the frame of a bill are deemed to be waived by the filing of an answer.16 The general rule is stated to be that, having answered, the defendant may not thereafter move to strike the bill.17 Similarly, having answered and gone to a hearing on the merits, an objection that the complainant is without right to sue comes too late.¹ An answer fully to the merits of a bill in chancery submits the defendant fully to the jurisdiction of the court notwithstanding any objections thereto reserved in the answer.19 The answer being a full statement of the defense limits the proof to such defenses as are pleaded; if the defense is not pleaded in the answer, evidence of such defense will not be admitted.20 But when an answer is filed which denies the making of a contract, the suit being one for specific performance, under this general denial, the defendant may prove the statute of frauds, for the plaintiff must prove a legal, enforceable contract; if the answer, however, admits that such a contract was entered into, then it must specifically plead the statute of frauds if evidence of non-compliance with the statute is to be received on the hearing.21

On a hearing, the answer will also serve to limit the evidence; thus the defendant is bound by the defense he undertook in his answer, and will not be permitted at the hearing to use facts offered in substantiation of the defense in the answer to establish a different defense from that which, by his answer, he has drawn the complainant's attention.22 In such a case the proper procedure for the defendant is to ask leave to file an amended answer; in the event of his failure to do so, the defendant will be limited to the defenses set forth in the answer, both in the Court of Chancery and on an appeal.23 vided for in Chancery Rule 84.
