117. Sufficiency of the Answer: Responsiveness. 

A general denial in an answer will not suffice. If a defendant submits to answer, he must answer fully, even though the bill contains no interrogatories, is not a bill for discovery, and waives answer under oath.24 Every material allegation in the bill must be answered. 

And the defendant must answer not only as to his knowledge of each fact so charged, but also, if he have no knowledge as to his information and belief.25 And it will not be sufficient for him to answer merely as to his information; he must also state his belief. As to immaterial facts stated, he is not required to state his belief of those statements. If the defendant has neither knowledge, information nor belief, he must plead the lack in plain, unmistakable words.26 

The reason is that whatever the defendant does not deny amounts to an admission that it is true, or that he does not mean to put it in issue as a part of the controversy of the cause. If the answer is argumentative or evasive, and lacking in the fullness of disclosure required by proper pleading, it will be stricken on motion.28 Under the above rule an answer to a material allegation of a bill, "having no personal knowledge thereof, [the defendant] leaves the said complainant to make such proof as he may be advised," is insufficient.² 27

118. Admissions by Answer. 

38 Admissions contained in the answer are binding on the defendant at the hearing; evidence tending to contradict these admissions, or denials by the defendant of facts admitted in the answer, will not be received in evidence at the hearing.39 Thus, in an action to establish a parol trust in land, an answer which admits the trust but does not claim the benefit of the statute of frauds, establishes the trust; the written answer of the defendant, even though unsigned by him, is regarded as sufficient memorandum for enforcement of the trust in equity.40 An unsworn answer, therefore, is evidence in favor of the complainant in so far as it tends to prove his cause of action by admissions or otherwise; in so far as it is against him, it merely raises issues of fact to be determined at the hearing.41 

If the answer neither admits nor denies, the truth of an allegation is deemed to be admitted.42 This is under the theory that if the defendant admits it, the court will admit it too, and the complainant is not put to proof as to such allegation.43 If the charge is as to a matter within the knowledge of the defendant, with a request for an answer, and the defendant fails either to deny or allude to the matter in his answer, the allegation is deemed to be admitted.4 Such a fact or allegation, when admitted for the purposes of the suit, is a fact of the same cogency as if it had been proved in the cause by uncontradicted testimony.45 Thus by failing to deny the allegations of a bill

Discovery will be compelled when a case for relief is made, although answer under oath be not prayed for. Thus when an action for accounting is brought and discovery is prayed for as incidental thereto, the complainant is entitled to discovery without having prayed for answer under oath.48 If, however, the bill is one of discovery alone, i.e., a pure bill of discovery, the bill cannot as such be sustained unless it prays for answer under oath.4 49 It is equally well settled that the inherent power of equity to afford discovery has not been abrogated by the statutory provisions establishing interrogatories and providing for discovery in that manner; these methods are cumulative and not exclusive.50 It is equally well settled that the authorizing of law courts by statute to grant discovery has not divested the Court of Chancery of its original jurisdiction to grant discovery, the jurisdiction of the two courts in this case being concurrent.51

121. Withdrawing the Answer.

123. Pleading to the Jurisdiction in the Answer. 

Want of jurisdiction in equity, in the sense that an adequate remedy exists at law, may be raised as a defense in the answer.81 In such a case proper pleading requires the defendant to pray the same benefit of the averment of want of jurisdiction as he would have been entitled on demurrer.82 Although, as has previously been stated, the defendant cannot both demur and answer the same part of the bill, yet a demurrer in the answer is proper when the answer and final hearing are necessary to determine accurately the question raised by the demurrer.83 But in so far as the defendant relies on facts stated in the bill which have been answered, such a demurrer must be considered as overruled by the answer, and the questions of law raised by it must be determined on the facts disclosed by the evidence adduced in support of the answer.84 Want of jurisdiction in the sense that the court lacks jurisdiction of the subject-matter may be raised by answer. 

But neither by failing to raise the question, nor by open consent in court could the defendant waive his right to raise this question of lack of jurisdiction of the subject-matter at any later stage of the suit.85 

Want of jurisdiction over the person of the defendant cannot be raised by answer, for an answer is a general appearance, and jurisdiction over the person may be conferred by consent.86 Nor can the rule be obviated by reserving in the answer the benefit of the objection to the jurisdiction of the court over the defendant's person.8

124. Sham or Frivolous Answers.

When an answer is sham or frivolous, a motion may be made on notice to strike the answer for that reason. 88 Such a motion is not in lieu of demurrer. It may, as in case of the plea, be heard on affidavits or other evidence. The statute makes no provision for the taking of evidence but the necessary implication of the statute is that evidence be taken. The universal practice is to deal with sham pleadings in a summary way by affidavits or documentary evidence without waiting for the formality of a hearing.89 The procedure on the motion is regarded as an inquiry as to whether there is a fact issue to be tried, and not a trial of the issue itself on motion.90 Similarly, the court may sua sponte strike an answer as sham. 

The power to strike pleadngs as sham on motion extends only to the defensive pleadings, viz., the answer and plea, and not the offensive pleadings, viz., the bill and counterclaim.91 If part of the answer is sham or frivolous, only that part will be stricken out and not the whole of the answer.92 When an answer is attacked as frivolous, the procedure is the same, i.c., by motion, but the motion is not heard on affidavits, the sufficiency of the answer being determined by inspection in open A motion to strike a frivolous answer admits, for purposes of the motion, the truth of the facts alleged by way of defense, but demands the judgment of the court on their sufficiency as a defense as a matter of law.93 Defenses that are trivial and palpably insufficient legally, and interposed merely for delay, are frivolous, viz., an answer by a defendant setting up usury when the defendant on the facts is estopped to plead the usury; 9 an answer setting up 94 "time as of the essence of a contract," when time was neither expressly nor impliedly made of the essence by the terms of the contract; court. 95 etc.96

125. Exceptions to the Answer. 99 Under the early practice a complainant could except to an answer for scandal, impertinence,¹ multifariousness and other formal defects. 

Exceptions would also lie for insufficiency of answer. By insufficiency is meant lack of responsiveness in the answer,2 and not that the answer fails in point of law to state an equitable defense. Of course, an answer that fails to state a defense is insufficient in a certain sense but not as here used. This legal insufficiency in failing to state a defense was not raised as an issue by exceptions; it was raised by setting the cause for hearing on the bill and answer, which was in effect demurring to the answer. Even before the adoption of the Chancery Rules of 1915,³ a motion had been substituted for exceptions to the answer, i.e., objections based on formal defects and insufficiency (i.e., lack of responsiveness). On a hearing on this motion,5 in lieu of exception, the proceedings were conducted just as if, however, they were proceedings on exceptions. The same would seem to be still true on a hearing on the present motion to strike an answer, provided it is not in lieu of demurrer.

126. Testing the Answer: An Issue of Law. 

From 1886 up and until 1917,13 a Chancery Rule permitted a motion in lieu of demurrer. The cases, however, uniformly held that the rule did not permit a motion to be addressed to the answer, or any part of it, because it failed to set up an equitable defense. The rule as the cases limited it was a substitute merely for an exception to the answer for scandal, lack of responsiveness, etc., and was not intended to allow a demurrer to the answer in the form of a motion. 

The approved procedure in case the complainant desired to demur to the answer was to set the cause for hearing on the bill and answer when all allegations of the answer would be taken to be true.¹¹

THE ANSWER 

181 The present practice with respect to demurring to the answer (or moving to strike in lieu of demurring) is well stated by Chancellor Walker: "Before the passage of the Chancery Act, a motion to strike out an answer on the ground that it disclosed no defense to the relief sought, did not lie. The then rule 213 of this court allowed objections to pleadings to be made by motion and this has been held to be the equivalent of a demurrer to a bill and of exceptions to an answer. Prior to the passage of the Chancery Act (1915), a demurrer to an answer did not lie in any form. 66 The language of the present rule 67 is a clear departure from that of the former rule 213. It is that any pleading may be objected to by motion on the ground that it discloses no cause of action, defense, or counterclaim. By its very terms it extends the motion to strike out to answers, for they are defensive pleadings, and the rule says that a pleading may be objected to because it discloses no defense. 

It must be apparent that the reason that demurrers did not spring into use contemporaneously with the institution of answers in chancery is that originally the complainant in the bill called upon the defendant to answer his allegations and make discovery on oath, and what the defendant set forth was therefore evidence in the cause. 

As the answer was formerly regarded as evidence (and still is, if the bill prays for answer upon oath), there sprung up a method of objecting to defective answers, known as exceptions, and exceptions lay for scandal, impertinence, and insufficiency. While a demurrer to an answer (whether or not under oath), insufficient because it disclosed no defense, might with propriety have long ago been substituted for an exception, the fact is that this departure from precedent was not inaugurated in our state until two years ago. "While the Lord Chancellor in ancient times performed strictly legal functions and held an ordinary legal court, yet the extraordinary court or court of equity-that is, chancery-had become a court of greatest consequence in Blackstone's day. And suits in equity in our state are probably now as numerous as those at law; and the parties litigate here at arm's length upon principles governing their rights residing in the great body of equity jurisprudence, which has been evolved in England and this country, and particularly in this state. There is therefore now as much reason that the defendant, being subpoenaed to answer a bill in chancery, shall set up in his answer a lawful defense to the complainant's claim, if any he have, as that a defendant in a suit at law, summoned to answer the plaintiff's demand, shall set up a valid defense in law. In other words,

there is no longer any reason residing in archaic notions of difference in procedure between courts of equity and of law that renders a demurrer to an answer in chancery inappropriate." "15 From an order entered on a motion to strike an answer, allowing the motion and striking the answer, the defendant may appeal.16 

Similarly, the complainant may appeal an order denying the motion.17 

127. Hearing the Cause on Bill, Answer and Replication: An Issue of Fact. 

The complainant may take issue with the answer on its truth, and by filing a replication, general in form, traverse its essential allegations. The procedure is thereafter to set the cause for hearing in the regular manner, to take evidence in the cause, and submit it thereon. On such a hearing, ie., on the bill, answer and replication, the averments in the answer will be taken as proved only in so far as they are responsive to the bill.18 Allegations that are not responsive, but by way of avoidance, must be established by proofs to be taken as true.19 But an answer, although responsive, is not necessarily, on that account, evidence for the defendant on a hearing on the bill, answer, and replication.20 The answer is deemed to be such only in so far as the responsive allegations go to facts which are within the personal knowledge of the defendant.21 Thus a responsive allegation founded on hearsay is not evidence for the defendant.22

It would seem to have superseded the older practice yet the practice continues to some extent.

130. Function. 

The only relief that a defendant can ask for in his answer is that he be dismissed with costs. If, therefore, he wished affirmative relief against the complainant, under the earlier practice, he must file a separate pleading along with his answer, praying for such relief by way of a cross-action. This separate pleading was known as a crossbill. Even though on the answer it appeared that the defendant was entitled to some affirmative relief, yet none could be accorded until, on leave to file obtained, on application and notice, a crossbill was actually filed seeking such relief.2 

Under the present practice in New Jersey, the counterclaim incorporated in and as a part of the answer has been substituted for the

132. Leave of Court to File. 

If a crossbill was filed at the time of filing of the answer to the original bill, or before replication has been made thereto, it was filed as of course without leave of court.26a If, however, after answer and a hearing, the defendant wished to file a crossbill, even though it was evident that he was entitled to affirmative relief, he would have on application and notice, first to obtain the leave of court to file the same under the old practice.26 Under the present practice in New 

Jersey, the defendant would necessarily file his counterclaim with the answer, for the counterclaim is a part of the answer. Should the defendant wish to incorporate in his answer a counterclaim, the answer already being filed, it would be a question of amending the answer, and subject in general to the rules relating to the amendment of pleadings allowing pleading out of time.26c But a party who is a stranger, a mere volunteer, with no interest in the pending cause, has no right to file a counterclaim, and the same will be stricken out on motion.20d

134. Must be Germane to the Original Bill. 

A requirement well recognized in the early practice in numerous cases was that the new matter set up in the crossbill must be germane to the original bill, related thereto, or arising out of the same transaction; and not foreign thereto-constituting a cause distinct from and unconnected with the complainant's cause of action.31 V. C. 

Stevens: "The crossbill is auxiliary to the proceeding in the original suit and dependent upon it." 32 V. C. Van Fleet: "The new facts which it is proper for a defendant to introduce into a pending litigation, by means of a crossbill, are such, and such only, as it is necessary for the court to have before it, in deciding the questions raised in the original suit, to enable it to do full and complete justice to all the parties before it in respect to the cause of action on which the complainant rests his right to aid or relief. If a defendant, in filing a crossbill, attempts to go beyond this, and to introduce new and distinct matter, not essential to the proper determination of the matter put in litigation by the original bill, although he may show a perfect case against the plaintiff or one or more of his co-defendants, his pleading will not be a crossbill, but an original bill." 38 Without this restriction, new matters might be introduced into a litigation, without end.34

This requirement is unaffected by the Chancery Rules of 1915. 

Although Rule 28 permits the defendant to counterclaim "any cause of action against the complainant," yet this rule is circumscribed by Rule 70, which permits only matter, "the proper subject of a crossbill" under the previous practice, to be set up by counterclaim.35 It may be taken, then, as settled, under the present Chancery Rules, that the counterclaim must, as heretofore, be germane to the original

135. What is Germane. 

38 In determining whether the matter of a counterclaim is germane to the original bill, no precise rule can be stated. It has been held that in a suit against an executor for a legacy the executor could properly show by way of counterclaim that the complainant had received funds from collecting a life insurance policy payable to the estate, sufficient to pay the legacy sued for; in an action by a mortgagee against a grantee, for a deficiency, usury in the mortgage is pleaded by way of counterclaim;39 that in a suit for specific performance of a contract to sell land, the defendants denying the contract could, as legatees, to whose legacies the land has been devised subject, demand the sale of the land by crossbill.40

In matrimonial causes, to an action for separate maintenance by the wife, the husband may counterclaim for absolute divorce.41 Similarly, to a petition for divorce, the defendant may cross-petition by counterclaim, for divorce, and for settlement of rights arising from a joint bank account.42 In foreclosure, the matter of counterclaiming independent and unrelated set-offs not germane to the bill is controlled by a special statutory provision hereinafter considered in detail.43 In other chancery actions, counterclaiming independent setoffs would be excluded under the rule that they are not germane to the cause stated in the bill. But where the cross-demand arises out of the transaction which gives rise to the cause stated in the bill (i.e., strictly matters of recoupment and not set-off), such cross-demands, whether liquidated or unliquidated, are allowable as a matter of inherent power of chancery.44

136. Must Raise Matter of Equitable Jurisdiction. 

Another rule early applied to the crossbill was that the crossbill, like the bill of complaint, must present matter strictly cognizable in a court of equity,-a matter of equitable jurisdiction.47 Thus, in an action to quiet title under the Act of 1870, the defendant may properly counterclaim a suit to set aside certain conveyances as fraudulent, both actions being strictly equitable in character.48 But a cause of action for which a cross-complainant would not be entitled to file an original bill cannot be enforced by a crossbill.49 So a crossbill setting up a purely legal claim, such as one for unliquidated damages for breach of contract, will be stricken out on motion as seeking to introduce matter not within the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery.50 

Like the original, so the crossbill was demurrable, or subject to the modern counterpart of the demurrer-the motion to strike, in case it disclosed a cause of action for which there existed an adequate remedy at law.51 By way of statutory exception to this rule is a legal title of the defendant asserted in an action to quiet title under the Act

139. Effect of Dismissal of the Original Bill on the Counterclaim. 

The rule is that ordinarily the dismissal of the original bill of complaint carries with it the dismissal ipso facto of the counterclaim. 

The rule as thus stated contemplates a counterclaim, or crossbill, filed merely as a means of defense. A counterclaim of this character must be distinguished, however, from one which seeks for the defendant affirmative relief, and not mere discovery in aid of the defense. So there is this exception to the rule that when affirmative relief is sought by the counterclaim against the complainant, the dismissal of the original bill does not carry with it the dismissal of the cross-action by way of counterclaim. When such relief is sought the crossbill will be retained for the purpose of affording the appropriate relief, but the counterclaim must exhibit a cause of action cognizable in a court of equity, otherwise the court would not be justified in retaining it.75

When a counterclaim is accompanied by interrogatories, and the complainant undertakes to answer thereto, but does not answer fully, the complainant may on motion dismiss the original bill with costs, but a motion to dismiss the cross-action will be overruled.76 The answer to the crossbill, of course, stands and there must be further answer, under the general rule governing the answer, that if a defendant submits to answer he must answer fully.77

The rule that the dismissal of the original bill by the complainant does not carry with it the dismissal of the counterclaim which prays for affirmative relief, save with the consent of the defendant, was

140. Defects of the Counterclaim. 

A crossbill which merely sets up matter which the defendant may make equally available and effectual as a defense by answer, is defective; for in such case the crossbill is not only unnecessary but useless. 

The only purpose it could serve in such a case would be to incumber the record and add to the expense of the litigation.81 Such a crossbill upon amendment would stand as the answer.82 A crossbill may be stricken on motion on the ground that it is objectionably multifarious, or involves a misjoinder of parties.8 83

142. Parties. 

A counterclaim may be directed at and make as defendants (1) the complainant in the cause, (2) a co-defendant or co-defendants, (3) outside parties whose interests are affected by the matter of the counterclaim and who must be brought in as parties. It was settled before the Chancery Rules of 1915 that outside parties may be made parties defendant to a crossbill,89 and it has been recently determined that there is no good reason why the same practice should not prevail where the counterclaim is substituted for the crossbill.90 Outside parties who are brought in a cause on counterclaim are called third parties." Against them subpoena must issue, the cause regularly matured as to them, they having the usual twenty days after the service of the subpoena within which time they may file an answer. 

Separate hearings may be ordered as to the counterclaim and third parties within the discretion of the court, and in any case in which the counterclaim cannot be conveniently disposed of in the pending action the court may strike it out.91 If the counterclaim fails to make as 66

144. Permissive or Mandatory.

In certain cases in actions at law the filing of a counterclaim is mandatory, and a failure of the defendant to counterclaim such claims will preclude the defendant from suing on them later. No such rule obtains in any case in equity practice in New Jersey, for the filing of a counterclaim seems to be in all cases a permissive mode of proceeding; failure to counterclaim, therefore, in equity procedure would not preclude a subsequent action on the matter that might have been counterclaimed.8 It would seem to be within the discretion of the court to order such matter to be raised on the pleadings, and additional parties that are necessary be brought in, if the defendant's failure to counterclaim would otherwise prevent a complete and final adjudication of the pending cause.

146. The Replication. 

A cause is brought on to a hearing on the proofs by the filing of a general replication traversing the answer, in the form that is provided for in the Chancery Rules.¹ The time for filing the replication is ten days, but the making of a motion to strike the answer suspends the time for replying.2 The time fixed for filing the replication may, as in other cases, be extended by the Chancellor for good cause shown. For failure to file a replication, the bill may be dismissed.* 

If the omission to file is inadvertent, the court may give leave to file same nunc pro tunc even after the hearing. If the complainant persists in failing to file a replication, the court may, on the defendant's motion to dismiss the bill for want of prosecution, put the complainant on terms. the bill may be dismissed for manifest default in pleading and inaction.5

The effect of the replication is to deny and put in issue every allegation of the answer not responsive to the bill including matters of avoidance set up in the answer. It also operates to prevent the complainant from thereafter objecting to the answer for insufficiency, scandal, and other formal defects, for upon the filing of the replication, it will be assumed that the defendant has answered fully and in proper form.

New matter may be set up in a replication only in two cases: First, when the answer sets up matter unanticipated by the complainant, to which he now wishes to plead other matter by way of avoidance, and only in this case upon leave of court; second, in answer to a counterclaim by the defendant. If a special replication is defective in form, it may be stricken on motion.10

Under the earlier practice, if the complainant joined in the answer on an issue of fact, he was thereafter precluded from raising on the answer an issue of law, no matter how deficient in point of law the answer might be. To overcome this rule, V. C. Garrison allowed the complainant to withdraw his replication.11 The present practice would permit this procedure in the interest of substantial right and justice.12 Withdrawal of replication would also be allowed to enable the complainant to amend his bill on leave granted by court.13

Ch. Magie: "This application, and others of similar nature, seem to require me to express my views upon the proper practice, and the power and duty of the Chancellor to intervene and to decline to act upon the advice of vice chancellors. The introduction of vice chancellors into our system of chancery jurisprudence arose from legislation based on the ancient right of the Chancellor to call upon the masters of his court for their advice as to his action in

denying an application for a rehearing;36 (c) in conviction by a vice causes and proceedings pending before him. When that legislation was first adopted, the business of the court had outgrown the power of the Chancellor to dispose of alone. For the purpose of enabling the court to deal with the increasing business therein, the Legislature gave authority to the Chancellor to appoint an officer, to be called a vice chancellor, to whom he might refer causes for trial, and who might try the causes thus referred upon evidence orally taken, and was required to report to the Chancellor his opinion, and advise what decree should be made therein. As the business of the court still further increased, the Legislature, with wise liberality, from time to time has authorized the appointment of additional vice chancellors, and by this system the Court of Chancery has practically been enabled to keep pace with its business. The utility of the system has been established in its existence of over thirty years, and its recognition by all departments of the state government, executive, legislative, and judicial, has given it a sanction beyond dispute or question. The legislation on this subject has not attempted to deprive, and it could not constitutionally deprive, the Chancellor of his right to make the decrees of his court. [See Ch. Walker's opinion, In re Vice Chancellors, 148 

Atl. 570.] Obviously, however, the purpose of this legislation could not, at the time it was originally adopted, and certainly cannot now, be made effective and useful in conducting the business of the court, if the Chancellor should deem himself compelled to review the opinion and advice of every vice chancellor in every case, on the mere demand of a party thereto. In all ordinary cases it is essential to the conduct of the business of the court that the Chancellor should decline to revise the opinion of a vice chancellor or to refuse to follow his advice, and this, in my judgment, was the plain intent of the legislation. Parties may well in such cases be left to obtain relief by review of the decree by appeal. "Yet I deem it equally obvious that there are, or may be, exceptional cases, in which it would be the duty of the Chancellor to review the conclusions reached by a vice chancellor, and to consider whether or not his advice should be followed. I can conceive of only two classes of such cases: One class, I think, would be composed of cases in which the decree advised is based upon a principle, or the conclusion reached is by a course of practice in direct opposition to previous decisions of the Chancellor, or of some vice chancellor whose advice has been acted upon by the Chancellor. The obvious reason is that the 

Court of Chancery must speak with one voice, and not discordantly. Another class would be composed of certain cases in which a rehearing has been applied for. Before the introduction of vice chancellors such an application was made directly to the Chancellor, and was dealt with by him on equitable principles, and the practice was regulated by rules of the court. Since vice chancellors have been made trial judges, the practice, on application for the rehearing of causes in which decrees have been signed on the advice of a vice chancellor, was pointed out by a rule of court which was promulgated in 1871, and is now Rule 148 [128]. 

If it is made to appear to the Chancellor that a rehearing has been practically denied by a vice chancellor, and that such denial deprives a party of the opportunity of presenting the case on an issue made by the pleadings, and thereby produces an injury which cannot be relieved by an appeal, it would seem that the Chancellor ought to intervene to the extent of protecting the objecting party from the consequences. There may be other cases in which the Chancellor ought to act, but I cannot discover any."

151. Reference to a Master. 

The reference to a vice chancellor is general; that to a master specifies the subjects upon which he is to inquire and report. Masters are of two kinds: (a) advisory, and (b) special. A master's authority is limited and controlled by the order of reference, and he is confined to the directions of such order.39 Thus a reference to report on the sum due one mortgagee, does not include the power to report on sums due another mortgagee and it would be irregular for the master to so report. 40 If the master files a report himself, or parts with it by delivering it to the solicitor of the complainant for filing, his authority is thereby terminated, and he cannot, thereafter, recall the case to himself, take further proceedings, and make a supplemental report.41 A master cannot delegate any of his authority to another but the use of the services of an expert accountant is not a violation of this rule.42 Masters in Chancery are appointed at the pleasure of the Chancellor and hold commission from him. CHANCERY PRACTICE IN New Jersey 153. Exceptions to a Master's Report. 

A master's report may be objected to by the filing of exceptions thereto.55 A hearing on exceptions is in the nature of a review, or an appeal from the master to the Court of Chancery. Ordinarily, the vice chancellor to whom the cause was originally referred, reviews and determines the validity of the exceptions.56 In matters of computation the report should show on its face the way the master arrived at his conclusion, so far as to enable the court to determine from the report itself whether his method was right or not.57 On exceptions to a master's report the only thing that can be considered is the validity of those exceptions, and the propriety of the reference cannot be considered because that is presumed to have been considered and determined when the reference was made.58 Where the evidence sharply conflicts, the rule of decision is to confirm the finding of the master who had first-hand opportunity to hear and value the evidence, unless he erred as to a matter of law, or plainly, as to the facts.59 When, however, the master's findings are based on a misconception of the law, the exception to his findings will be sustained.60

On a hearing on the exceptions, the burden of proof is on the exceptant.61 Where there is the slightest evidence of improper dealings between the master and the successful side, and the dealings have a tendency to influence his action, the master's report will be set aside.62

154. The Order of Confirmation. 

Ordinarily in the absence of exceptions to the report of the master, it will be confirmed. 155. The Kinds of Decrees. 

Remittitur.

Decrees are classified as: (I) Interlocutory, (II) Final. They may also be classified as: (I) Appealable, (II) Non-Appealable. 

An order in a cause is in a sense a decree; it is merely a decree of lesser importance going usually to routine matters in the conduct of the suit, viz., an order of reference, an order of designation. They are interlocutory in character. Decrees go to some decisive adjudication with respect to the substantial merits of the suit. An interlocutory decree is a decree entered in a pending chancery action and prior to final disposition which does not dispose of the whole merits of the cause but leaves important questions for further examination and future judgment of the court.¹ Orders and decrees relative to pleadings and adjudications incidental to the suit, are interlocutory in character.2 A final decree is the decree entered on the final hearing.³ There can be but one final decree in a given cause, no matter how numerous the parties or the issues. But on separable and distinct issues in one cause, final decrees on one or more issues may be entered separately.5 A decree in equity may be in character interlocutory as to some of the parties to the cause and final as to others: viz., the so-called interlocutory decree in a bill of interpleader. 

Ordinarily, however, only one final decree is entered in a cause, whereas a number of interlocutory orders may be entered. The most important distinction between interlocutory and final orders

lies in the different time for appeal allowed in each case, viz., forty days on an interlocutory order, and one year on a final decree.7 

A decree is a judicial decision of a litigated cause entered in a court of equity; the word decree is also applied to the determination of causes in admiralty and probate courts; a judgment in a strict sense is applied to the decisions of a law court, although it may be accurately used in a broad sense to include the decisions of the courts of law and equity.S

An order nunc pro tunc (now for then) is entered to supply some omission in the record of an order which was actually made but omitted, its function being to correct the mistake so as to make the record show the order as of the time when it was actually made.⁹ 

The power to enter orders nunc pro tunc cannot be exercised for the purpose of giving effect to a mandate of the court as of a time anterior to that when the order was in reality made.10 

The power to correct a decree, nunc pro tunc as to clerical errors, errors of form or mistakes in the drafting of decrees, as distinguished from judicial errors, is not affected by a pending appeal from the decree so corrected.11 Other kinds of decrees are, decrees nisi,12 consent decrees,¹ decrees pro confesso,14 etc.

158. The Final Decree. 

The final decree of the Court of Equity is often alluded to as a judgment, the two words in this respect being synonymous in spite of some marked distinctions between judgments at law and in equity.50 The Court of Chancery is a court of record and its decrees are pleadable in bar of another suit between the same parties for the same cause.51 A chancery order entered after due notice to all parties in interest, is res adjudicata until reversed or modified and cannot be collaterally impeached by parties or their privies.52 A final decree of the Court of Chancery has the same force, operation

159. Conformity. 

A decree in chancery must conform to the case as presented on the pleadings, as well as to the proofs.63 A decree that does not conform will be reversed on appeal.64 Not only that but such a decree as to matters not set up in the pleadings is void even in collateral proceedings.65 It should be noted that the old rule requiring a prayer for general, if relief other than that specially prayed for is to be granted, has been changed by the present Chancery Rules; any appropriate relief may be accorded under a prayer only for special relief. A complainant is not entitled, therefore, to relief that is not comprehended within either the allegations or prayers of the bill, or facts proven at the trial." 67

But after a decree has been enrolled, the Court of Chancery will not vary or alter it in a material point except upon a bill of review or a rehearing. It will, however, on petition amend an enrolled decree when the amendment is necessary to give full expression to its judgment, and is matter which without doubt, would have been incorporated in the decree when made, if attention had been called to it.70

225 decree, although they may be stated in the recital preceding the decretal paragraph, or may be omitted entirely.76 But there should be an adjudication in a decree of the rights to which a party or parties are entitled. This does not include negative adjudications against a complainant on which he is unsuccessful; it is only necessary that a general adjudication in favor of the defendant, so far as he is successful, need be made, unless of course there are specific matters to be awarded to him, and which cannot appropriately be the subject matter of an omnibus adjudication.77

In the ordering part of the decree it is usual to recite that the decree is made upon motion of counsel naming them, for the party entering the decree. If the decree is in part only for the complainant, being negative substantially in favor of the defendant, then it ought not recite that it is made on motion of complainant's counsel when, in truth, it is not. Nor should a decree contain alternate recitals of motions made on behalf of complainants and defendants, naming counsel as moving for the respective parties. It should merely recite in the presence of counsel, but not on the motion of counsel.78

Decrees in general consist of four parts: (1) The date and title; (2) the recitals; (3) the declaratory part, if any; (4) the ordering or mandatory part.79 Under the Chancery Act it is provided that the decree shall not contain any recitals from the bill, answer, or other pleading.80 The evidence is never set out in the decree, although the facts proved are generally and always properly, stated. Final decrees in equity do not, to be valid, have to show on their face that all jurisdictional requirements have been complied with. In a decree in chancery, there need not be, furthermore, in the ordering or mandatory part, an adjudication of the existence of facts warranting the making of such decree, although they may be stated in the recitals preceding the decretal paragraph, or may be omitted entirely. It is usual and proper, and the better practice, however, to set out sufficiently the findings of the court in the recital part of the decree, and if omitted, the omission may in the discretion of the Chancellor be supplied by an amendment.81

162. The Decree as a Conveyance. 

Section 45 82 of the Chancery Act provides that where a decree shall be made for a conveyance of land and the party against whom the decree is entered fails to comply therewith within the time appointed in such decree,83 then the decree shall be taken to have the same operation and effect as if an actual conveyance had been executed conformably to such decree. This operates in spite of any disability, such as infancy, lunacy, or coverture.84 Nor does the pendency of an appeal to the Court of Errors and Appeals operate to prevent the application of the statute.85 The effect of the statute is to work a transfer of the legal title both at law and in equity whereas formerly and independent of the statute, the decree operated only in personam.86 Although the statute applies alike to conveyances both of personal 87 and real property, its most usual application in the practice is to decrees directing conveyances of land by the vendor in suits for specific performance of a contract for the sale thereof brought by the vendee.88 The statute, however, has no application to a decree entered in a suit by the vendor, directing that the vendee take title, and decreeing specific performance in favor of the vendor, when the vendee is unwilling to comply and refuses to obey 82. 1 C. S., p. 426, § 45. The statute also applies to a release or an acquittance. For a history of the statute which goes back to 1799, see Amparo 

Mining Co. v. Fid. Tr. Co., 74 N. J. Eq. 197, 71 Atl. 605; Hannan v. Wilson, 101 N. J. Eq. 743, 139 Atl. 165.

Naugle, 97 N. J. Eq. 110, 127 Atl. 263. See FORM 137: Decree for Conveyance in Suit for Specific Performance.

163. Duty of Obedience: Contempt in General. 

When a decree has been entered in a cause, it is a party's first duty to obey the decree, for it is a principle of law that a party who does not obey the decree cannot take any steps to be relieved of the decree by vacating the same.93 Even when a decree is improvidently entered, or irregularly obtained, it is not open to any party to question it by disobedience; it must be respected until it is annulled or set aside by proper authority on direct proceedings brought for that purpose.94 

The fact that a decree is founded on error of law or fact is no excuse for not obeying it.95 The lack of jurisdiction to enter the order may be shown, however, and that hence there was in legal effect no order.96 A person may be in the position of a contemnor of court by

164. Duty of Obedience (Continued): Effect of an Appeal. 

Whether or not, an appeal to the Court of Errors and Appeals suspends the duty to obey a decree of the Court of Chancery, depends on the nature of the decree appealed from.¹ If the decree is prohibitory in character, or if the object of the decree "is the preservation of a status quo on which the determination of the appeal may act effectively," the decree stands even though appealed from.2 If, on the other hand, the decretal order, or injunction, by whatever name known, calls for an alteration in the status of the parties as previously existing, the effect of the appeal is to suspend the operation of the decree and the duty of obedience. Within this latter rule would fall a mandatory injunction even though prohibitory in form, a decree of specific performance, an injunction prohibiting the continuance of a going business, etc. If the defendant desires to obtain from the Court of Chancery a dissolution of the injunction not appealable. 165. Justification of Contempt: Defective Service: Etc. 

The duty to obey a decree presupposes (a) valid service on the defendant of the decree or order disobeyed, or, (b) notice or knowledge of the decree. Notice to be sufficient must (a) proceed from a source entitled to credit, and (b) inform the defendant clearly and plainly from what act he must abstain.10 With respect to valid service as an excuse for non-obedience or disobedience of a decree, an important distinction is to be observed between disobedience of a mandatory and prohibitory order; in the former case, knowledge or notice of the order is not sufficient to create a duty of obedience; the order must be served by the exhibition of the original order and not merely by the delivery of a certified copy.11 Whereas in cases of prohibitory orders, the defendant will be found guilty of contempt if notice or knowledge of the decree be established.12

166. Direct and Consequential Contempts Distinguished. 

Contempts may be either (a) direct, or (b) consequential. Direct contempts are those usually referred to as contempts in the face of the court, i.e., in facie curiae, but this does not mean that such contempts must necessarily be committed while the judge is presiding in open session in the courtroom.20 It may be a contemptuous interference with judicial proceedings in which the judge is acting as judicial officer.21 Consequential contempts are those which do not openly insult or resist the powers of the court, or the persons of the judges, but which without such gross insolence and direct opposition, The lack of intention in a servant to contemn a decree as between the master and servant may be a ground of exculpating the servant, but of course not the master. The distinction between these two kinds of contempts is important in two particulars: (a) In direct criminal contempts, in facie curiae, there is no right of appeal, whereas a right of appeal does exist in cases of all indirect contempts not in facie curiae.23 (b) Furthermore, in cases of contempts in facie curiae the court may proceed to adjudge and punish in a summary manner without notice and without a hearing, whereas in consequential contempts, the defendant is usually entitled to a hearing on a reference with the safeguards as to taking of evidence, cross-examinations, etc., that attend the usual criminal hearing.24 

167. Civil and Criminal Contempts Distinguished. 

Contempts may be further classified as, (a) civil, and (b) criminal.25 A civil contempt in the Court of Chancery is a remedial step in a cause for the coercion of one party for the benefit of the other.26 

A criminal contempt, however, is not remedial nor a step in a prior cause the proceedings are independent of the prior litigation, punitive in character, in which the alleged contemnor is entitled to all the substantial rights of a person accused of crime that are consistent with the summary nature of the process of the tribunal in which it is administered.27 Proceedings to punish for criminal contempt must be brought as a separate cause and failure to do so is a fatal procedural infirmity.28 The pleadings, or cause, is entitled: "In Chancery of New Jersey. Aside from the procedural differences between civil and criminal contempt heretofore explained, the real substantial difference lies in the nature of the order contemned: if the order is an affirmative one to do an act commanded (i.e., a mandatory injunction) which is remedied by imprisonment until the party perform the required act, then the contempt is a civil contempt.41 In such a case, the contemnor can liberate himself from prison at any time by doing the act commanded, and thus "as quaintly put," the imprisoned man "carries the keys to his prison in his own pocket.” 42 On the other hand, if the order be prohibitory in nature, i.e., forbidding the doing of an act, and the order is violated, the contempt is an affront to the dignity of the court; in such a case the imprisonment would be for a definite term, the contemnor could not by performance liberate himself, and the contempt would be criminal.43 It is an offense against organized society which although it arises in the course of private litigation, is not a part thereof, but like any other criminal offense, raises an issue between the public and the accused.44 The jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to convict for contempts criminal in character is inherent, existing in every superior court of record, and under the Constitution of 1844, the legislature cannot constitutionally deprive the Court of Chancery of this jurisdiction.45

170. Reference in Contempt Proceedings. 

Under section 140 of the Chancery Act, it is provided that whenever a person is cited for contempt of any order issued out of the Court of Chancery, or for contempt of the court, the citation shall be referred for hearing to a vice chancellor other than the one by whom the original order of restraint was issued. Expressly excepted, however, from this rule are orders (1) which relate to specific performance of contracts or enforcement of covenants, or (2) relate to restraining an action at law, or (3) trespass upon land, or (4) restraining waste, or (5) concerning the administration of trusts, or (6) writs of habeas corpus, or (7) for the payment of alimony, or concerning other domestic relations relating to the care and custody of children, or (8) the relations between husband and wife.12

The usual procedure for enforcing the payment of a fine for contempt, outside of the coercive effect of the imprisonment, is by a writ of sequestration.15 In case an order to pay a sum of money is contemned, and the contemnor is imprisoned, it may not be a violation of the constitutional prohibition of imprisonment for debt "unless in cases of fraud.” 16

In suits by the vendor against a vendee for specific performance, the practice is not to enforce the decree against a recalcitrant vendee by contempt process, the reason being the constitutional prohibition against imprisonment for debt.¹7 

A corporation in contempt can be punished only by fine, but the responsible officers if duly convicted, can be punished by imprisonment for their own contempt.18 Where no want of intention or effort on their part to secure obedience to a decree can be imputed to the officers, failure to secure obedience is visited on the corporation, and not the officers personally.19

176. Enforcement of Decree: Writ of Fi. Fa. 

Originally the Court of Chancery could enforce its decrees only in personam, because there were no other means. Now, however, writs of execution may issue out of the Court of Chancery against the personal or real property of the defendant with like force and effect as those issuing out of the Supreme Court.35 Decrees in equity for the payment of money may be enforced against the judgment debtor by the usual writ of fieri facias directed either to a sheriff or a master in chancery. When the land to be sold under the writ is situated in two counties, the practice is to direct the sale by a master.3 

But unless the Chancellor shall order otherwise for good reasons presented to him, every execution shall be directed to a sheriff. 36

178. Statutory Sequestration of Assets of a Non-Resident. 

In 1919 by supplement to the Chancery Act86a it was enacted that in any action in which a money decree is sought against a defendant, and it is made to appear by affidavit that the defendant is a nonresident and has property within this state, the court may upon the bill or petition, or at any time thereafter, issue a writ of sequestration directed to the sheriff to take into his possession such property and hold it subject to the orders of the court.8 The purpose of this statute is to create in chancery an analogous procedure to that existing at law under the Attachment Act.88 The action is quasi in rem;' service on the absent defendant may be by publication, and its constitutionality with reference to the "due process clause has been 87

249 sustained. The statute is remedial in purpose and is to be liberally construed.90 It contains no limitation on the type of equitable action in which the writ may issue other than that a money decree must be sought.91 It issues whether the amount demanded is certain or uncertain.92 It issues in favor of a resident or a non-resident, on a claim arising within or without the state.93 The suit begins as one quasi in rem.

Should the defendant enter a general appearance, the effect is to transform the suit into one commenced by subpoena: it proceeds thereafter as a suit in personam, remaining, however, a suit quasi in rem as to the property seized under the writ of sequestration.94 In such a suit the writ of sequestration stands as a summons; it acquires jurisdiction against the defendant to the extent that a decree in the action may operate against the property seized and also by bringing the defendant into court to give bond to secure the release of the property sequestered, the defendant appears generally.95 The defendant may, however, appear specially and move to quash the writ.96 In such event, the procedure is by petition for leave to appear specially, and on order obtained, the defendant may move to set aside or quash the writ.97 A special appearance entered without prior leave of court amounts to a general appearance.⁹8 

Similarly, a motion to strike or dismiss the bill would be a general appearance.99 The writ of sequestration binds real estate in the state from the time of its recordation in the Supreme Court; in the county, from the time of its recordation in the office of the county clerk.¹

180. Writ Ne Exeat. 

The function of a writ ne exeat is to maintain the presence of the defendant within the state for the purpose of keeping him amenable to the orders and decrees of the Court of Chancery and thus securing the practical application of legal process.18 The writ, both in its body and by indorsement thereon, 19 fixes the sum for which the defendant is to give security, and if he fails to do so, directs the sheriff to take the defendant into custody.20 A bond of this nature in chancery is held to be the equivalent in legal import to bail furnished at common law to the sheriff to insure the appearance of the defendant to answer the suit, and therefore is considered as equitable bail.21. The condition of the bond 22 as required by Chancery Rules is that the defendant cause his appearance to be entered in the suit, and continue such appearance by a solicitor of this court, residing in this state; and shall at all times render himself amenable to the orders and process of this court and shall appear before this "' 23 The writ issues out court "6 when so required 

18. Foote v. Foote, 102 N. J. Eq. 291, 140 Atl. 312, rev'g 101 N. J. Eq. 122, 137 Atl. 851.

Originally designed to restrain the subject from departing the realm (ne exeat republica, let him not go out from the republic) so that he might be able to respond to the demands of the king in the event of war, it was later applied by the Court of Chancery to secure appearance of a defendant to answer process in a civil cause. Foote v. Foote, supra; 19 R. C. L. 134.

The effect of the failure thus to indorse the writ seems not to have been considered in any New Jersey cases with reference to a ne exeat bond and indorsement. But under § 26 of the Divorce Act a bond with indorsement as in cases of ne exeat bonds is required on a writ of sequestration, and it was held that the failure to indorse the writ as required by the statute rendered the writ not void but voidable at the instance of the person against whom the writ was directed. Applications to the vice chancellors may be heard without order of reference.42 The writ may issue on application even before the bill is filed and no suit is pending.43 In all cases the demand must be supported by affidavits for the Chancery Act 44 requires "satisfactory proof" that the defendant "designs quickly to depart from this state." The affidavit of the petitioner alone is sufficient if its facts disclose that the defendant's departure will defeat the claim, and also that the defendant intends to leave the state.45 This intention may be disclosed by threats or declarations of such intention, or facts evincing it. But mere apprehension that the defendant is about to leave will not warrant the issuance of the writ.47 It is not necessary that the defendant be actually within the state when the application for the writ is made, nor is it necessary that he be a resident of the state. 48

When the writ issues against a non-resident temporarily within the state, it is not necessary that it appear that he intends to depart the jurisdiction, if it be shown that his departure will defeat the suit.49

255 The procedure in moving against a surety for the payment of the penalty of a defaulted ne exeat bond is a summary proceeding by a petition for an order to show cause served upon the surety.62 The bond is not breached, however, by failure of the defendant to perform all the orders or decrees in the cause; it is breached only when the defendant does not remain amenable to jurisdiction.63 The sureties, when sued thereon, cannot defend that the bond is not in strict conformity with the rule of the court.64 Nor are they discharged by entry of a final decree, nor by reason of the fact that the defendant is in custody for failure to comply therewith.65 Nor may the sureties secure their discharge by the surrender of their principal.66 If, however, after the giving of the ne exeat bond, the bill is amended to state a new and different cause of action than that set out in the original bill, the surety on the ne exeat bond is entitled to an order cancelling and surrendering the bond.07 Also in the event a more stringent bond is given than is required by the Chancery Rules, it is within the province of the court to determine whether on breach thereof, the bond will be declared forfeited.68 

Process of contempt cannot be used to enforce payment by the surety where no special equities exist, for the ultimate result of contempt proceedings is imprisonment which falls in this situation under the constitutional ban against imprisonment for debt unless in cases of fraud.69

writ is sometimes called "equitable ejectment" since it operates to dispossess one in possession of land. It issues out of chancery as a matter of inherent power and practice without regard to any statutory authority.72 Its issuance is allowed on the principle "that a court of equity will, when it can do so justly, carry its own decrees into full execution without relying on the co-operation of any other tribunal." 73

The granting of the writ is addressed to the sound discretion of the court never to be exercised in a case of doubt.74 

Nor will it issue to try a question of legal title to land.75 Its denial, however, is to be based on some reasonable ground in equity,76 viz., when purchaser's title is derived through a sale conducted under suspicious circumstances," or, when the property sold was insufficiently advertised,78 or, because of a waiver or estoppel against the petitioner arising from more than mere delay or lapse of time in applying for the writ.79 If the writ is denied, appeal may be taken to the Court of Errors and Appeals.80

187. Award of Costs and Counsel Fees. 

The award of costs is within the discretion of the Court of Chancery.13 When awarded, payment of costs may be enforced by a writ of fieri facias or capias ad satisfaciendum, or by subpoena and attachment.14 But no execution shall issue for costs unless by special order of court.15 Where costs are directed to be paid by an interlocutory order which cannot be enforced by execution, payment may be enforced by writ of attachment for contempt; if awarded as incidental to the final decree in the cause, payment can be enforced only by those methods which the law designates for the enforcement of the decree itself.16 Under Section 84 of the Chancery Act, the statute formerly permitted the award of costs only to the successful party to the suit,17 but by the Supplement of 1915, costs may be awarded the unsuccessful party against the successful party in any

188. Appeal: In General. 

The right of appeal from the Court of Chancery to the Court of Errors and Appeals is created by statute and confirmed by the Constitution of New Jersey.53 Appeal proceedings, therefore, must be within the time fixed by the statute, to-wit, within forty days from an interlocutory decree,54 and within one year from a final decree.55

189. Who May Appeal: The Party Aggrieved.

190. Non-Appealable and Appealable Decrees. 

Appeal lies only from decrees and orders that are appealable; if an order or decree pertains to the routine conduct of a chancery suit and is addressed to the discretion of the court, not affecting the substantial rights of the parties, it is a non-appealable decree.84

191. Effect of Appeal. 

The Chancery Rules provide (a) that an appeal from an interlocutory order does not stay proceedings in the cause without an order of either the Court of Chancery or the Court of Errors and Appeals;13 (b) that an appeal from a final decree stays process on such decree obviating the necessity for any special order staying execution, provided the appeal [i.c., the notice of appeal] be filed with the Clerk of the Court of Chancery within ten days after the filing of such final decree (unless otherwise ordered); if later than ten days, special order, on good cause shown, is required as in the case of appeals from interlocutory orders.14 To be taken in connection with these provisions of the Chancery Rules, is the rule laid down by C. J. Beasley to the following effect: that even in the absence of a special order staying execution, in any case, the appeal shall operate to suspend a decree or order, whenever such construction is necessary to preserve the subject of the appeal in such a condition as to enable the Court of Errors and Appeals to render

Under the above rule, an appeal taken from a part of a decree only, is ground for a stay of execution of the decree in its entirety if the appellant, appealing one part of the decree seeks to enforce that part from which no appeal is taken.17

Notwithstanding the principle above explained that an appeal may operate per se to suspend execution of a decree, the usual practice is to apply for an order in the Court of Chancery, or in the Court of Errors and Appeals [see FORM 205: Order Staying Execution of Decree Appealed From.], to stay execution of a decree whenever it appears that execution would destroy or impair the subject of the appeal.18 In the hearing on the application to stay, the Court of

193. Steps of Appeal: Notice of Appeal. 

The notice of appeal is filed by the appellant with the Clerk of the Court of Chancery within the time allowed for appeal; this notice states shortly the parts of the order or decree complained of as erroneous, and is signed by counsel; it states that he conceives it to be a good cause for appeal (and if appeal is taken from an advised order or decree, the notice so states, naming the vice chancellor or advisory master advising the decree); a copy thereof is served on the solicitor of the adverse party if he prosecuted or was defended by such.32 [See FORM 215: Notice of Appeal.] It is the notice of appeal filed in the Court of Chancery that is the appellate act giving the Court of Errors and Appeals cognizance of the case.33 It operates, therefore, to oust the jurisdiction of the chancery court,34 and to fix the time of the appeal for purposes of the limitation thereon.35 Should the appellant fail to file the notice of appeal as is required, the appeal on the petition of appeal is coram non judice and will be dismissed.86 

194. Steps of Appeal (Continued): Petition of Appeal. 

The petition of appeal is filed within twenty days after filing the notice of appeal; it briefly states the order or decree complained of, the grounds of appeal being explicitly stated; a copy of the petition of appeal must be served within five days after filing the same on the solicitor of the adverse party, if there be one; if not, on the adverse party if to be found in this state.87 If the appellant fails to file the petition of appeal within the prescribed twenty days, the appeal shall be deemed to be waived, and the cause may proceed as if no notice of appeal had been filed.38 The petition of appeal must set forth

The answer to the petition of appeal is filed by the respondent within thirty days after service of the copy of the petition of appeal, and making of the deposit of costs required by the rules of the Court of Errors and Appeals; in event it is not filed within the prescribed time, the appellant may enter a rule as of course in vacation or termtime with the Clerk of the Court of Errors and Appeals, for the hearing of the appeal.43 The answer of the respondent puts in issue only those errors alleged in the appellant's petition: in so far as the answer alleges errors prejudicial to the respondent, the appellate court has no jurisdiction over such, since the respondent has not perfected an appeal in the manner prescribed by the rules of court.44

277 68 appeals from the Court of Chancery the Chancellor does not sit as a member or have a voice in the hearing or final decision but shall inform the court in writing, of the reasons of his order or decree." 

The rule on an even division of the Court of Errors and Appeals, is to affirm the decree of the Court of Chancery, a majority being required to reverse.69 There is no decision on the legal question involved, the result depending on the fact that the question put is whether the decree shall be reversed.70 The party appealing must have at least an arguable case; the appellate court has inherent power to dismiss an appeal that is manifestly and palpably frivolous and without merit.70a

The rule is that on an appeal, great weight is given to the findings of the Chancellor (or vice chancellor) on questions of fact.71 The reason for this rule is that the Chancellor (or vice chancellor) saw the witnesses, heard them testify, and had a better opportunity to judge their credibility than the appellate court.72 This rule does not operate, however, to impose any restraint on the Court of Errors and Appeals in determining whether the general finding is consistent with the facts.73 If the finding of the Chancellor is supported by the [great] preponderance of the evidence it will not be disturbed.74 

Nor will a reversal be predicated on harmless error,75 but exclusion by the Court of Chancery of competent testimony is ground for reversal.76 The question on appeal is not whether the reasons assigned for its action by the Court of Chancery are correct, but whether its action was proper. An appeal from a final decree brings up for review all interlocutory orders made prior thereto in so far as they involve the merits of the case;79 but not those orders relating merely to the sufficiency of the pleadings, and not affecting the merits of the suit.80 This latter type of interlocutory orders which are merely incidental to the suit, are not reviewed on appeal from a final decree; they become conclusive at the end of forty days there being no appeal taken therefrom.81 

An appeal from a part of a decree adverse to the appellant, does not carry up for review the entire decree; and an affirmance of the part appealed from does not affirm that part of the decree from which no appeal was taken and which was in favor of the appellant.82 

But on a review that portion from which no appeal is taken will be assumed to be correct, appellant not being aggrieved thereby.83

If matters are assigned as grounds in the petition of appeal and are not set forth either in the brief or argued at the hearing, they will not be considered by the appellate court, the presumption being that the appellant abandoned such grounds.87 Several exceptions, however, have been made from the rule that the appellant cannot assign at the hearing any other grounds for reversal than those contained in the petition of appeal and raised and argued in the Court of Chancery: viz. (1) Where the Court of Chancery was without jurisdiction either of the person of the defendant against whom a decree in personam was entered, or without jurisdiction of the subject matter, this objection can be made on an appeal even though not argued in the Court of Chancery and not set out in the petition of appeal.8 (2) Simi- larly, non-joinder of a party necessary and indispensable to a valid and efficacious decree.89 The procedure of the appellate court on objection properly taken on appeal to the lack of a necessary party is to remit the proceedings to the Court of Chancery for the purpose of introducing into the proceeding the omitted parties.90 Parties cannot be added on appeal, even though necessary, since the jurisdiction of the 88

Court of Errors and Appeals is strictly appellate with reference to Chancery matters.91 Nor can new facts be introduced by testimony; the appeal is decided upon the case as it was before the Chancellor.92 

On appeal, the reviewing court will not consider questions that are merely moot or academic; nor where by reason of change of circumstance, any appellate action would be futile and nugatory under the circumstances;94 nor will the appellate court review any order of decree entered with the consent of the appellant,95 or any order or decree to which objections have been waived by failure to object in the Court of Chancery ;96 nor any matters not passed on by the lower court and thus outside the record;97 etc. 

On an appeal from the award of a preliminary injunction, the order awarding the injunction will not be dissolved unless the case is free from doubt.98 The appellate court will not presume that there has been any change in the circumstances of the case since the award of the injunction, and will hear the appeal on the same evidence as was before the Court of Chancery.99 But this rule will not operate to prevent the Court of Errors and Appeals from exercising that discretion upon which the allowance or refusal of an injunction rests.¹

281 On an appeal from a jury issue, the fact of the award of such and the verdict rendered in the cause on which the final decree rests, does not operate to take away or limit the control of the appellate court over the decree.2 On the appeal, therefore, the appellate court may decide the issue, or send it back with instructions for a new trial.³ 5 If after an appeal, the appellant dies, the appeal may be revived either by a notation on the record, of his personal representative, or, under the old practice, by a bill of revivor, or by a bill in the nature of such. If the respondent on appeal dies, the death is suggested on the record, and by order his administrator and heirs are made parties. If the respondent die after the argument but prior to the rendition of the opinion of the appellate court, the decree of the appellate court will be entered nunc pro tunc, as of the date the cause was argued. If the appellant without explanation fails to appear either personally or by counsel at the hearing, the appeal will be treated as abandoned, and the order appealed from will be affirmed.?

66 The order of remittitur is the concluding portion of the judgment rendered in the Court of Errors and Appeals, remitting or returning the record in the cause to the Court of Chancery for further proceedings according to the law and practice of that court." [See 

FORM 225: Remittitur on Affirmance; FORM 226: Remittitur on 

Reversal.] The remittitur contains a copy of the decree of the appellate court, and is annexed to the petition of appeal and the matters thereto annexed, under the seal of the appellate court and signature of the clerk, are filed in the Court of Chancery.13 Unless there be a special order therefor, the record is not actually remitted to the Court of Chancery until after the expiration of ten days from the entry of the remittitur.14 When the cause is regularly remitted to the Court of Chancery, the jurisdiction of the Court of Errors and Appeals ceases; further proceedings must be had in the Court of 

Chancery.15 It then becomes the duty of the Court of Chancery to execute the judgment of the reviewing court in accordance with the mandate, without amendment, modification,16 or interpretation.17 If the judgment of the Court of Errors and Appeals be misentered in the minutes, it must be executed by the Court of Chancery according to its terms; the proper practice, in such a case, is to apply to the appellate court to rectify the entry of such a decree.18 

On a remittitur of affirmance no further decree of the Court of Chancery is necessary since the original chancery decree remains in full force and effect; on a remittitur of reversal, however, since the appellate decree does not in and of itself alter the original chancery decree, it becomes necessary for the Court of Chancery to enter a new decree pursuant to the mandate of the Court of Errors and Appeals. In such cases, either of reversal or modification, the practice is not to enter a new chancery decree in words at length or in special form, 13. Rule 38 (Err. & App.).

202. Costs on Appeal. 

Under the statute, the Court of Errors and Appeals may within its discretion award costs.22 And under the rules of the Court of 

Errors and Appeals, the party prevailing on appeal is entitled to costs incurred in both the lower and appellate court unless the court in terms adjudge the contrary.23 On a reversal, when a complainant is unsuccessful in the Court of Chancery, but successful on appeal, the Court of Chancery under Section 91 of the Chancery Act, may award counsel fees to the complainant for services rendered in the Court of Chancery, to be included in the taxed costs.24 Counsel fees for services on appeal are ordinarily awarded by the appellate court, and application therefor must first be made in the Court of Errors and Appeals.25 If, however, (a) application be first made in the

Court of Errors and Appeals and no action is taken thereupon;26 or if (b) through inadvertence the application is not made while the case is before the reviewing court on appeal, then after the remittitur, the Court of Chancery has jurisdiction to grant counsel fees for services rendered on appeal.2 27

203. Definition. 

The term judicial sale embraces any sale made by an authorized officer, such as a master or commissioner, of a court of competent jurisdiction, in connection with some pending proceeding in that court, and which is inchoate until confirmed by the court.¹ In Chancery such judicial sales are usually in connection with foreclosure suits, suits to sell infant's lands, partition proceedings, creditors' suits to sell land, receiverships, administration of estates, etc.2 It embraces properly a sale on a writ of execution in equity in New Jersey when the writ is issued to a master in chancery. It also would seem to embrace a sale by a sheriff under execution since confirmation of such a sale is required.4 3 

1. 35 C. J. 7; 16 R. C. L. 5; Jersey Land Co. v. Goldblatt, 104 N. J. Eq. 425, 146 Atl. 198 (sale pendente lite to prevent deterioration). 

2. The term judicial sale is sui generis and is not construed to be within the prohibition against a voluntary sale. Similarly in interpreting a statute, a provision that required a pro-rating of taxes in a sale of land was held inapplicable to a judicial sale. Title Guar. & Tr. Co. v. Goeller, 93 N. J. Eq. 612, 117 Atl. 

831. The provisions of the Uniform Sales Act are ordinarily inapplicable to a judicial sale, particularly Section 4 (the statute of frauds) and Section 24. 27 

C. J. 230; Robertson v. Smith, 92 Va. 450. 

3. The Court of Chancery may issue its writ of fieri facias to a master as well as to a sheriff. 4 C. S., p. 4678, § 12; 1 C. S., p. 427, §§ 46 et seq.; In re 

Rhodes, 100 N. J. Eq. 370, 136 Atl. 408 (land in two counties). 

4. 1 C. S., p. 447, § 94. Cf., Tulane v. Deane, 4 N. J. L. J. 23. Query:

204. Necessity for Prior Court Order. 

Before a judicial sale can take place, ordinarily a decree ordering the sale must be entered, referring the matter to a master who is designated by the court.5 In a foreclosure suit where the property is of such a character or is so situated, as to make it liable to deteriorate in value, or that its care and preservation will be difficult or expensive, under Section 62 of the Chancery Act, the Court of Chancery has the power to enter an order for the sale of the mortgaged premises pendente lite. The officer is limited by the terms of the order and can act only in accordance therewith. When the parties make no objection to an appointment of a master to conduct the sale, the right to object is waived. Should the decree ordering the sale be reversed on appeal, subsequent to a sale, the reversal will not affect a bona fide purchaser's title, in so far as title to land is concerned. 

If the sale is void, the purchaser is protected to the extent he has paid off valid liens, or that his purchase money has been used to discharge the debts of the debtor, by being subrogated to the rights of the creditors.¹ 10

287 Where personal property is being sold, there is no rule that each article must be sold separately. If all the articles constitute an entirety having a value as such, and greater value than if sold separately, then they will be sold as a unit; if they have no such unital value, and it is likely that there would be bidders on the articles separately, then they will be sold separately.25 Similarly when personal and real property are being sold, they will be sold as an entirety or separately according to whether under a separate sale, the owner's interests will be best protected.2 26 The terms of the sale may be prescribed in the decree ordering the sale, and may be either for cash or on credit and terms that the court may deem best.27 A master in equity charged with the conduct of a sale has considerable latitude in prescribing such terms, not contrary to those prescribed in the decree, and which will exclude puffers and encourage bona fide bidders.28 Such terms going to a down payment, with security for the balance may be adopted as will amply secure compliance by the bidder with his bid.29 But the master may not impose conditions that will increase the liability of the purchaser with respect to the property sold, greater than would otherwise be imposed by law.30 Rigid conditions not called for under the facts and designed to oppress and injure the purchasers are equally illegal.31 

206. Order of Confirmation. 

Judicial sales of land conducted under a decree of the Court of Chancery and a reference to a master must be confirmed before they are binding on the court. The master must within five days thereafter report the sale to the court and the court will confirm the sale as valid and direct the execution of a good and sufficient deed to the purchaser if the court is satisfied that the land has been sold for the highest and best price it would bring.32 On objection to confirmation in a foreclosure sale, the only question that can be raised is that the property did not bring the highest and best price obtainable.38 All other grounds of objection must be made by independent action by

208. Rights of the Purchaser: Defect in Title. 

Formerly the rule was that judicial sales were subject to caveat emptor.48 But under the Sale of Land Act, the purchaser may petition the Court of Chancery to be relieved of his bid if before the delivery of the deed he can satisfy the court of a substantial defect or encumbrance which would render the title unmarketable.49 If, however, the notices of the sale describe the defect or encumbrance, or if the court undertakes to remove the defect or encumbrance, out of the proceeds of the sale, the purchaser will not be relieved.50
