209. Grounds for Avoiding: Suppression of Competition. 

An agreement between the bidder and others who are prospective bidders, to suppress or stifle the bidding is a ground for avoiding a judicial sale.61 But the fact that several bidders unite to bid, when the property is so large that no one is able to buy all of it, does not vitiate the sale.62 Similarly, one who has an interest to protect may agree to refrain from bidding, without offending the rule.63 By-bidding, i.e., to increase the price by fictitious bids, is a fraud on the purchaser and ground for avoidance.64 

210. Grounds for Avoiding (Continued): Inadequacy of Price: 

Upset Bids.

The English practice permits the opening of a judicial sale when an offer on security is made to pay a greater sum for the property than was bid at the sale. This enables a subsequent bidder, somewhat unfairly it would seem, by an "upset bid," to trade on the judgment of the original successful bidder.65 The practice above stated is disapproved in New Jersey, where the rule is well settled that mere inadequacy of price is not a sufficient ground for setting aside an order confirming a sale even though substantially more is now offered for the property." The language of the statute, that the court must be satisfied that it was the "highest and best price the same would then bring "67 has been construed not to change the previous rule against upset bids; the statute is interpreted to permit interested parties to attack the sale on the ground that the property did not bring the "highest and best price" that was then obtainable.68 Prior to confirmation, however, if a material advance in price is offered secured by a deposit or bond, the sale will sometimes be opened and further

211. Grounds for Avoiding (Continued): Fraud, Mistake, Irregu larity, etc.

The usual grounds for attacking a judicial sale are fraud, mistake, irregularity, or lack of jurisdiction: Fraud, or impropriety in the sale, is a ground for setting aside the order of confirmation even though a deed has been delivered to the purchaser.73 Surprise created by the officer conducting the sale is ground for withholding. confirmation.74 But not when merely resulting from the neglect or inattention of the party complaining. When the sale is to be avoided on that ground, it must be a mistake as to a material fact and not a mere mistake of law.75 Irregularity and mismanagement in the sale so as to discourage bidders and result in considerable sacrifice, will justify the Court of Chancery in withholding confirmation although the purchaser had nothing to do with such mismanagement.76 When a sale is attacked on the ground of fraud, the objector has the burden of establishing the fraud. 212. Liability of the Purchaser: Resale to Charge Defaulting 

Buyer.

The purchaser is liable for the purchase price, if unpaid, only after confirmation. If after confirmation, the purchaser fails or refuses to pay, the sale will be set aside and the purchaser held for damages. 80 

An order for a resale will be entered which does not operate to release the original purchaser who remains liable for the deficiency.81 

But the price obtained at the second sale, to fix the liability of the defaulting bidder, must be on conditions and terms, the same as at the first sale, and the property offered must be identical in substance and description.82 It is not necessary, however, to fix the liability of the defaulting bidder that a resale be ordered. The down payment may be declared forfeited, and the bidder proceeded against by petition or motion to enforce payment in full at the agreed price.83 

The complainants in such a suit are the commissioners, and the proceeding is ancillary to the sale.84

214. Sale of an Infant's Land. 

Where an infant is seized of land corporeal or incorporeal or entitled to any term to come or any interest under a deed of trust wherein no power of sale is given to the trustee, the infant by guardian or next friend, may apply to the Chancellor to have the land sold.92 The Chancellor may inquire into the merits of the application in a summary procedure by a reference to a master, and should it appear that a sale would promote the infant's interests, the Chancellor will direct a sale, subject to the confirmation of the Court of Chancery. No sale will be ordered if contrary to the provisions of any will devising the land to the infant. The sale will be made by guardian and no deed can be executed until the Chancellor has confirmed the sale. The proceeds will be reinvested for the benefit of the infant and a report thereof on oath must be filed by the guardian with the clerk of the Court of Chancery. 

Under the New Jersey statute, any future estate limited over to an infant, also may be sold upon application, by the person owning a vested interest therein, to the Chancellor if the interests of the infant would be promoted thereby. The statute also applies to persons not in esse with special provisions for service in such cases.93 

A petition must be filed in the Court of Chancery by some person owning a vested interest in the land." Twenty days' notice must be given each person having any interest vested or prospective. Nonresidents may be reached by publication. If the infant in interest be under fourteen years, service may be made on his guardian, father or mother. An order of reference to a master is next entered to inquire into whether the sale would promote the infant's interests. 

On a satisfactory report by a master and confirmed by the Chancellor an order of sale is entered. The funds realized from the sale are paid into court and re-invested in real estate mortgages, securities of the United States or of the State of New Jersey.

215. Discovery: In General. 

Originally a pure bill of discovery would lie in equity compelling answer under oath. The answer in such a suit would be evidence in the defendant's behalf. The practice of praying for answer under oath is obsolete under the present practice but a bill may be filed for discovery waiving answer under oath, and seeking discovery incidental to other equitable relief.¹ A bill for discovery should allege either a pending action at law, or a contemplated judicial proceeding, to enforce a legal right, in aid of which discovery is necessary.2 Discovery as incidental to other equitable relief is more usual than a pure bill of discovery, as is illustrated by the following equitable actions: discovery as incidental to an accounting,³ as incidental to a bill to annul or set aside a conveyance, etc.5 Discovery will not be compelled, however, when such will incriminate the person from whom discovery is sought or subject him to a penalty or forfeiture; nor compel him to violate the privilege of confidential communications between husband and wife; nor against third persons who have no interest in the suit. The Court of Chancery also possesses inherently the power to compel the inspection and copying of records that are in the possession of the adverse party.11 The granting of an order compelling a party to make discovery on oath of books, papers or other documents which are in his possession or under his control relative to any matter in question in the cause is discretionary with the Court of Chancery.12

216. Statutory Interrogatories. 

Section 19 of the Chancery Act permits the complainant to annex to the bill, interrogatories calling for answer by the defendant under oath. The answers must be full and responsive, and a defendant omitting to answer may be compelled to do so. In the event that the defendant fails to answer, the allegations in the bill on which the interrogatories are founded are taken to be admitted, and a decree may be made accordingly. Due to the fact (1) that statutory interrogatories must be annexed to the bill, and (2) may be filed only by the complainant, and (3) before the cause is at issue, the more usual procedure is to proceed under the Chancery Rules which allow interrogatories more conveniently.15 

217. Interrogatories Under the Chancery Rules. 

The Chancery Rules also provide for interrogatories. In two respects the procedure under the rules is different from that prescribed in the Chancery Act: (1) Either party may address interrogatories to the opposite party. (2) Interrogatories may be filed after issue has been joined. Interrogatories must be in writing and relate to any matter material to the issue." Written answer must be served within ten days after the service of the interrogatories.. The

Their use in this respect is to be distinguished from the function of a bill of particulars which permits discovery of an opponent's case with greater particularity than is disclosed by the pleadings, and may be sought in chancery before or after answer.17 

The practice under the Chancery Rules was designed to provide a simple and expeditious method of examining the adverse party before trial similar to the practice at law. There is no requirement under this practice that the bill be sworn to.18 The practice is not, however, to file interrogatories addressed to strangers to the suit even though joined as a party for that purpose: a defendant to be compelled to answer interrogatories must have some interest in the suit for the rule allowing interrogatories was not designed to permit the prying into the records of strangers.19 When an action is brought by the guardian of a lunatic, the lunatic is the real party in interest, and the guardian, for purposes of the rule is a stranger to the suit, and cannot be compelled to answer interrogatories.20 Interrogatories in all cases will be confined to the issues raised by the pleadings, and must be material to the issue.2 They should not seek the names of witnesses, nor be designed to pry into the adversary's case, but should be of such a character that with a responsive answer, they will constitute competent evidence in behalf of their proponent.22

CHAPTER XIII. 

THE BILL OF INTERPLEADER. 

220. Grounds of Strict Interpleader.

225. Bill in the Nature of a Bill of Interpleader. 

219. Function. 

A bill of interpleader in equity is an action by a stakeholder who with respect to several claimants, is indifferent to their claims. It is proper in cases where two or more persons severally claim the same thing under different titles or in separate interests, from another person who not claiming any title or interest therein himself,¹ and not knowing to which of the claimants he ought of right to render the debt or duty claimed, or to deliver the property in his custody,2 is either molested by actions brought against him or anticipates injury from their conflicting claims.3 In such a case the debtor, or custodian, may file a bill of interpleader in the Court of Chancery and avoid the vexation of several suits and the risk of being compelled to render the same duty or thing to several claimants. The relief in equity is liberally accorded the honest stakeholder who without full information of the conflicting rights, fears to make a decision by which he may incur liability. The ultimate issue, however, after the claimants have interpleaded, is to whom does the fund or thing belong. A typical interpleader action is one brought by a bank as a depository of funds being claimed by the executor of the now deceased depositor and an alleged donee under a gift inter vivos.

220. Grounds of Strict Interpleader. 

The grounds for a strict interpleader action in equity are: (1) that the same duty, debt or thing is claimed by all of the parties against whom relief is sought; (2) that there is privity of contract or duty between the complainant and the different and conflicting claimants;8 (3) that the complainant does not have nor claim any interest in the subject matter; (4) that the complainant stands indifferent as to the respective claimants;10 (5) the claimant must be in possession or control of the fund or thing in dispute;11 and (6) the complainant must not have incurred a personal obligation to any one of the claimants, independent of the title or right to possession, for in that event there would be a claim against the complainant-stakeholder, not common to all the claimants.12 If one of these essentials is lacking then the complainant must defend himself as best he may, against each of the claimants.13 Nor can the complainant interplead a fund when there is a dispute as to the sum for which complainant is liable.14 

221. Parties and Service. 

The complainant in a bill of interpleader is the debtor, obligor or custodian of the fund or thing in dispute and since the action is for his relief, he is a necessary party. All persons claiming an interest in the subject matter in dispute are also necessary parties.15 The legal representative of any such claimant is a necessary party. But persons who claim no interest therein are improper parties.16 At

Bill in the Nature of a Bill of Interpleader. 

A bill in the nature of a bill of interpleader is one in which the complainant asks some relief over and above a mere injunction against suits by conflicting claimants, and states facts which entitles him to relief independent of the fact of the adverse claims of several claimants.30 Such a bill states substantial grounds of equitable jurisdiction. In such an action it is not true, of course, that the complainant claims no interest in the subject matter; but his interest must not be such as he hopes to acquire as the result of the litigation.40

A claim of a lien for storage charges by the complainant would be such an interest as would defeat a strict interpleader suit.41 

This bill need not be supported by affidavit of non-interest and noncollusion as in the case of a strict interpleader.42 If an action is brought as a strict interpleader and at the hearing proofs are offered to establish a claim by the complainant in the subject matter interpleaded, the bill must be dismissed. For a bill of interpleader cannot be amended to be an action in the nature of an interpleader because this would be equivalent to allowing a new cause of action by an amended bill.43 [See FORM 235: Bill in the Nature of a Bill of Interpleader.]

CHAPTER XIV. 

THE BILL OF REVIVOR. 

SECTION 226. 

Function. 

227. Form of a Bill of Revivor. 

228. Distinguished from a Bill in the Nature of a Bill of Revivor. 

226. Function. 

When an action in equity abated by reason of the death of a party thereto, the action under earlier chancery practice was revived by a bill of revivor. With reference to a pending action when no final decree had been entered, the personal representative could revive in the event of the complainant's death; similarly, if the defendant died, the complainant could revive against the personal representative of the decedent defendant.¹ But when no decree had been entered, either in the event of the complainant's death or the defendant's, there could be no revivor by the defendant, or the defendant's personal representative.2 If final decree had been entered, however, a defendant having a beneficial interest therein, the defendant, or his personal representative, as well as the complainant, or his personal representative could exhibit a bill of revivor, for purposes of prosecuting an appeal.3 When either party died after the final argument but prior to the entry of final decree, the court may order the decree to be signed nunc pro tunc as of the death of the party-thus enabling the defendant to revive. If, however, a bill of revivor be filed for the purpose of reviving to prosecute an appeal, and it appears that the right of appeal is lost, the bill will be dismissed: the court will not do a nugatory act.5 Even in early practice, the formal bill of revivor was superseded by motion for an order of revivor as a simpler mode of procedure. And under the statute, proceeding by a formal bill of revivor is still permissible procedure in the event the parties prefer that course of practice."

227. Form of a Bill of Revivor. 

When a bill of revivor is necessary, the requisite allegations and prayers may be made in the form of an addition separately filed by way of supplement to the original bill, and in such case service of process on any new parties shall be made, as in the case of an original bill, and service of copies of the addition, by way of supplement, shall be made on all of the defendants to the original bill affected thereby, including all defendants who have appeared to or procured copies of the original bill, and the complainant may thereupon proceed with the cause, as if the addition, by way of supplement, had been made in a supplemental bill, which contained a recital of the allegations and prayers of the original bill and the proceedings thereon.8 

Bills of revivor or supplemental bills shall not restate any of the statements in the original suit unless the special circumstances of the case require it. No formal written appearance need be filed by an answering defendant along with an answer; and the clerk shall not file any such appearance unless requested so to do by the solicitor of the answering defendant or by such defendant personally." 

228. Distinguished From a Bill in the Nature of a Bill of Revivor. 

J. Story: "We have seen that a bill of revivor, properly so called, lies only in cases where a death interferes, and it is necessary to bring the proper representatives of the deceased party in the realty or in the personalty before the court.

In each of these cases, there is no other fact to be ascertained, than whether the new party brought before the court has the character imputed to him. If he has, the revivor is of course. But there are many cases, in which there are other facts, which may be brought into litigation, besides the mere question of the character of the new party; and to such cases, therefore, the simple bill of revivor does not technically apply. Under such circumstances, an original bill, in the nature of a bill of revivor, is the appropriate process to bring those facts before the court, and to put the original proceedings again in motion, and to enable the new party to have the benefit of the former proceedings." 10

229. Function.

The object of a bill of review is to procure the reversal, alteration, correction or annulment of a decree entered in a former chancery suit. It may be filed only by a party to an ended chancery cause and to reach a final decree which has been signed and enrolled. Under the early practice, if the decree sought to be reversed was interlocutory and had not been enrolled, then the proper procedure would be to file a petition to rehear, or a bill in the nature of a bill of review.¹ 

Judge Story thus states the difference: "The distinction between a bill of review and a bill in the nature of a bill of review, though important in England, is not felt in the practice of the courts of the United States, and perhaps rarely in any of the state courts of equity in the Union. I take it to be clear that in the courts of the United 

States all decrees as well as judgments are matters of record, and are deemed to be enrolled as of the term in which they are passed. 

So that the appropriate remedy is by bill of review." 2 It is the established practice in New Jersey, and has been for more than a century, to proceed by petition for a rehearing even though the decree has been enrolled provided the time for appeal has not ex-

2. Dexter v. Arnold, 5 Mason 310. 307

If, however, the time for appeal has expired, then the complainant under a long line of established cases would proceed by a bill of review.5 Whether or not he can also proceed by a petition for a rehearing even though the time for appeal has expired, will be considered in detail in a following section. 

Such is provided for by the Chancery Rules.*

234. Grounds: Newly Discovered Evidence. 

A petition for leave to file a bill of review on the ground of newly discovered evidence must be supported by affidavit that the evidence is new and could not have been discovered by reasonable diligence before the hearing. The court must be satisfied upon an examination of the petitioner's application for leave that the evidence (a) is new; (b) that it could not have been discovered sooner with reasonable diligence;27 (c) that it is of such a character that if brought forward in the suit, it would probably have altered the judgment;28 (d) that it is not merely cumulative.29 Where former counsel made an error of judgment or mistake of law as to the pertinency or force of certain evidence, the substitution of new counsel who might make a better showing on the facts and a more persuasive argument than his predecessor made, is not a sufficient ground for a petition to rehear.30 

In the event that evidence is overlooked at the time of the trial by reason of the negligence or laches of the petitioner, such will destroy any right he may have to relief by a bill of review.3 

Matters of public record accessible to the defendant at the time of the suit, not at that time searched for and properly presented in the case, cannot later be made the ground of a bill of review. Such cannot be called newly discovered evidence merely because it did not occur to the defendant to search the records at the time of the suit.3 

But a controlling decision handed down by the Court of Errors and Appeals subsequent to the entry of the decree for which a rehearing is sought is newly discovered matter which will warrant reopening the decree when it is of such a character as to influence the result.3 33 

31 32 Query: Whether a petition for a rehearing is appropriate procedure when the ground for the rehearing is fraud? See § 232, n. 19, supra.

235. Effect of an Affirmance on the Right to Petition for a Rehearing.

Formerly, the practice was to proceed by bill of review and not by petition, following an affirmance by the Court of Errors and Appeals of a decree entered in the Court of Chancery. The practice was to proceed in the same manner as in the case when the time for appeal had expired.34 The present practice, however, following an affirmance by the Court of Errors and Appeals, is to proceed by petition and order to show cause. 35 The effect of an affirmance by the Court of Errors and Appeals does not prevent the Court of Chancery from entertaining a petition to review a decree nor does any rule of practice require it to obtain the consent of the appellate court. In one respect, however, the affirmance limits the Court of Chancery in a review of its decree to the ground of newly discovered evidence.36 

Following an affirmance there can be no review of a decree on the ground of error of law apparent on the face of the decree.37 

236. Appeal From an Order Denying a Rehearing. 

A petition for a rehearing is addressed to the discretion of the Court of Chancery.38 In the event on an application for a rehearing, an order is entered denying the rehearing, ordinarily the order is not appealable, for the appellate court will not substitute its discretion for that of the Court of Chancery.³ 39 But if it be established that the order entered by the Court of Chancery was an abuse of discretion, or was the result of mistake or imposition, an appeal will lie and the order denying a rehearing will be set aside.40

A bill of review is not an appeal proceeding, but is a proceeding addressed to the court of first instance. Putnam v. Clark, supra. Eckhouse v. Berwyn Estates, supra, n. 35.

237. Distinguished From an Original Bill to Impeach a Decree for Fraud.

An original bill to impeach a decree for fraud is filed as a matter of course whereas a bill of review is filed only upon leave of court.41 

Decrees of foreign courts, which to some extent constitute a class to themselves, are reached by original bills to impeach,42 but in case of domestic decrees, the policy is not to commence an original, independent and expensive suit, but to file a bill of review subject to the discretion of the court when this mode is adequate. This latter method, if not exclusively prescribed, is to be encouraged in all cases where such procedure will accomplish justice, in that it gives to the court of equity a wholesome control over the proceeding. It would seem then, that the line between original bills to impeach a decree for fraud, and a bill of review for the same ground, cannot be sharply drawn. The latter seems to include the former.43 

The nature of the fraud necessary to warrant an original bill to impeach a decree is described as "extrinsic and collateral to the matter tried by the first court, and not to a fraud in the matter on which the decree was rendered." 44 The jurisdiction of a court of equity to give relief against a judgment or decree which has been procured by fraud, whether it be of a tribunal standing above or below, is well settled. Where a bill alleges fraud of the character that might have warranted an original bill to impeach, and combines therewith grounds which might have been presented in a bill of review, the bill is to be treated as a bill of review rather than as an original bill. 

Such latter grounds cannot be rejected as surplusage in determining the character of the bill.45 A bill of review is necessarily addressed to the same court wherein the decree was entered and enrolled. 

Where a decree has been obtained in absence of the other party, upon a hearing entirely ex parte, and the defendant now comes forward and alleges surprise, lack of opportunity to make a defense, and offers proof that fraud was practiced which deprived him of a defense, then no bill of review is necessary even though the decree

238. Miscellaneous Rules. 

Every petition for a re-hearing shall set out concisely the special matter or cause on which such re-hearing is applied for, and shall be signed by counsel; and if a re-hearing is ordered, the party who complains of the decree or order and applies to have it corrected, shall be entitled to open and close the argument. A copy of every petition for a re-hearing shall be served on the opposite party, with a notice of presenting the same. If a petition for re-hearing shall be presented to the judge who heard the cause before a final decree shall have been settled upon application, or within ten days after filing any final decree not settled on application, and a caveat against signing and enrolling the same shall be filed with the clerk of the court, such final decree shall not be signed and enrolled, or any process issued thereon, until the said application shall be finally disposed of. No order for a re-hearing shall stay proceedings on any interlocutory decree or order, unless by the special direction of the court. A re-hearing of decrees, signed upon the advice of a vice chancellor or advisory master, may be had in the same manner and upon the same terms as in cases heard by the Chancellor.49

239. Function.

A bill to quiet title to land, or a bill quia timet to remove a cloud from the complainant's title, is a statutory action in New Jersey.¹ 

This action is a constitutional extension of the early, inherent jurisdiction of equity to entertain a bill to remove a cloud from title to land.2 The statute was first adopted on March 2, 1870.3 The creation

of the statutory remedy did not, however, abolish the old procedure: the Court of Chancery may now as formerly, entertain a bill to remove a cloud from the title to land independent of the statute.* 

In practice, the statutory suit is the usual procedure although instances of the older suit are not infrequent.5 

For purposes of distinguishing the present statutory action from the old bill to remove a cloud, it should be noted that in both suits the complainant is required to show possession of the locus in quo.º 

The distinction is this: that whereas before the statute of 1870, a prior determination of the complainant's title in an action at law was a condition precedent to the filing of the bill in equity, such is not required as a condition precedent to the statutory remedy. The statute, therefore enlarges the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, in that it gives the complainant a right to come into chancery in advance of a determination of the title at law." 

The purpose of the statute is to enable one in peaceable possession of land in this state to clear his title thereto by compelling all claimants to appear in the Court of Chancery and have the title adjudicated, settling forever all disputes and doubts concerning the title.s 

Like other equitable remedies, its further purpose is to afford relief to one who is unable to bring ejectment at law, and who is accordingly without adequate remedy at law:9 and to avoid multiplicity of suits and vexatious litigation by the settlement in one action of the claims of several disputants.10 The action is not limited to the

242. Statutory Requirements: Title of Complainant. 

The statute specifies (a) the qualifications of the complainant, (b) when he may sue, and (c) what the bill must contain.47 With respect to the qualifications of the complainant, the statute requires that he have peaceable possession of the land, under a claim of ownership, to which an adverse claim or right is asserted, or is reputed to exist. The complainant must assert in himself some title or ownership but he is not required to establish his title until the defendant has at the final hearing, shown prima facie the title or adverse interest which he the defendant claims.48 A complainant may proceed under the statute although he does not claim as owner of the fee.4 49

And a person holding merely a record legal title in trust for another is also a proper party-complainant.50 Similarly an executor can proceed under the statute to quiet title to the lands of the testator;51 also one claiming by adverse possession;52 a judgment creditor if in peaceable possession may file the bill;53 also, the owner of an undivided interest.5 And by the amendment of 1896, an action may be maintained by one vested of an estate in remainder.55

243. Statutory Requirements (Continued): Peaceable Possession in the Complainant. 

The complainant in order to proceed under the statute must also be in peaceable possession of the land, title to which is to be quieted.57 

The bill in each action must on its face disclose as a jurisdictional fact such peaceable possession in the complainant; otherwise, the bill will be dismissed.58 By peaceable possession is meant peaceable with respect to the defendant: the test is whether the defendant in setting up an adverse claim or title, has so interfered with the complainant's possession of the premises by acts of such a character that a suit at law by the complainant based on such interference would involve the defendant's adverse claim or title to the land.59 Where the defendant's act has produced such interference as is suable at law, then the possession of the complainant is not peaceable within the meaning of the statute, and the Court of Chancery is without jurisdiction under the statute.60 For example, where the defendant set up an alleged right of way, which was, if without legal justification, a trespass for which an action of ejectment would lie at law, such a defense would bar the complainant's action in equity to quiet title, since it shows the lack of a jurisdictional fact, viz., peaceable possession in the complainant; similarly, on the defendant's show-

245. Peaceable Possession (Continued): Presumptive: Wild Lands. 

Pomeroy classifies statutes allowing an action in equity to quiet title, in two classifications: (1) Complainant is required to be in possession, (2) Not so required.73 The original act of 1870 was amended in 1901 to permit one not in possession of "wild or wood or waste or uninclosed or unimproved lands" to quiet title thereto, upon the payment of taxes on such lands for five consecutive years immediately prior to the commencement of the suit; the complainant is presumed to be in peaceable possession within the meaning of the statute.74 To this extent, the New Jersey statute of 1870 as amended falls in Pomeroy's second classification. The payment of the taxes for the period fixed by the statute, does not, however, establish the complainant's right to the land by. adverse possession; the effect of the statute is merely to permit the complainant to file a bill under the statute, and come in and attempt to prove his adverse possession.75

The fact that the land is not separately assessed for taxes to the complainant does not preclude the complainant from coming in if he has paid the taxes for the required five years.70 support the old bill quia timet to remove a cloud independent of the statutory action. 246. Peaceable Possession (Continued): Effect of Denial by the Defendant: The Preliminary Hearing. 

If the defendant denies the peaceable possession of the complainant, a preliminary issue of jurisdiction is raised which must be first heard and determined in the Court of Chancery." The complainant must be found to be in peaceable possession on this issue before jurisdiction over the issue of title can be assumed.78 The defendant has the right to have this preliminary issue determined at a separate hearing before he can be called upon to defend his title at a trial at law. At this hearing no jury trial at law can be demanded by either party and the hearing is strictly limited to the issue of jurisdiction at which hearing the question of the respective titles will not be considered.79 Although conceivably the Chancellor might empanel a jury in "aid of his conscience," (ie., a feigned issue under the old practice) on the question of the complainant's peaceable possession, the practice, however, is for the Chancellor to decide the issue of peaceable possession without the aid of a jury.80 At this preliminary hearing on jurisdiction, the complainant has the burden of proof in establishing his peaceable possession.81 If he fails, the bill ordinarily will be dismissed.82 But an appeal can be taken forthwith by either party on an adverse ruling on the question

325 of peaceable possession.83 It should be noted that a denial by the defendant of the complainant's peaceable possession of a part only of the land, raises as a preliminary issue, a question of jurisdiction with respect to the whole of the premises.84 

An objection by the defendant that the complainant is not in peaceable possession of the premises (or denial of any jurisdictional fact) comes too late at the hearing on the title.85 In the hearing on the issue of peaceable possession, or other jurisdictional fact, the complainant has the affirmative, or burden of proof;86 whereas at the final hearing on the title, the position of the parties is reversed and the defendant has the affirmative and the position of a plaintiff.87 

In establishing at the first hearing, jurisdictional facts such as the complainant's peaceable possession, the degree of evidence required is described as "satisfactory.' " SS If in the answer the defendant admits the peaceable possession of the complainant (and other jurisdictional facts), this admission will operate to dispense with proof by the complainant, and the cause will proceed forthwith to a final hearing on the title without a preliminary hearing on jurisdiction.89 

Peaceable possession may be shown by (a) acts of possession done without dispute, (b) under claim of title, and (c) occupation and use in so far as the nature of the land permits." Attempts to sell and convey, or the cutting of timber therefrom, would constitute possession of wild lands at any rate, under the statute.91 As to what constitutes peaceable possession in all cases, no comprehensive definition is possible: ordinarily quiet occupation is sufficient.92 Verbal denials by the defendant do not prevent the possession from being peaceable.93 But if ejectment will lie, the complainant's possession is not peaceable.94

247. Statutory Requirements: Non-Pendency of Another Action. 

The statute permits a complainant to proceed thereunder only when no prior suit is pending to test or enforce the adverse claim.95 

By the adverse right is meant the alleged right of the defendant.96 

But if the pendency of another suit is to defeat the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, the object of the pending suit must be to enforce or test the validity of the title which is now denied or disputed in the equity action to quiet title. Thus a bill to quiet the title from the alleged lien of a judgment at law would proceed in spite of the issuance of the Court of Chancery of an execution founded on the judgment.98 The defendant, if he wishes to deny 'the non-pendency of another action, must make a preliminary issue thereof; otherwise, it will be assumed that the statute is satisfied in this respect; he cannot raise the issue at the hearing on the title.99 

248. Essential Allegations in the Bill. 

The statute prescribes that the bill to quiet title must (a) describe the land clearly, (b) name the person who asserts the adverse right, or is reputed to hold it, and (c) must call upon him to set forth and specify his title or lien, and how or by what instrument his claim is derived or created.¹ The bill must allege further, (d) a claim of ownership of the title in the complainant,¹ª (e) the complainant's actual and peaceable possession of lands within the state, and (f) the non-pendency of any action to enforce or test the validity of the defendant's adverse claim or lien.3 The precise and proper form for

If any of these jurisdictional allegations be omitted from the bill, the form of the bill is bad and the defendant may move to strike the bill in lieu of demurring thereto. The inclusion, however, in the bill of a needless statement of the defendant's claim or title, although bad pleading, is readily cured by amending the bill,12 or may be treated as surplusage.13 Even if the defendant moves to strike the bill (in lieu of demurring thereto), the complainant is not bound by his statement of the defendant's title.14

The bill further need not specifically describe the suit as one to quiet title, nor need the statute be specifically pleaded.17 The bill may proceed as one brought under the statute, if the essential jurisdictional allegations are included, even if the action be styled as one to set aside a deed,18 or for the partition of land,19 etc. Conversely the misdescription of the bill as one to quiet title under the statute, is not fatal to a suit, which independent of the statute, is cognizable in equity.20

251. Affidavit to the Bill.

253. Process: The Ticket.35 

Defendants in this action are served in the usual manner with a subpoena ad respondendum.36 The statute also requires that a ticket be issued and served with each subpoena.37 This ticket must (a) describe the lands involved with precision; (b) state the object of the suit; and (c) call on the defendant, if he claims any title, interest or incumbrance on the land, to answer the bill of complaint, but not otherwise.38 The failure to include a ticket with the subpoena is not a ground for motion to strike the bill: it is merely an irregularity of service, and if promptly objected to, may be taken advantage of by motion to set aside the service.39 [See FORM 30: Ticket in Suit to Suit to Quiet Title]. Absent and unknown parties may be served by order of publication in the usual manner.40

256. Hearing on the Adverse Claim of Title: Burden of Proof. 

In this final hearing only questions concerning title can be raised; there can be no denial of the complainant's peaceable possession or other jurisdictional fact.61 The practice is not to award an issue at law on title until all questions of jurisdiction have been settled. 

Should the question of title turn on adverse possession, the establishing of the complainants' peaceable possession preliminarily is not important as that decision was merely for purposes of acquiring jurisdiction.62 Regardless of whether the issue of title is tried at law or in equity (issue at law being waived), the statute puts the defendant under the burden of establishing title, requiring him to assume the affirmative on the issue of title. And the complainant is not required to establish his own title by proof until the defendant has made a prima facie case for the adverse title he claims.6+

258. Nature and Object. 

Partition is a matter of right¹ but only when the complainant is sui juris. A partition proceeding in equity is not strictly an action in rem, where the property itself, conceived of as having done the wrong or having been the instrument of its commission, is being proceeded against; it is rather a suit quasi in rem—where the suit is against the person in respect to the res. Its object is to avoid the inconvenience from a common possession, and to enable the persons entitled thereto, to take possession in severalty and improve their respective shares.* 

259. When the Bill Lies. 

Partition may be had in equity of any class of property, real or personal, of rights held in co-tenancy, viz., by coparceners, joint

7 tenants or tenants in common.5 A life-tenant is entitled to partition against co-life-tenants but not as against the remainderman since the life-tenant and remainderman do not have a joint and common right to the possession. When owners are seized of an estate by the entirety, as between husband and wife, there can be no partition, for here the estate is not held by moieties, but both are seised of an entirety. But there may be, not an absolute sale and partition of the premises, but a sale of the right of possession during the joint lives of husband and wife. The partible share held by a co-tenant may be for a less estate than a fee, or may be limited over after an estate for life.1 When an estate in remainder or reversion is owned by tenants in common, one or all of whom desire partition, then no partition may be had without the consent of the particular life-tenant then in possession.11 That is to say a reversioner, remainderman, vested or contingent, no one of whom has possessory rights in praesenti nor entitled to such in severalty in case partition should be made, cannot compel partition unless the holder of the particular estate, such as a life-estate, for a term, etc., consents thereto.12 Thus 10

An estate by the entirety between husband and wife amounts in its essential features to a tenancy in common for the joint lives of the parties, with remainder to the survivor. When the husband conveys to a grantee his interest for life, such grantee may maintain partition against the wife, the partition is limited, however, to the joint estate for their lives without affecting the right of survivorship. Schulz v. Ziegler, supra.

Where there are undivided shares owned in common, each share being vested in two persons who as between themselves are tenants by the entirety of their respective shares, then partition may be had of the two undivided shares. 

In case partition in kind is impossible, the proceeds of the sale will be held by the court to await the death of the husband or wife, and when the question of survivorship is determined, the principal will be paid to the survivor.

plainant.

Title in the Com- 

A bill for the partition of land will not lie where the title is denied or depends on doubtful facts or questions of law.28 Generally the complainant to maintain partition in equity must disclose in his bill of complaint such legal title as would sustain an action of ejectment.29 

If the complainant's bill discloses only an equitable title but with a present right to a conveyance and possession, and he is in possession, equity will regard that as done which ought to be done, and decree partition.30 If the title of any party is disputed on equitable grounds, the legal title not being contested, equity will retain jurisdiction and settle such dispute in partition.31 If the bill discloses color of title with the right of immediate entry to vacant lands, then actual legal title and possession is not necessary. 32

A co-tenant who has mortgaged his undivided share has a sufficient legal title to entitle him to maintain partition proceedings.33 If the Court of Chancery can see that there is no valid objection to the title of the complainant-that the objection made is an illusory one it will proceed to decree partition.34 But if the objection is a substantial one, putting the legal title to lands in issue, the Court of Chancery will in its discretion either dismiss the bill or retain it to allow the title to be settled in an action at law.35 The practice in New Jersey is quite universal to retain the suit until the determination of the legal title at law, the denial of the legal title being regarded not as a bar to the proceeding in equity but merely as a cause for staying it pending settlement of the legal title at law.36

Possession in the A bill in equity for partition will not lie if the bill does not disclose that the complainant is in possession of the land to be partitioned.37 

A tenant in common who has been disseised is not entitled to partition as against his disseisor where there has been an actual ouster by him, or those claiming through him.38 But a partial dispossession does not prevent partition of the whole tract.39 A plea that merely sets out that the complainant is not seised of the premises is insufficient; it must show further-" why and wherefore" the complainant is not seised.40 An heir cannot demand partition when co-heirs are in possession under a mortgage by which the complainant has conveyed possession of the premises to them.41 The complainant must establish a right to the possession, which, especially in the case of vacant lands, if undisputed, is sufficient, without establishing actual possession.42 

265. Essential Allegations (Continued): Infant's Land. 

When partition of land is sought in equity in which there is an interest belonging to an infant, the bill must allege that partition would be for the benefit of the infant.13 In this case partition is not of right.44 This allegation presents a preliminary issue of fact,-on which on reference, an advisory master takes evidence and reports whether or not partition would be for the benefit of the infant.45 

The practice when infant's land is sought to be partitioned, is to take proofs in open court.46 Proceedings to partition infant's land may also be instituted on application in the Orphans' Court, upon four weeks notice of the filing of the application.47 Where a suit for partition of an infant's land is actually pending in the Orphans' Court, a bill for partition may not thereafter be filed in the Court of Chancery.48

266. Partition by Division. 

When the land is partible and it is not disclosed by the evidence that actual partition, i.e., partition by division (or partition in kind, as it often is called) is inequitable, then partition will be by actual division, and not by sale and division of the proceeds.49 Partition need only be made so that each party in interest will have his share in value, and not so as to give each party a share in every part of the property.50 It is desirable, however, that a part of each distinct kind of property should be assigned each tenant, especially of property that far exceeds the other in value, in so far as such is practicable.51 Equity may require one party to pay money to others to equalize the value of their respective shares.52 

Distribution of parcels by drawing of lots, in making an allotment of shares to the respective owners, is impracticable, and where resorted to by the commissioners making partition, is not obligatory upon the Court of Chancery.53 54 In making partition, where the interests of the two co-tenants is in the ratio of five to one, the question is not whether the land can be divided into six equal divisions, but whether the land can be divided into two shares having the ratio of value of five to one. 

Under the Partition Act, the Court of Chancery may in its discretion, to gratify the desires of those co-tenants who elect to, set their shares off in one parcel without partition inter sese,—who for purposes of division are treated as one owner of the aggregate of their total interests.55

The usual procedure is to refer to a master the question of the partibility of the land, for a report on the practicability of actual partition without prejudice to the owners. Where it is doubtful whether partition can be equitably made,56 or if a sale would be accompanied by a great loss, then partition by division will be established, not by the giving of notice, but by the actual filing of the application.

267. Partition by Division (Continued): Commissioners. 

Commissioners, three in number, having been duly appointed and sworn as directed by the court, enter upon and inspect the land and divide it into portions of equal value.59 Commissioners are not like arbiters whose conclusions are binding, but their report may be set aside for inequality, favoritism, or fraud.6⁰ Commissioners are entitled to a reasonable compensation.61 The report of the commissioners must be confirmed by an order of court. A survey will not be ordered unless clearly necessary. 62 To set aside the report of the commissioners on the ground of mistake, the mistake must be serious and clearly proved.63 The Court of Chancery is reluctant to disturb an actual partition by commissioners. The report is attacked not by exceptions but by a motion to suppress or quash the report.65

271. Disposal of Proceeds. 

The Partition Act authorizes the sale of any owner's individual share free of any lien or encumbrance thereon, transferring the lien to the owner's share of the proceeds, thus protecting the liencreditor.87 A creditor even after a sale under a bill for partition may intervene by petition, and have his debt paid out of the proceeds of the sale provided that his claim was enforceable against the land.88 

The land being subject to the claim, the proceeds are equally so.89 

The Partition Act also provides that the judgment will operate as a lien on the proceeds if gotten "at any time prior to the distribution of the proceeds of such sale," provided only that the judgment would have been a lien on the interest of the debtor if owned in severalty.90

For purposes of descent and distribution, the proceeds of the sale retain the character of real estate.⁹1 Similarly for purposes of satisfying a mortgage.92

Where a female co-tenant who is married has an interest in land, the husband has a contingent estate in remainder-a right to possible succession to the wife's interest if she predeceases him,93 which right is not defeated by a sale in partition, for the share of the proceeds representing the wife's interest is conserved and protected to meet the husband's ultimate estate by curtesy should it ever become consummate.94 Similarly, in the sale of a male co-tenant's interest who is married, the proceeds will be protected to meet the wife's dower interest should she outlive her husband.95 A joint interest held by entirety will be invested, the principal to go to the survivor upon the death of the other party.96

The Partition Act permits a decree when it appears that the personal property is insufficient to pay the debts, authorizing the sale of land of a decedent debtor free of claim for such debts, transferring

272. Relief Incidental to Partition. 

Other equitable remedies are often prayed for in a bill for partition, and even though not prayed for, are often allowed as incidental to partition.2 Equity in decreeing partition does not act ministerially and in obedience to the call of those who have a right to partition, but administers relief er aequo et bono, according to its own notions of the rights between the parties. The following are the more usual cases of relief that are properly incidental to partition: Accounting against tenant in possession for rents and profits in favor of tenants out of possession; 4 appointment of a receiver to collect rents, pay taxes, and make necessary repairs, etc.; 5 issuance of an injunction restraining waste by the co-tenant in possession during the pendency

273. Defenses: Power of Sale. 

A discretionary or optional power of sale in the executors of an estate is not per se an obstacle to the partition of land.17 The right to partition, however, is not absolute in such a case, for if the suit is brought vexatiously, as when the executor is himself about to sell, the bill will not lie.18 When the power of sale is imperative, there is a conversion of realty into personalty, and partition will not be permitted.19 Similarly, partition will not be allowed to end an active trust, which would defeat the testator's intention, when the cestuis que trustent cannot agree on and do not all consent to partition.2 

But equity may partition a trust estate decreeing that the share of each cestui be held in severalty.21 If a trustee fails to convey to heirs of a decedent as directed under a trust instrument, the heirs are entitled to partition just as if the conveyance had been executed.22

But the mere fact that the lands of a decedent are for one year subject to the debts of the decedent is no reason for denying partition, since the purchaser under the sale takes title subject to such liability as the statute imposes.30

276. Bill to Set Aside a Fraudulent Conveyance: In General. 

A creditor may file a bill to set aside the fraudulent conveyance of the debtor made with the intent to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors.¹ The jurisdiction to entertain such an action is exclusively in the Court of Chancery. The suit is brought under the provisions of the Uniform Fraudulent Conveyance Act adopted in New Jersey in 1919, which repealed the earlier statute applicable to fraudulent conveyances to the extent that they are inconsistent.4 The Uniform Act as a whole has been held to be constitutional.5 Under the statute, the bill may be filed either for the benefit of the single creditor complainant, or for the benefit of all other creditors who may come in, 6 1. If the debtor's intent was merely to postpone sale until it could be sold to better advantage, it is void as delaying creditors. Semenowich v. Melnyk, 93

277. Idem: Party Complainant. 

A creditor must obtain a judgment at law before he may proceed in equity to set aside a fraudulent conveyance.9 Section 10 of the 

Uniform Act purports to give a creditor a right to proceed in equity without having reduced his claim to judgment.10 This section was held to be unconstitutional without, however, affecting the constitutionality of the act as a whole.11 But under the Uniform Act it is not necessary that the complainant be a lien judgment creditor.12 

Prior to 1919, the rule was contrary.13 With respect to the question of whether the creditor obtained judgment prior or subsequent to the time the conveyance sought to be set aside was made, it is settled that a creditor who reduces his claim to judgment after the conveyance may sue to set it aside on the theory that such a judgment, when once obtained, relates back and establishes a debt as of the time the original debt was created.1 .14 It is also true that a creditor whose debt or right of action, as well as the reduction thereof to judgment, was subsequent to the making of the alleged fraudulent conveyance, may file a bill to set aside the conveyance, for the attacking creditor need not have been in the actual contemplation of the debtor at the time of the conveyance: it is sufficient if the intent was to defraud some creditor, existing or subsequent.15 A creditor is defined by the act to be a

The act made no change in the law with respect to conveyances designed to cheat creditors. Such a conveyance may be set aside by either present or subsequent creditors.25 But the fraudulent intent (ie., in cases of actual fraud) is not presumed: the burden is on the creditor to prove actual fraudulent intent by the evidence.26 The creditor may succeed by showing either an intent to defraud a creditor existing at the time of the conveyance, or an intent to defraud not any particular creditor, but subsequent creditors generally.27 If actual fraud is established on the part of both the grantor and grantee, the question of the presence or absence of a valuable or adequate consideration becomes unimportant.28 Nor is the question of whether the conveyance produced insolvency or left the debtor with insufficient capital important.29 Independent, however, of the statutory grounds for setting aside a fraudulent conveyance, the Court of Chancery has no power under any "broad powers of equity to set aside a conveyance at the instance of a complaining creditor.30

281. Idem: Voluntary Conveyances: Gifts. 

The Uniform Act does not in terms cover conveyances by way of gift (i.e., voluntary, or for a nominal consideration, or for love and affection), except in so far as they are made with actual fraudulent intent, or are constructively so, in producing insolvency, leaving insufficient capital, etc.43 With respect to such voluntary transfers, where there is no fraudulent intent, actual or constructive, the transfer is a valid one.44 But when there are existing debts, when the debtor conveys out of love and affection to a relative, the courts are quick to hold such fraudulent as to such existing creditors.45 But there is no presumption of fraud arising from a gift to a wife, whether directly made or through an intermediary.40

The fraudulent grantee, however, is not entitled to any allowances on account of improvements, as against creditors of the fraudulent grantor.60

The wrong of a fraudulent conveyance is not so much a wrong accomplished as a wrong planned; thus a transfer in anticipation of an insolvency which does not occur is obnoxious to the statute as made with intent to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors.01 Similarly, a purchase by a debtor of land taking title in the name of a third person to defraud creditors; the debtor, and those claiming through him, are not entitled to a conveyance from such third person, nor to a resulting trust in the property.62

286. Writ of Habeas Corpus. 

The writ of habeas corpus issues out of chancery as a matter of inherent jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery.87 Applications for the writ may be made to the Chancellor or to vice chancellors sitting as the Chancellor.ss Such applications may be heard without order of reference by vice chancellors, and when properly made otherwise may be entertained by either the Chancellor or vice chancellors at any time.89 Application should be made to a vice chancellor sitting in or near the locality where the cause of action arose. There is no requirement that the application be heard in open court, nor any that notice be given to any person who may be interested in the application.91 90 92 Under the Habeas Corpus Act, the Chancellor, as well as the vice chancellors, are empowered to issue the writ of habeas corpus.9

When the vice chancellors act under the statute, they sit as statutory agents or magistrates, and not as headmasters of the Court of Chanvery.93

In both cases, however, the pleadings are entitled in the Court of Chancery.94 In matters touching the custody of infant children, a distinction seems to be taken as to the jurisdiction of vice chancellors sitting as statutory agents, viz., that the application in such a case could be entertained by a vice chancellor only when "sitting

287. Writ de Lunatico (Idiota) Inquirendo. 

The Court of Chancery has jurisdiction over all cases of idiocy and lunacy to be determined on a commission of idiocy or lunacy which issues out of the Court of Chancery, and is returnable thereto.25 

The object of these proceedings is to hold an inquest on an alleged lunatic to determine whether (a) such person shall be allowed liberty or taken into custody, or (b) whether such person shall be allowed to exercise ownership over his property.26 Proceedings are initiated by the filing of a petition by a relative or some party in interest praying that a commission issue.27 This petition shall be accompanied by the affidavits of two or more persons evincing the lunacy.28 A com- mission in the nature of a writ de lunatico inquirendo thereupon, if allowed by the Chancellor, issues from the Court of Chancery.29 

This commission names three commissioners to hold an inquisition. 

Thereupon they, by precept, require the sheriff to summon a jury to try the alleged lunatic.30 Ten days' notice of the hearing must be

The vice chancellor may further appoint a custodial receiver without notice to the corporation to continue for such short time as the order may designate.43 The rule to show cause in such case issues to the corporation to show why at the hearing the receiver should not be made permanent. The cause is heard in a summary manner, but any statutory provision dispensing with notice to the corporation would be unconstitutional.44 The petition is supported by affidavit and should disclose a statutory ground for the appointment of a receiver, viz., (a) insolvency, (b) suspension of ordinary business for the want of funds to carry on the same and is not about to resume within a short time, or (c) business has been or is being conducted at a great loss and to the prejudice of stockholders and creditors. Forthwith, on proof of the allegations in the petition, (a) an order is issued restraining the corporate officers from exercising corporate privileges, and (b) an order is entered appointing a receiver. The Court of 

Chancery may also appoint a receiver for a corporation under its inherent power independent of statute.45 Such a receiver is called sometimes an "equity receiver" to distinguish the case from that of a "statutory receiver" appointed under the statute. 

289. Bill by Purchaser of Tax Certificate to Foreclose. 

An act entitled "Tax Sale Revision " 16 provides two methods by which a purchaser, or his heirs or assigns, of a tax sale certificate, may cut off the right of an owner, mortgagee, occupant, or other person having an interest in lands sold for municipal liens, to redeem 47 the same. One method is by notice in writing at any time within twenty years after the purchase to all persons¹7a interested in 

43. Chancery Rule 111a. (Basis “immediate and irreparable injury" will result before notice can be served and a hearing had.) See Chancery Rules 

111b, 111c, 111e, 111f, and 111g. 

44. Shaw v. Standard Piano Co., 87 N. J. Eq. 350, 100 Atl. 167; Morse v. 

Met. S. S. Co., 88 N. J. Eq. 325, 102 Atl. 524; Chancery Rule 111a. 

45. In re N. J. Refrigerating Co., 95 N. J. Eq. 215, 122 Atl. 832. Similarly, the Court of Chancery has inherent power to appoint a receiver for a foreign corporation. Hill v. Dealer's Credit Corp., 102 N. J. Eq. 310, 140 Atl. 569.

MISCELLANEOUS PROCEEDINGS 

367 the land, calling upon them to redeem, either within two years after the sale or within six months after service upon them of the notice, depending upon whether the notice is served within eighteen months after the sale or not, 48 or else be barred.49 The other method, which is in addition to and not exclusive of the other, whether notice to redeem has been given or not, is by a bill in equity to foreclose the right of redemption.50 This bill may be filed at any time after the expiration of the term of two years. It is interesting to note that a bill to foreclose is the only method available to bar the right to redeem of an infant under the age of twenty-one years, or an idiot, or a person of unsound mind.51

Proof must first be submitted to the satisfaction of the court that all subsequent municipal liens have been paid to the time of the commencement of the suit. A notice of the suit must be filed in the office of the collector of taxes, and the court may, upon application at any time after bill filed, allow reasonable search fees, disbursements, counsel fees, etc.52 Redemption thereafter shall be made in said cause only. In the foreclosure, the validity of the tax sale, etc., is conclusively presumed unless the defendant in his answer sets up as a defense the invalidity of the sale.53 The filing of such an answer stays proceedings for four months from the date of such filing, or for such longer time until a writ of certiorari, if one is granted, is discharged. If such a writ to review the tax sale, etc., is not granted within the four months, the court will strike out such part of the answer as denies the validity of the tax or legality of the proceedings to sell, or the legality of the sale, and shall proceed as if no such defense had been interposed.54 A writ of certiorari shall not be allowed after the time to plead has expired.55 The decree rendered by the Court of Chancery is final upon the defendants, their heirs, devisees, and personal representatives, and their or any of their heirs, devisees, executors, administrators, grantees, assigns or successors in right, title or interest, and bars their interest in and to the

lands described in the decree only.56 Application to reopen said decree must be made within three months and only upon the grounds of lack of jurisdiction or fraud in the conduct of the suit. The final decree cannot be collaterally attacked,57 and the proper procedure to open. a final decree is not by notice of motion with affidavit attached, but by petition for rehearing, on which order to show cause may issue,58 the allowance of which is a matter of discretion of the court.59 

Upon a showing by affidavits that the land covered by the tax sale certificate is wild or wood, or waste or unenclosed, or unimproved lands, and that after due inquiry and a search of the records of the surrogate, register of deeds and mortgages or, if none, of the clerk of the Court of Common Pleas, and of the Secretary of State, the person foreclosing is unable to ascertain the name of the owner or owners of said land, the Court of Chancery will allow the suit to proceed against the "unknown owner, his heirs, devisees and personal representatives and their or any of their heirs, devisees, executors, administrators, grantees, assigns or successors in right, title or interest." Notice of such suit shall be given under order of the court, by publication, according to the law and practice of the Court of Chancery, directing such unknown owner or owners to appear and answer the said bill within such time as the Chancellor shall direct, not less than two nor more than four months from the date of the order of publication. At the expiration of the time limited in said. order, the Chancellor shall make such decree as if they had been personally served, and upon their failure to redeem they shall be barred. Notice of the date limited for redemption, etc., shall be posted upon the lands affected by the suit at least twenty days before the date so fixed.60
